summary_html:
“Three sessions.” Khaslana says at least, with his empty doll eyes under the shadow of the trees, he looks more like a ghost than ever. “I give you three sessions. If you don’t get to paint something I like, I leave.”

“Hm, you really think I can’t.”

“I know you can’t.”

How terribly arrogant. Mydei grins, wild and prideful, heart thumping with what might be either adrenaline or anger. “Three sessions.” He agrees.

They say whoever attempts to make a muse out of Khaslana goes mad. Mydei thinks that’s fine. He wants less of a muse than he likes a challenge. Somewhere along the way, he falls in love.

chapters.title: Chapter 1: The abyss down below us
chapters.html:
A drop of paint falls to the floor.

The sound it makes as it collides against the stone is faint. A silent drip drowned by the bustling of the city down below, but in the emptiness of the balcony, its non-existent echo spreads all the way from the tip of his fingers to his ears.

Mydei’s eyes shift down to it. A small little round thing of blue, quickly losing its bright shine as it dries. He doesn’t bother cleaning it. A futile endeavor made redundant when in view of the splats and stains of dried paint that covered the original marble stone like a tapestry. An accidental thing rather than a stylistic choice; the balcony is, after all, famous among artists—frustrated artists, to be exact, an old thing at the top of a cathedral of a long forgotten god turned cafe that oversees the city’s plaza.

A view of inspiration, one of the reviews that appeared when you searched the name and was trying a little bit too hard to be poetic read, the gentle breeze of the air carries along the lives of millions of strangers right to the infinity of the canvas.

It’s not the sort of place Mydei frequents; not the sort of place Mydei ever envisioned turning to. Inspiration is not something he tends to struggle with. He paints what he wants and what he wants he paints. Simple as that. Thoughts, feelings, views, whatever. It never takes much effort to press a brush against a canvas.

It didn’t, at least.

It’s not that nothing seems to catch his interest. It’s not that nothing seems to spark in his mind. There are ideas, sure. There are wants, because a human never truly stops wanting, and Mydei has never been one to deny himself. There’s inspiration, but it is accompanied by the uncanny abstinence of the burning urge to paint that usually latches onto him like a second skin. Months upon months of the same blank canvas staring back at him.

He peers back at the plaza, eyes trailing on different people. A woman pushes an ice cream’s cart around, a child runs after the pigeons another is throwing seeds at and scares them all off, the kid that was feeding them proceeds to hit the other, a girl kisses a flower before braiding it into another girl’s hair, a bunch of construction workers with different princess backpacks at their feet laugh loudly as they eat while on break, and one cafe worker chases a haggard old man throwing tomatoes at the cathedral with claims of blasphemy with a broom. He could paint any of it. It wouldn’t take much effort.

Another drop falls to the floor.

Mydei looks down at it again, then to the sky, now bleeding with reds and oranges as the purple hues of night start creeping in, and then to the canvas. Blank. An expanse of white. The brush dipped in blue, tip weighted under the wet paint, merely a breath away from it, but the quiet mundanities of the city fail to close that gap.

Another drop falls.

Mydei sighs and sets the brush aside.

In practiced motions, he picks all the tubes of paint and brushes placed on the wooden table and puts them back into his paint case; a smooth, black box that would look professional were it not to have a bunch of ugly-looking chimeras in the sides that all his friends in Castrum Kremnos had painted before he moved out the country.

The thought of ever cleaning them off has never once crossed his mind, but the blue paint on the palette has long dried.

He hauls the case by the handle, takes the blank canvas and leaves the balcony right before the old bell perched in one of the towers of the cathedral tolls, signaling the pass of another hour with ear-deafening clarity. It’s the third time it has happened.

The old woman behind the counter looks at him sympathetically at the sight of the white canvas under his arm and throws an extra piece of sweet bread into the plastic bag as he buys a loaf. It’s still warm. He thanks her and starts eating it on the way out.

The last bits of light still cling to the sky, but the streetlights have already been turned on by the time Mydei makes it out the plaza. Feet trailing on well-worn cobblestone and a maze of paths and streets as he makes his way to the public parking lot. A stray dog raises its head towards him from where it is lazing on the floor and Mydei throws it the last bite of bread in his hand. Its tail wags against the floor as it eats it.

He keeps walking.

On the fifth avenue, two streets before the parking lot, lies The Irontomb, a military base turned art gallery1, still open despite the hour. Mydei blinks at it, checks the time on his phone and, after a second of consideration, turns in its direction.

The man at the reception doesn’t look up from his cheap gossip magazine as Mydei walks inside. His body casts long shadows on the porcelain floors with intricate designs thanks to the light of the chandelier up in the ceiling —lavish, as the rest of the Irontomb is, a hard attempt to scrub out the remnants of the military off its metal walls, but nothing can’t quite erase the structural industrialization of its corridors. A nitpick only architects and the like would go on about, most only come to gaze at the art.

Mydei doesn’t come often to this place. He finds the art on display, frankly, too miserable; wannabe edgy. It’s not to discredit the art, all the works are all masterpieces in their own way, all too visceral and all too real, but the contents portrayed all tether on hopelessness of some kind, thriving on destruction. Perhaps that is to be expected for a place named The Irontomb.

For a while, Mydei simply walks through the corridors in quiet contemplation, eyes trailing on the different pieces, not particularly thinking of anything, but not particularly thinking of nothing either. Maybe hoping for the urge to paint to strike him down. Art lives of art, as his mother used to say.

He walks through the east wing, past the board propped on an easel promoting an upcoming art competition and through artworks named on some variations of Black Tide, Okhema’s Final Days, A Cat’s Lie, and the like. He skims past Calculation 032at the center of the gallery, disinterest born from having enough of a lifetime having to write artistic analysis on it, in favor of turning into the west wing.

And the painting of a crumbling statue at the end of the hall stops Mydei dead in his tracks.

A somber mix of blues, blacks and whites broken by bright golds sweeping out the statue like blood. Marble skin breaking apart, piece by piece, revealing nothing but a deep hollowness inside. It is falling, submerging in a deep abyss of blacks as a crumbling hand reaches up to the last vestiges of blue above.

A dying, lonely thing.

His eyes linger on the statue’s face; strangely familiar, like a stranger met in a dream, a person only seen from the corner of the eye. It’s undoubtedly beautiful, sharp features, otherworldly etherealness, but it is all overshadowed by the molting gold of his eyes, melting in terrible sadness.

Thus Burns the Dawn, the name reads.

Mydei stares at it until the echo of the bell toll resonates through the Irontomb’s walls like a death knell and its doors come to close and when he steps outside the sky outside is black like liquid obsidian. No moon that night.

The turned lights of hotels, houses, restaurants, shops and the like mix with the bright, yellow old shine of the streetlights along the attention grabbing neons of ads and illuminated signs. It pollutes the night, erases the natural light of the stars, but the few, stubborn little dots of white that refuse to be outshined remind Mydei of crumbling marble.

His fingers twitch.

━━━━━━━━━━

The bright shine of the sun reminds him of burning, grief-stricken eyes.

His eyes trail over the smooth walls of the gym as he works out, replacing oranges and teals with blues, whites and golds, even if his pace doesn’t falter once as he continues his morning’s regime.

The articulations in his hand tense and relax, tendons and veins moving, skin stretching, and it is easy to picture the places where cracks would form first.

He saves references of statues and sculptures, most marble, on his phone; anything he can find, from famous things like Veiled Virgin, Aphrodite of Milos, David and Belvedere Torso, to the metal or plaster sculptures hidden in some unsuspecting turn of the city, and the unnamed things found on some corner of the web.

His dreams, ambiguous things, lost in the sea of conscience, all feature the last vestiges of a marmoreal heart sinking in the puddles he walks past.

It clings to him. The painting. Intimately.

Mydei is not obsessive by nature. Dedicated, yes. Stubborn, passionate and, at worst, terribly intense, that, he can admit. He knows himself well and isn’t afraid to do so. He recognizes the fixation, the fascination, the twitching of his fingers and the reasons the canvas stays blank despite it— He doesn’t want to recreate it. He could, rather easily. But he has never been the type of person to settle—but he fails to understand where said fascination comes from. He’s never been Pygmalion, not to say that the analogy falls flat when Thus Burns the Dawn is another’s Galatea; and he does not indulge in either naiveness nor romanticism as to believe in proclamations of love at first sight, much less with a statue, nor the transcendence of a pure heart.

The first piece clicks eight weeks after, amidst the smell of paper, wood and paint of an art store that is most definitely a mafia front close to Mydei’s home. Paintings hung on cloth hangers on the ceiling like dead men. A vase with spider lilies dripping blood3, a study of birds, a boat on the side of the coast and a statue stepping out a room.

The last one catches his attention. Gently, like a tap on the shoulder. Mydei’s eyes skim past that painting to the one next to it just to come back a second after. It’s a simple thing—left unfinished, giving the sensation it was made in haste. The room isn’t finished, crude strokes of brown melting to white, like it was falling apart while the blacks and reds of the night peeking outside the door overlapped with the door’s frame. The statue, back turned, has a foot already set outside, a hand on the handle as it closes it behind it. Picture caught mid-action.

“Thirty-three million, five hundred fifty thousand, three hundred thirty-six.” Says a man with far too polished of a suit, a cigarette and a fedora as puts a set of brushes and tubes of different shades of blue paint in a plastic bag. Mydei makes a sound in the back of his throat and, “The painting.” He clarifies.

“Weird name.”

“It’s the number in the barcode on the sticker on the back. It doesn’t actually have a name, but I need it to call it something.”

“Where did you find it?”

“Why, does it interest you?”

“I’m not buying it.”

“Heh, then I guess we won’t know.”

Mydei doesn’t say anything and neither does a single muscle on his face so much as twitch. He simply shifts his eyes down to stare at the man and he cracks immediately. “On the trash.”

“Mm.”

“It’s not that strange.” He says, suddenly feeling a whole lot chattier. “Most of his paintings do—The model’s, I mean. No worth to an incomplete thing.”

His? A part of Mydei thinks, looking up at the painting once again, eyes trailing to the figure in the center. Clothes made crudely of three strokes of blue and white, a bright yellow circle shines on the neck, overshadowing white hair, hiding grief-stricken eyes, crumbling marble.

Painting left discarded.

Ah.

“Khaslana.”

“Know him?” Mydei huffs, making a motion to the general direction of the art supplies he’s buying, almost offended. There’s no artist in this city worth their name that hasn’t heard about Khaslana. “Personally, I mean.”

“No.”

“Gonna try your hand at it?”

Mydei arches an eyebrow. “Do I look that desperate?" He asks. It comes out condescending.

“No, you look captivated.”

His fingers twitch.

“You aren’t the only one.” The man continues, not as a consolation, and shrugs. “Can’t say I understand the appeal, frankly.”

“You dug his painting out the trash.” Mydei replies.

He taps the end of the cigarette against the end of the table, gray ash falling down to the floor as he replies, “Madness sells well.”

━━━━━━━━━━

Every place has its stories. Every place has its blood. Every place has its whispers. This city is no different, held between the corners, the soil and the eyes, tales of golden butterflies kissing trees, black dogs that lick the mouths of the drunk, Bartholos’ tricks and the like abound.

And between brushes and paint, the stroke against a canvas whispers that whoever attempts to make a muse out of Khaslana goes mad.

Mydei isn’t one for gossip, but he is observant; not to mention one would have to be both blind and deaf not to notice the lonesome figure with a sun on his neck and snow for hair portrayed on thousands of works left discarded. Found in the trash, found in an alley, found at garage sales, found in unsuspecting art stores, found in random shops, restaurants and cafes— but never in galleries, exhibitions nor museums.

Works all incomplete. Featureless.

With the exception of two. Thus Burns the Dawn, made by the Irontomb’s curator, an Antikytheran named Lygus, and an unnamed piece made by the Ruin Author, Nanook4, that never saw the light of day.

It’s like watching a corpse in the ocean at night, an old man with trembling hands told Mydei once, an untold story hidden between crinkled, warm eyes, the wish to paint him before he sinks hooks you by the throat like a vice and you don’t realize you are sinking too.5

Yesterday, tall tales, Mydei used to think, Zagreus likes to mingle with the people. Today, he looks down and watches the water reach his calves.

A lesser man would be consumed. A coward would fear it. Mydei is neither.

He still thinks of crumbling marble, burning suns, the vestiges of a ghost, the canvas remains empty, but he doesn’t obsess over it. He does not search up and high for Khaslana, he does not go to gaze upon Thus Burns the Dawn for hours at a time, he does not search and buy every painting of Khaslana he can find and, likewise, he does not shy away from them. Even when they seem to cling to him insistently.

Hauntingly.

A painting on the bakery he goes to every week, another next to the bin of his neighbour’s trash. Here, on the feed of some app on his phone. There, through the window of some shop he walks past. The cathedral-turned-cafe in the center of the plaza has one hung next to the door; featureless, as always, the shape of a head up to the neck. Mydei can’t remember for the life of him if it was there before.

I could paint you, he thinks, more than a little pridefully, refusing to bend as he watches shapes across paper, but you can’t sink me.

━━━━━━━━━━

Mydei meets Khaslana three weeks after, outside the entrance of some old mall without one wall at the side that the owner insists is an aesthetic choice and not the result of poor planning that had resulted in said wall crumbling down after a tame earthquake some years ago.

It’s completely by chance. A thing almost lost under the hustle of his day-to-day if not for the loud ‘splash!’ that catches his attention as he walks past and makes him turn his head around—just to see a man waist-deep in a man-made pond.

He doesn’t recognize him, at first, more used to the unfinished things made of crude strokes of paint, before he catches sight of snow hair and a burning sun on a neck, hidden under a leather choker but undoubtedly there. All-consuming, all-alluring.

Mydei’s breath does not hitch when he sees him. His body doesn’t look in and on itself, and neither does his heart skip a beat. Instead, there’s a single thought that comes to him with stark clarity and bone-deep certainty.

Found you.

Even though he wasn’t looking for him in the first place.

Khaslana makes his way further into the pond. His movements disrupt the stillness of the waters, looking as if he might dissolve and disappear into them any minute now, like an apparition, like a ghost.

A pink plastic ball floats in the middle and a few kids stand anxiously at the edges. Khaslana grabs it, turns, and throws it back to the kids. One of them catches it, and they all yell some variation of ‘Thank you, Mister!’ before scramming off as Khaslana gives them a little wave of hand.

How surprisingly kind.

Or, perhaps, not so surprisingly.

Mydei finds himself strangely curious about what other things whispers and rumours fail to say.

A pair of well-worn white sneakers with black socks rest right on the edge of the pond. They dangle precariously, and Mydei drags them further into the concrete as he waits for Khaslana, who is making his way back in strides, head turned down, seemingly careful not to step nor kick onto any of the koi fish swimming lo and about.

Khaslana comes to a stop just a few steps away from the edge, just below the shadow Mydei’s body casts onto the waters, and he turns his head up to see him.

His eyes aren’t gold.

It startles him, for some reason.

Molten gold of bleeding eyes and scorching suns fade out of his mind like seafoam onto a lightless blue. Khaslana’s eyes aren’t bright. Not one bit. They are deep, murky things, swallowing all light. The surface of a lake, an ocean, hiding an unfathomable abyss below. Glossy, almost doll-like. Nothing but Mydei’s own reflection staring back at him.

His skin, too, is much like a doll’s. White, porcelain-like, stretching over sharp features with seemingly no imperfections if not for the way pale lips are chapped and bitten. Mydei could probably go into more detail, if not for the way his eyes keep going over to set on his eyes.

Empty, enticing things, like the bottom of a well without water.

One you could fall into at any moment.

Maybe that wouldn’t be so bad.

The thought is stark, like a bolt of lighting. Mydei bites the inside of his cheek hard enough to taste blood and the pain—The pain is grounding. A push against the pull. He blinks, and finds that he has to take a step back to avoid falling into the water, feet dangling precariously over the edge.

Dangerous.

The thought shouldn’t thrill him so.

Khaslana is still watching him, silently. Somehow, looking as if he’s seeing past him at the same time he’s boring into his very soul. His face an emotionless, cold thing.

He’s still on the pond.

Wordlessly, Mydei extends a hand.

Khaslana blinks; empty-well eyes shifting down from his face, to the extended hand, again to his face before settling back onto his hand one last time. There’s a long beat before his right hand raises and an even longer beat before his hand stops simply hovering over Mydei’s palm and grabs it. His skin is both too far hot and far too cold.

Khaslana’s feet make a loud splat as he steps back onto land along a faint drip, drip, drip. The water darkens the concrete under him. He’s drenched up to the end of his white, loose shirt and his black pants cling onto his legs. On his left hand, Mydei notes, a long, dark purple glove with butterflies reaches all the way to his shoulder. It seems out of place.

Mydei doesn’t let go of his hand.

His fingers twitch.

“Thank you.”

And the second piece falls into place. An idea sparks in his mind. Competitive, greedy, and more than a little bold. Dangerous.

“I want to paint you.”

“Eh?”

Not one to be ashamed of his desires, Mydei repeats, shamelessly. “I want to paint you.”

There’s a long, long pause and, slowly, almost deliberately, Khaslana lets go of Mydei’s hand and lets it fall limply to his side.

“...And you are?”

Chapter End Notes

FOOTNOTES

1. Lots of places have been repurposed in this town, truth be told, to the point that it’s kind of ridiculous. It cuts costs, for sure, but Mydei thinks whoever is making these decisions should take a long look at themselves when they decided to have children running around in a playground that once was an execution ground. Not even Castrum Kremnos is that careless with their dead.Back 2. Calculation 03, drawn on a chalkboard that covers a whole wall with a cheap piece of red chalk, it’s less an artwork than it is a long equation, written in a way that shows a hyperrealistic bird eye’s plane of the whole country of Amphoreus being swallowed by code. It’s the last and most famous piece of the series Calculations made by the all elusive mathematician Nous on a single evening. Artists praise the talent, but mathematicians and the like have gone mad trying to solve it. There’s exactly one person that has achieved it, the genius turned serial killer, Polka Kakamond, though she didn’t share the result— Madam Herta has gone on record saying she also did it but the result was so boring you might as well have asked her what two plus two was.Back

3. That one will be bought and burnt soon after.Back

4. Known for their portrayals of destruction in its most visceral form. It is said that gazing upon the Ruin Author’s works is enough to instill the idea that existence itself is a mistake. Ash to ash, dust to dust. Indifferent to most works, upon walking into The Irontomb, the Ruin Author had stopped to gaze upon Thus Burns the Dawn for a whole minute before asking about the model. They went on to paint Khaslana after that—an experience that, reportedly, ended up with someone being stabbed with a palette knife, a bucket of paint being swung to a head and a burnt mansion. All parties involved refuse to comment on the matter, though, it is said that the Ruin Author’s eyes noticeably soften upon reminded of the experience.Back

5. It had been hailing, that day, the tiny specks of ice threatened to break the glass ceiling of the tiny ice cream shop everyone had crammed into. The old man had come to sit on the same table as him and started talking once he saw the paint stuck under Mydei’s nails with the same abandon old people always have—Mydei doesn’t remember what he answered, but he remembers the laugh he got in return. “Boy, you don’t reach my age without learning how to swim. Besides, I only draw pigeons.”Back

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Pull of the waters
chapters.html:
Drops of water fall onto the floor, one after another and yet another one after, darkening the pavement below from ash to black like a burnt down wasteland before they dry. Unable to leave its mark the way paint does, forming shapes that don’t last.

Here one moment, gone the next.

A sun forms, or perhaps it is a flower, maybe both, maybe neither. Maybe it doesn’t matter.

Mydei’s eyes flick away from it to see Khaslana instead.

Paint and shapes reflect in lightless blue eyes, works and arts Mydei has done over the years. He takes his time. Lingers long on each and every one. Sun-ringed pupils shifting from one side to the other as he observes all the different details that create a picture like a puzzle instead of simply scrolling through Mydei’s phone and catching a glimpse or two.

—And yet, despite the amount of care he has, it somehow still feels as if he’s looking right past them.

Mydei’s mouth twists, just barely. The world spins, time flows and the wind that pushes white locks of hair back doesn’t do much to stab off the quiet stillness that surrounds Khaslana. His breathing is slow, blinks sporadically, and his face doesn’t change. Expressionless features carved out of marble. Unmoving, unchanging, eternally.

A statue, a picture caught in time.

He should be able to paint the slope of his nose in one single stroke of the brush, he believes; dust the tip with a little pink, maybe, to give some color to his complexion—though, that could make him look as if he’s cold. It could work, paint him in the snow. Add some vibrant colors to avoid him blending into the background, maybe paint in gold the sun on his neck.

For the lips, a faint pink will suffice, with small red tears close to the cupid’s bow to portray the places where he has picked at them. The general texture of broken skin may be hard to recreate, but Mydei can already think of a few ways to do so.

For his eyes, those—those shift up to him.

And Khaslana stares.

Mydei doesn’t look away.

There’s no particular embarrassment or startle at being caught watching so blatantly. Of course he’s going to do so, he wants to paint him. He has already made this desire well-known, and, even if he hadn’t, it wouldn’t stop him from watching Khaslana, either way. Mydei is not a self-conscious person and neither is he a coward as to hide when he finds the abyss staring back at him, threatening to sink him down, down, down.

Khaslana doesn’t comment on it. He doesn’t say anything, in fact, and neither does Mydei. Silence growing and drowning the rustle of the leaves, the rumble of cars, the steps, and conversations as empty eyes trail onto every nook and cranny of Mydei’s face with the same attention he watched the paintings on his phone. Careful, but distant, still.

Mydei wonders what he sees, what he’s searching for, whichever realm he finds himself in and threatens to disappear into at any moment now like mist in the night.

They still don’t say anything, maybe words have simply stopped existing.

Time stretches, twists and turns. A minute might have passed, or maybe two. The eternity of a second and the fleetingness of year. All in one, before Khaslana's head tilts. The movement much like a doll’s whose neck’s articulations couldn’t hold on the weight of its porcelain head. White hair follows the motion, a few strands going over his eyes.

Khaslana looks away first.

In careful movements, he looks through a few more images of his paintings before he shuts down the phone and gives it back to Mydei, fingers shy of touching.

Then, wordlessly, silently, he bends down and plucks the socks out of the white shoes resting on the floor. The sun on the concrete has faded between one blink to the other and the drops falling from Khaslana’s drenched clothes like quiet rain don’t form any other shape.

He still doesn’t say anything.

The silence should be unnerving, perhaps even nerve-wracking. It’s hard to know whether to interpret the lack of answer as judgement, condescension, or simply lack of care, but Mydei isn’t concerned.

He knows his paintings are good.

It’s not vanity—ha, Nikador forbid the thought—but simply self-assurance. A fact. Skill crafted out of years of practice and passion. A warrior who doesn’t recognize their own strengths isn’t better than the one who overestimates them.1 So, he lets such silence stretch. Mydei has spoken his words and it is turn for Khaslana to respond. He’s patient.

In lieu, Mydei watches in silence as he turns around his black socks with ugly yellow-green patterns sewn at the sides. Fabric covering soles tinged in faint red from where the heated stone had started to burn Khaslana’s feet before they moved onto one of the wooden benches placed under the trees.

A beat passes.

And Khaslana sighs. A quiet thing. Bursting silence like a bubble. Breath stolen by the wind, which pushed along the branches of the big, big trees with their big, big leaves, shifting shadows through space, looming like nooses to be hung.

He says, “There are easier ways to learn how to paint people.”

“Excuse me?”

“I said, there are easier ways to learn how to paint people.” Khaslana repeats with the exact same tone and inflection. There’s no particular sneer to it, but the monotonous timbre of his voice makes it sound awfully pretentious.

A flicker of a flame licks against his ribcage. “I know how to paint people.”

“I never said you couldn’t.”

“Didn’t you?”

“Maybe.” Khaslana shrugs, makes a general direction to the phone in Mydei’s hand. “You just don’t seem to paint people often.”

“Hmph. I’m not the kind of person to paint just anyone.”

“But you want to paint me.”

Khaslana is hardly the type one would describe as ‘just anyone’, let alone a ‘person’. They both know it. None of them mention it.

“I have already said that I do.” Mydei replies instead.

“Why?”

“I want to.”

Khaslana’s eyes lower. “That’s not a real answer.”

“It is.”

“Is it?”

“Yes.” He repeats, firmly.

Another sigh. This is one stolen, too, as if the wind itself wanted to take him. Marble turned to dust.

“What a rather simplistic view of life.”

“I’m a simple man.” Mydei shrugs. “And I don’t think it necessary to justify the whys of our wishes and wants.”

“So, you agree.” Khaslana says. The shadows of the trees shift around him. “That it’s not as simple as just wanting to paint me.”

“No, I think it is.”

Khaslana hums. “Mm, could it be that you don’t know why?”

No. Mydei knows. The fact that he’s simple—or, at least, thinks of himself that way—doesn’t mean he’s oblivious. Repression is a vice and ignorance a weakness. He knows his wants and he knows his whys. It’s hard for him to put them into words, action always speaks far more honestly, and neither is it necessary, so he settles on an unceremonial, “I like a challenge.”

And Khaslana—

—Stops.

It’s not the quiet stillness from earlier, though it is ever present, but something else. He blinks, blinks and blinks again. His mouth opens with the beginnings of an answer before closing and pressing into a line. The movement stretches and shrinks one of the red tears in the commissure of his lips.

The thought of tearing it further comes unbidden. Dig a nail into it or rip the wound further with his teeth and lap the blood with his tongue and paint torn reds over a white linen.

Mydei lets out a low, deliberate breath.

Dangerous, how easy it is to sink.

“...A challenge.”

“Mm.”

“A challenge.” He repeats, as if it was the first time he has ever been told that, before he shakes his head and, a little pointed, he adds, “You do know that none has been able to paint me.”

“None of them are me.”

“You speak as if you don’t have a brain.” Khaslana replies. He doesn’t scoff, but the sound he makes comes close to one. “Haven’t you thought there’s a reason why that is? Next you will say you are going to win that stupid art competition on The Irontomb with me as your model.”

Mydei raises his chin. “Is that a challenge?”

“Well, you sure like those, don’t you?” Khaslana crosses his legs, places his elbow on his knee and rests his cheek on his palm. He’s all sharp edges and jagged ends, a flicker peeking under a cold exterior. “Even when they are far beyond your level.”

“Far beyond my level. Ha, what’s that supposed to mean?”

He shrugs and, almost disinterestedly, he says, “You just don’t paint people often,” and the words are light but the bite sure isn’t.

“Doesn’t mean I can’t.” Mydei repeats.

Khaslana’s eyes narrow at the edges, just so, and the sound he lets out is a condescending thing, perhaps even a little mean. Meant to bruise. “That you can do it doesn't mean you are any good at it. I have seen a whole lot better.”

A part of him, ever observant, ever sharp, ever piercing, recognizes the jab, the lie, a performative dig to get at him, but another part can’t help but fall for it either way. He has never taken kindly to being looked down upon in any way shape or form. He clicks his tongue and says, just as pointed, “At least they aren’t in the trash.”

Khaslana’s expression doesn’t fall.

It doesn’t shatter, nor does it twist, nor does it stutter, nor does it freeze. It doesn’t change. It remains in that impassive, porcelain expressionless from earlier. Unmoving, unchanging, eternally—But the hand on his cheek tenses, fingers curling, before he goes to pick at a scab on his lips, chipping marble.

“That’s exactly where yours will finish too.”

He’s very adamant about that, if Mydei didn’t know better, he would think he was, “Scared?”

Khaslana’s eyes shift sharply, looking as if he would have Mydei dead more than a million times over. An array of cold, blue colors won’t suffice to paint them. It wouldn’t be enough. Fire encased in ice, Mydei thinks, maybe a dot of orange hidden and dissolved between the blues, like a flame—not because there’s any light on those empty blue eyes, but because Khaslana seems to be burning inside out. It’s hidden, carefully, but it’s there.

Silence stretches, melts and crashes. Somewhere, a child laughs. Somewhere, a car honks. Somewhere, people talk. The hot embers of, well, maybe not anger, but annoyance, still sizzle in his gut, but he swallows whatever scalding retort and prod bubbling on his tongue. He knows, with the sharpness of a predator, when to strike and when to wait.

He reclines against the bench, head thrown back, and looks up into the sky through the little crooks of the green leaves rustled by the wind. Above, the clouds twist into one dream or the other as they continue their slow travel to some corner of the world to cry onto.

From the corner of his eye, he catches the general impression of a motion. Khaslana still picks at his lips, and, despite the fact that the embers haven’t quite cooled yet, he says, “You are going to draw blood.”

A beat passes.

Khaslana’s hand falls.

Mydei waits.

The silence that befalls afterwards isn’t particularly comfortable. There’s still tensions, words heard yet left unsaid, the beginnings of a crack, yet the rustle of the winds and the quiet mundanities of the city soften it. A laugh, a step, a hum, a yawn, a life. The quiet drip of water drops falling to the floor much like paint on an empty balcony.

A lifetime or two may have passed before Mydei lets his head roll to the side, leaving behind ambiguous forms in the clouds to the drifting form of Khaslana. Empty eyes fixed on some spot on the ash concrete, trailing onto the drops of water that don’t make any shapes without really seeing them.

A few more lifetimes pass before he starts to put his shoes on. The sound of scraping stone rising where he’s digging and wiggling his feet into them, crushing the heel tabs. For a moment, Mydei thinks he will simply go with shoelaces left undone, but it seems he’s not without his pride.

The shadows shift and,

“Three sessions.” Khaslana says at least, with his empty doll eyes under the shadow of the trees, he looks more like a ghost than ever. “I give you three sessions. If you don’t get to paint something I like, I leave.”

“Hm, you really think I can’t.”

“I know you can’t.”

How terribly arrogant. Mydei grins, wild and prideful, heart thumping with what might be either adrenaline or leftover anger. “Three sessions.” He agrees.

━━━━━━━━━━ “I forgot to mention,” Khaslana says in lieu of a greeting at half past three o’clock sharp of a gray Sunday afternoon. “I don’t do nude. Will that be a problem?”

He’s one hour and half late.

The three little knock-knock-knocks cling into the gaps of terracotta bricks; not like echoes, but like a cavity in a tooth. Unnoticed, unseen, but all-present as it digs and digs in. Mydei looks at Khaslana, standing at the edge of the second stone step that gives way to his house with his messenger bag, sharp tongue and doll eyes, and, instead of mentioning his lateness, answers with a deadpan, “Good afternoon to you too.”

“Good afternoon, Mydeimos.” He replies just as deadpan. The bastard. Mydei shouldn’t be so charmed by that. “I don’t do nude.”

“Yes, I heard you the first time.”

“And you didn’t answer the first time.”

This guy. “No, Khaslana.” Mydei says through a breath, making a motion as he steps aside in silent invitation for him to enter. He doesn’t budge, and so, “It’s not a problem.” He adds.

Khaslana hums, takes a step forwards, and stumbles when the last stone step wobbles under his weight. Mydei should fix it, he thinks as the other’s arms jerk upwards to maintain balance, it’s been loose for a while now, rock slowly grinding out the floor with the passage of the years.

His soles collide against the stone of the second step with a harsh ‘bam!’ that is far, far too loud for someone as quiet as Khaslana. He doesn’t fall. Mydei gets the impression his body would shatter like glass if he did. Little pieces scattering across the street. Never to be found again.

Mydei extends a hand towards him. Khaslana doesn’t grab it. Instead he takes a long stride with long legs and skips the wobbly step and just like that—He’s in his house.

He shuts the door.

It closes like a casket’s lid.

“Do you want anything to drink?”

Khaslana’s eyes wrack through the expanse of his house; through the terracotta bricks, through the kitchen’s door, through one of the paintings his mother made for him hung on the wall2, through the long brown couch, through the book with a story about bugs left on the coffee table next to a glass with red drops of pomegranate juice sliding down. He lingers a tad longer on the vase in the center but the glassy sheen never truly leaves his eyes, as if the world always reflected on them instead of sinking in.

As such, it takes a couple more seconds for his question to reach him, and his answer is a simple shake of head.

Mydei nods, tells the other to follow him, and starts leading him in the direction of his art studio. Khaslana walks after him, steps silent against the wooden floor to the point that Mydei has to fight the urge to look back to check if he’s still there.

A couple of more steps pass in place of the clock hands until Khaslana says, “I was late.”

There.

It’s just a matter of patience, really. Don’t mention it and, eventually, they will bring it up themselves—if they care, and it seems Khaslana is not as inconsiderate as he tried to make himself out to be.

Mydei already knew, of course, otherwise the other would have simply put his shoes back on and disappeared into the wind with soggy socks and wet feet the other day.

“You were.” Mydei replies simply. “Had me thinking you weren’t going to come for a second.”

“There was a—Cat.”

The sentence ends abruptly. Mydei turns around to see Khaslana standing still, eyes turned upwards as he stares at the cat perched proudly from his position on top of the stairs leading up to his room, looking haughtily down at him.

“That’s Kopopo the Third.”

“Kopopo?”

“The Third. Address him correctly.”

Khaslana’s eyes shift from Kopopo The Third to Mydei. Expressionless, but once he realizes Mydei is serious, he says, flatly, “The Third.”

Mydei nods.

“You were saying?”

“Cat.” He repeats.

“Brilliant observation. Kopopo The Third is a cat.”

“There was a cat. Another cat.” He says. Adamantly. A little annoyed, maybe. “It was hurt. I took it to someone who will take care of it.”

What a terribly sweet reason. It’s unexpected, but not particularly surprising for a person who dipped into a pond to retrieve a ball for a bunch of kids he probably didn’t know. Still, Mydei can’t help but ask, “And that took you hour and a half?”

“Cats don’t really like me.”

“What?”

As if on cue, Kopopo The Third, who at some point had decided to walk down the stairs and dignify them with his presence, hisses and swipes a clawed paw against Khaslana’s ankle before darting away like a bullet— which is strange, to say the least, because Kopopo The Third might be terribly haughty in the way all cats seem to be, kind of rude and overall unwilling to let new people close, but he has never been particularly aggressive.

Khaslana doesn’t bat an eye at his cat’s actions, though, and the delayed little ouch he lets out is possibly the most blandest thing Mydei has ever heard.

It’s almost funny.

A beat passes before Mydei starts going into the corridor next to the stairs, Khaslana trailing close behind. “A head’s up would have been nice.” He tells him.

“I don’t have your number.”

“Whose fault is that?”

“Who gives their phone number to a stranger?”

“You won’t give your number to a stranger,” Mydei pauses, baffled by the logic. “But you will agree to go into their house?”

“You were the one who gave me your direction.” He says. It feels judgemental, which is irritating, because Khaslana had been the one that suggested they do it in Mydei’s house, not him.3

Mydei opens his mouth, thinks better of it, and sighs. No use starting an argument, frankly. He continues.

Now, situated on the left, in front of the door under the stairs that leads to Mydei’s library, lies his art studio. It’s nothing big, much less impressive, a little room nestled within his life like a heart in a ribcage, because ostentatiousness and vanity are not needed to create, just a soul and a will.

It’s a little messy, maybe, the warm rich reds of the terracotta bricks splattered with stains and little dots of paint here and there, not enough to cover them, but just enough to make constellations on the walls. It smells of dried paint and strong coffee. He likes to paint with that, sometimes. Mydei turns on the lights and walks into it with familiar steps. There’s four tubes of paint placed on the floor next to the easel in the center of the room. White, blue, black and gold. Remnants of a haunting that made Mydei invite a ghost into his house.

He goes to one of the cabinets to take out some more. Orange, most definitely. Purple, for the silk glove in his hand. Blue, because Khaslana’s soft-looking sweater edges on it like a washed-out thing. Red, for some reason—and a couple dozen more.

Khaslana hasn’t entered the room.

He places the tubes of paint on the black table next to the easel, where an empty canvas is already propped onto. The same one he has been carrying like a second skin around with him from months on end, from the studio to the cathedral’s balcony to the edge of a lake to an errant food stand to the top of a car and into this room once again. It has a few stains of mud and mustard on the back.

He bends to pick the paint on the floor with one hand before placing them onto the table next to the others. Plastic against wood with a harmonized tap. Khaslana still doesn’t enter; glassed gaze fixed on the line that separates the art studio from the corridor. Maybe he will crumble into salt the moment that he enters, sea foam in the night.

Mydei walks to another cabinet, picks out some brushes and a palette from the shelf.

Khaslana doesn’t enter. Mydei doesn’t say anything.

His fingers twitch.

The light in the art studio is a low, yellow thing. It warms Khaslana, but the darkness of the corridor cools him, claws into him like desperate hands. It’s a pretty nice contrast, if a little ominous. Not a bad thing to portray. Mydei thinks of riverfalls falling from his eyes, filling the room, drowning it, sinking it, like an ocean tipped down, but his bottom well eyes have long, long emptied of any water.

There’s a breath, like the last exhalation of a dying man, and Khaslana steps into the room.

Mydei still doesn’t say anything, watches him walk through the art studio like smoke from a cigarette that might vanish soon enough; watches him look at the paint clinging to his floors, to the dozens of canvas laid across the room like bones holding a body. Some empty, some half-finished, some finished. Gloved fingers graze gently the beginnings of the aftermath of a battleground reclined on the wall before tilting it forward and catching a glimpse of an empty piano in a bar behind it.4

He stares at that one for a long time.

How, is the question, does an entity like Khaslana, made out of white linen, wet paint and incomplete brushstrokes, regard art?

“Do you even like art?” Mydei asks.

“Why wouldn’t I?” Khaslana mutters, fingers leaving the painting. It’s a terribly melancholic sight.

He lets the messenger bag fall onto the floor with a loud ‘thud’ immediately after before walking to Mydei. One of his hands rolls a brushstroke absentmindedly through the table as he asks, “How do you want me?”

“Whichever way is fine.”

Khaslana nods and goes to sit on the stool in front of the easel. He crosses his legs, gloved hand around his calf and places his elbow on his knee; resting his cheek on his palm, the bandages around his hand5 looking coarse against porcelain skin. He positions himself in a way where he isn’t looking directly at Mydei as he paints.

Mydei takes a seat too, right in front of the empty canvas as he picks up the palette and the brush the other was rolling on the table. He dips the end of it in a bit of orange, mixes it with white and raises the combination to the center of the canvas. Merely a breath away from it. The weight of the paint lowers the strands and the beginnings of a drop start to form, but before it can fall, Mydei takes a look at the Khaslana.

And the gap closes.

The first stroke against the canvas feels like the first beating of a heart that had been dead for months.

━━━━━━━━━━

…Just for it to die again a few hours later.

A paintbrush hovers in the air, close to the canvas. White paint shining under the yellow light of the studio as a couple of drops fall onto the floor. Drip, drip, drip. Mydei ignores it all, eyes staring intently at the shapes and colors that conform Khaslana on the canvas.

“Can’t finish?” He says, voice quiet. The first sound uttered in the room ever since they started.

Mydei blinks, feeling his eyes burn with dryness as he does so, before his gaze shifts from the painting to Khaslana. “What makes you say that?”

“Don’t they all?” Khaslana mutters, as if answering a question of his own before he says, louder, “You have been still for a while now—and I thought the one that wasn’t supposed to move here was me.”

Mydei huffs, “It’s not that. It’s just…” He falters and the action is so terribly uncharacteristic of him that he finds himself frowning—and yet, he finds himself repeating, “It’s just…”

…What is it?

He can’t put a finger on it.

His eyes trail to the painting, then to Khaslana, and back to the painting. By all intents and purposes, it is finished. A lonely figure sat in the middle of an art studio, with empty doll eyes and a marble expression. White hair that falls like snow. One hand with a purple glove with butterflies and the other with coarse bandages. Long legs with thick thighs crossed. White shoes with shoelaces undone that hover above the floor. Bitten lips. A burning sun in a neck tucked under black, tight leather that bulges out the skin at the edges in temptation.

It’s done.

But the canvas feels no less empty for it.

Maybe, “There’s something missing.”

“It’s not the painting.” Khaslana replies, closing his eyes. “Not really.”

“What?”

The hand around his calf falls. It reveals the beginnings of three thin scars and a stain of red smudged onto porcelain skin. Mydei’s eyes zero on it. The brush in his hand dips into red paint, covering the white.

“You will see.”

Chapter End Notes

FOOTNOTES

1. Long has the era of warriors, heroes and odysseys come pass, but, at their core, Castrum Kremnos will always be a nation built on Strife, and so they shall continue teaching their blood as such. What is life if not a battlefield, after all? Back

2. It’s of a lion cub sleeping on top of its mother’s back, basking in the sun. Despite the blood sticking to her paws and the meat between her teeth, the look in her eyes as she watches her son is a terribly gentle thing. It’s unnamed, of course, because that sort of love doesn’t need words to be understood. Back

3. More accurately, he had interrupted with a dry ‘yours is fine’ that left no room for argument when Mydei was giving him a few more public options because he understands the cautions a person should have to a stranger asking them to paint them on the street. A part of him wonders if he should worry about Khaslana’s sense of self-preservation. Back

4. It had been raining, that night, but the bar had been warm with his friends’ dumb laugh and Hephaestion’s arm around his shoulder. It had been the day before he moved out of Castrum Kremnos and the sight of the empty piano had stuck him, for some reason. The imprint of someone who should be there but wasn’t. He sketched it onto a napkin with a yellow crayon made out of clay and forgotten about it until it fell from the pocket of a jacket on the floor of a house that wasn't home yet. Back

5. Cats really, really don’t like Khaslana. It’s fine. He was always more of a dog person anyways—Except that dogs don’t really like Khaslana much either. Not anymore. Now, birds, though, different story, they absolutely love the guy. Also lizards, for some reason, which is great, frankly, because lizards are awesome. Back

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Try and swim
chapters.html:
Blacks and blues and whites and golds cling onto the decolored plastic palette in Mydei’s hand, slowly drying like cloths of coagulated blood. The paint on the yellowing strands of the old, rooting wooden brushes falls and dissolves through the once clear waters held in a white ceramic cup without a handle, slowly dyeing them into a dirty murky, gray that tethers and edges to turn onto the all-consuming black held in the middle of Khaslana’s empty, empty eyes.

The time on his phone marks four thirty-four in the morning of a date with no relevance to the story at hand in the Month of Freedom in big, bold white numbers. It changes to four thirty-five before the screen turns off on its own.

The painting is nowhere near done.

Khaslana had left once the clock marked eight. Time come notice by the astringent sound of his alarm phone. It had gone off like a gunshot through the dead silence that had befallen onto the art studio. Mydei had startled, a spasm of his hand around the brush, but he hadn’t flinched. Neither did Khaslana, who only blinked hard, as if awakened from a long, long slumber —though he did not look any less distant than he did before.

He had settled the painting brush onto the table at his side with a strangely harsh ‘clack’ whose echo had drowned over the sound of the still-going alarm that Khaslana had yet to turn off, leaving it to rang and rang, rang and rang, rang and rang.

A whole minute rang and rang before it died on its own.

The silence that followed was sharp.

“I can stay a little longer.” Khaslana had said, quietly, though not kindly. Words only heard, maybe, because there was no wind to steal them away. “If you want.”

Mydei had wanted. Instead, recognizing shifting waters, he answered, “It’s late.”

“I don’t have anywhere to go.”

The blood stained and swept over the delicate fabric of the purple glove in his hand, darkening it, and the bleeding in his calf had stopped, but the dry reds still smeared white porcelain skin1. Kopopo the Third, from where he had come settle on the edge of the room, had hissed and hair arisen as Khaslana walked past him, messenger back slung on his side and a curt, “Saturday. Same time.”

Mydei had stayed.

Now, he yawns and his eyes burn.

He scrubs them until voids eating constellations form under his eyelids and melt onto his vision, swallowing bits and pieces of the painting sitting coldly in front of him as the tip of the brush nestled on his index and middle finger taps onto his knee. It doesn’t stain the fabric of the clothes there. The red on it has long dried and hardened each and every single strand.

There isn’t any paint dripping onto the floor.

He gazes at the expanse of the empty canvas in front of him yet again, as he has done countless of times already, like an alarm that rings and rangs and rungs over and over.

It hasn’t changed throughout all this time.

The lonely figure is still sitting in the middle of an art studio instead of standing up and disappearing into the darkness of the night. White hair falling like snow. One hand with a purple glove with butterflies and the other with coarse bandages. Bitten lips. A burning sun that threatens to scorch it all into ash in a neck tucked under black, tight leather that bulges out the skin at the edges in temptation. White shoes with shoelaces undone that hover above the floor. Long legs and a calf with wounds painted with way too much care that bleeds and bleeds and threatens to flood and drown the low of the art studio in red, red, red.

But it’s not done.

It feels—dull, almost. Incomplete. Wrong.

Mydei’s eyes fix on empty doll eyes and marble expression. Devoid of any emotion, distant, fleeting, a perfect replica of its own but also not because something is missing, intrinsically, intimately, viscerally.

Something misses.

It’s the face, maybe. The expression. Mydei’s eyes sure can’t stop going back to it when he isn’t adding more red onto the floor.

The time on his phone reads six thirty-eight.

He twirls the brush on his fingers, once; presses it over the drying lump of white paint on the palette until the stiff strands crack and bend under the force, little specks of red dust scattering around. Kopopo the Third lets out a terribly loud yowl as Mydei lifts it over to the canvas once again.

And then, in one quick stroke, Mydei covers Khaslana's face—turns him into a stranger, a vessel with no eyes to see, no mouth to speak, a blank slate, and it is easy to realize then, the fact he didn’t draw a person to begin with, but merely a crumbling statue bleeding in the middle of an art studio.

He breathes and resists the urge to throw the painting in the trash.

━━━━━━━━━━

Through the mist, through the fog, through the incompleteness and through the sudden itch, not to create in brushes and paint, but to destroy in reds and linen, twitching and biting into the tips of his fingers, Mydei goes running the next evening.

It’s not running away, but merely, running. Jogging. A moment of solicitude from the paint sticking under his nails and the figure of a statue undoing sat on a room taken in rhythmic steps, burning joints, and cold air hitting against his face; through pavement and cobblestone, through paths that twist like mazes, stores, little’s ‘uh, I didn’t know that was there’ and through the dog in the fifth intersection that always jumps out the window when it sees him and chases him for ten streets straight ever since Mydei beat up his owner once2.

It’s grounding. Exerting. Maybe even cathartic. Thoughts and emotions checked, sharpened and put away in the same way a hunter would put away his arrows. Swimming against the current that laps and shifts around the oddity that is Khaslana.

In the distance, the red light on top of The Irontomb flashes once, against the oranges and yellows that paint the sky as the moon comes up, it looks like a second sun—A man-made one, that is, surrounded by the shiny blacks and grays of metal and wires. The sarcophagus of technology and logic defiled by arts and emotions.

There’s a second of pause, a second of contemplation edging on hesitation, strange, maybe, for someone like him, but, present, nevertheless. Though, is to be expected, he thinks, when haunted by a ghost. Still, a man does not choose what he feels, but he can sure choose how to face it, whether to be controlled, heart dictated; whether to escape them, soul trembling.

Mydei chooses neither, of course. He squares up shoulders, raises his chin, and turns in its direction.

It takes a while, maybe, maybe not. It doesn’t matter much. His feet still going on that rhythmic plam, plam, plam against cobblestone and rock as he jogs over.

He finds an old bending machine nestled like a mirror in between streets and when he tries to get a can of apple juice, what falls is the one next to it.

It doesn’t have a label, just a pink liquid that looks radioactive but tastes surprisingly good. It’s the last one, and the machine looks abandoned, so it is probably both the first and last time Mydei ever gets to taste it. A romanticist would sing for the fleeting joys lost, Mydei simply tips it back, throws it in a trashcan and licks his teeth with the aftertaste as he reaches The Irontomb.

The man at the reception doesn’t look up from the newspaper on his desk as Mydei walks inside, one hand tapping incessantly at the table. To his left, a couple of pamphlets with bright blues and greens read in bold red letters and the most egregious font he has ever laid eyes upon, ‘Join the competition!’

Oh, right.

“Next,” Khaslana had said, “You will say you are going to win that stupid art competition on The Irontomb with me as your model.”

Oh,

Right.

Mydei grabs one of the egregious colored pamphlets.

“Six letters,” The man at the reception says, without looking up at him, “Maestro.”

Mydei blinks, egregious colored pamphlet in his hand, and peers down onto the paper. Ah, a crossword. “Teacher.”

The man at the reception writes it down before his face scrunches. “Those are seven.” He twirls the pencil and starts erasing as he asks, “Gonna join?” But doesn’t wait for an answer before he pads around on the table for a clipboard, not looking from the crossword. He lets it fall onto the reception desk with a loud ‘blam!’, “Five letters. Subsided.”

“Maybe.”

“What does that have to do with subsided?”

“Just lend me the pencil.”

“No.”

Mydei lets out a bland, “Mm.”

A sigh and, reluctantly, the man at the reception gives him the one he has. It’s all chewed up. His fingers drum against the table as he mutters words to himself, and Mydei peers down onto the names written on it. He knows some, others don’t, faintly, he registers the Polyxia in elegant calligraphy. Hm, good to know she’s giving it a try again.

He writes his name underneath.

“Remember to have fun or whatever. Don’t feel obliged to participate. There’s always next year. You know the rest. Subside. Abate?” He mutters to himself once he gets back his pencil. Mydei gets a glimpse of him sighing and abating as he takes his phone to look it up while he turns onto the corner.

His steps are firm as he walks towards the end hall on the west wing, through old brushstrokes and images of destruction, past people chatting and pointing to a piece or another, past a girl sitting in front of Goldweaver’s Last Bath with an empty document that merely reads ‘Art Analysis’ in a laptop scrolling through her phone, and an Antikytheran looking at Calculation 033. It's surprisingly full for it to be a Tuesday evening, but it isn’t crowded either. Mydei, drenched in sweat, with his black shorts and loose, red sleeveless shirt, sticks out like a sore thumb— it’s a good thing, then, the fact he has never cared about stupid inanities like that.

Thus Burns the Dawn is just the same as he remembers from all those months ago. The breathtaking picture of a crumbling statue weeping gold in a somber mix of blues.

It’s strange, but firm, the sudden sensation that strikes him when his eyes set onto golden ones, the knowledge that the being in the linen is as much as it is Khaslana as it isn’t. The traces, the factions, the face, the eyes, the emptiness. Empty, empty, empty. It’s all him. Undoubtedly so—But, whatever seems to be burning Khaslana up hasn’t extinguished just yet, no.

Because the hand Mydei held the day had met, faint, as it had been, had had a pulse4.

He taps the egregious colored pamphlet in his other palm a couple of times, contemplating. The end goal of the competition, it writes, is to create a collection of different pieces featuring the same model in some form. And, so, it would be easy, he thinks, to create a collection of statues, a collection of dolls, a collection of corpses, with empty eyes and snow hair, but he’s no sculptor, neither is he a toy maker, and much less a mortician.

He’s a painter. A human that merely wants to paint another.

He didn't ask Khaslana to model for him just to bury him.

━━━━━━━━━━

Time tick-tock-ticks and Saturday comes in the eternity it takes a person to blink. All too slow and all too sudden. Seconds slipping by like grains of sand scattered through the wind along the smell of drying paint, white linen and an unmoving figure left undone burning into the back of his eyelids— until time freezes once again when a knock-knock-knocking arises like bubbles popping underwater at one o’clock sharp.

Khaslana is much the same as last time, standing at the edge of the same wobbly stone step that gives way to his house with the same messenger bag, same sharp tongue, same deceptive doll eyes, same all-consuming allurement—except, he’s not terribly late today.

“No cats this time?” Mydei asks, skipping formalities he does not care about as he steps aside to let him pass.

Khaslana stares at him for a pause too long, searching, Mydei’s form reflecting on stagnated water instead of sinking in, before he replies, simply, “No cats this time.” And, without further preamble, walks inside his house.

Mydei lets out a sharp ‘cht’ clicked between closed teeth before Kopopo the Third lunges at Khaslana with bared fangs from where he is hidden under the couch as he closes the door. His cat lets out a loud cry but stays put, because he may be spoiled rotten but that certainly doesn’t mean Mydei raised him badly.

Khaslana hums. “Except that one.”

“Don’t be dramatic.”

“It’s easy for you to say,” Khaslana says, plainly, already walking to the art studio as if he owned the place. Jackass. “You are not the one at risk of getting your tendons sliced.”

It’s a cat, Mydei thinks of replying, but, frankly, Kopopo the Third can be a force to be reckoned with. The kind of creature rhapsodes of old would sing lo and about myths of strife about. Mydei wouldn’t have it any other way.

Instead, he asks, as he follows, “How’s your calf?”

Khaslana falters, for some reason.

“…Fine.”

There’s something weird in the way he says it. Kind of quiet, kind of hesitant, kind of small. Mydei’s brow furrows and his eyes trail down to Khaslana’s ankle. It is covered by the long legs of his white pants—Their length is not quite right, ends of cloth frayed and dirty where the back of his shoes step onto it with every single stride he takes5.

His shoelaces are undone today too.

“It was a cat’s scratch,” Khaslana continues, reincorporating rather quickly. “Not a battle wound.” He says, lifting one end to let Mydei see the tree thin white lines, almost lost against his pale skin. The hand that lifts it, now without the coarse bandages, is also donned in similar little scars.

“Hm.”

“Mm.”

Khaslana doesn’t hesitate this time when crossing the threshold of the art studio, making a beeline directly to the canvas with his image propped on the easel. Mydei follows, again, coming to stand merely a breath away from him, scanning his face rather than the painting he knows is incomplete.

Khaslana's expression doesn’t even twitch. Instead, he lets out another little, “Mm.”

“I know.”

“Mm.”

“If you want to say something, say it.”

“No, I think you know.” Khaslana replies. Mydei feels the beginnings of a headache pulsing in the space between his eyes. It only grows when Khaslana adds, plainly, “I don’t like it one bit.”

“Neither do I.”

Khaslana’s eyes shift to him before his face does. The look in them is distant, as ever. “At least you are honest.” He mutters, before he catches onto the egregious colored pamphlet placed on the black table next to the easel. “What’s this?”

“A pamphlet.” Mydei says, dryly, unable to help himself.

“And you know what it reads?” He shoots back, brow furrowed, just barely, before his face falls onto the same blank muteness of always. The words don’t. “Or did the pretty colors on the cover merely caught your attention?”

Khaslana, it seems, is allergic to not having the last word. Mydei scoffs, and replies, not fully raising to the bait, “The composition on the cover is awful.”

“Ah, so it was the colors.”

“I’m an artist, in case you have forgotten.”

He mumbles something that sounds suspiciously like ‘unfortunately’ while he opens the egregious colored pamphlet6. Mydei leaves him at it, rounding the table to come sit on the stool. There’s already some water, a few brushes and tubes of paint propped on the surface. He uncaps the white one and places some of it on the palette.

“The end goal of the competition,” Khaslana reads out loud, words that Mydei already knows, at the same time he uncaps the orange paint. “Is for each intrepid artist to create a collection of different pieces featuring the same model in some form over a few months.”

The silence that follows is pointed. A little incredulous, perhaps even accusatory. Mydei can’t offer anything else, truly, nothing that the pamphlet has already said, and when it is made obvious he won’t elaborate, Khaslana says, “A collection.”

Mydei hums an affirmative.

“You want to make a collection.” Khaslana repeats, slowly, as if talking to someone stupid. Mydei’s eyebrow twitches. “With paintings of me. Do you need it spelled out?”

“Do you?”

“Do I?”

“You were the one that brought it up.” Mydei reminds him, reclining his elbow on the table as he turns to look up at him. “And I did say I like a challenge.”

Khaslana opens his mouth, closes it, and his eyes narrow. “I can’t tell if you are stupid, arrogant, or merely a very good liar.”

“None.”

“Stupid, then.” Khaslana huffs. Mydei contemplates, in complete seriousness, throwing the water in the porcelain cup at him. “The competition starts next Sunday, you know?” He says before Mydei can decide whether to do it or not. Dull eyes go to the egregious colored pamphlet to confirm the date before going back to him. “And you only have that.”

There are a couple of things Mydei could answer. All excuses. He’s not that type of man and, as such, he answers, “I still have two sessions.”

“And that’s enough?”

“That’s enough.”

The silence that follows is charged. Heavy. The beginnings of a sizzle as piercing gold eyes met deep blue ones—Broken abruptly by the loud ‘thud’ of Khaslana letting the messenger bag fall crudely onto the floor, right next to the table. The force makes the tubes of paint shake and brushstroke roll and fall onto the floor.

“How do you want me?”

Mydei thinks about it. “Same as last time.”

Khaslana’s head tilts, movement reminiscent of a haunted doll. Mydei tries to cut the comparison short to no avail.

“You are going to try finish?”

“Why wouldn’t I?”

Khaslana doesn’t answer that, instead, he turns to the painting and asks, “Have you ever heard of Icarus?”

“Are you the sun, now?”

The look that crosses Khaslana’s face is weird and, before he speaks, a small sound escapes him. It sounds like a crow’s cry, like someone who doesn’t remember how quite to laugh.

“Maybe.”

“I don’t have any wings.”

Neither does he need them.

“Yes,” Khaslana replies. “I can see that.”

He goes to the stool in front of the easel without further word. Mydei bends down to pick up the brush that fell. Once he straightens, is to see Khaslana already sitting down, crossed legs and elbow on his knee as he rests his cheek on his palm, positioned as to not look directly at Mydei as he paints. It’s a perfect copy of his position on the canvas.

Except, that he swapped both the leg he crossed and the arm propped on his elbow.

“Are you doing it on purpose?”

His tone is monotone when he answers, “Doing what on purpose?”

He absolutely is.

━━━━━━━━━━

“The vase in your living room is fake, by the way.” It’s what Khaslana says in lieu of a farewell when the clock hits eight once again, already disappearing past the corner of the art studio.

His head feels as if it is underwater, fuzzy and groggy, and so it takes a second for the words to reach Mydei, another before their meaning dawns on him, and yet another before he musters the force to settle the palette with whites that, at some point, have started to resemble more porcelain instead of skin, aside.

It’s hard, surprisingly so, to set foot outside the room, away from the painting—It’s better, than last time, much better, but still nowhere near done —But he still manages to catch up to Khaslana just as a pale hand closes around knob of the door that gives way to the exit with a bland, “What?”

Khaslana turns to him, “That vase,” He repeats, pointing at the red vase with golden accents picturing an image of the last King of Castrum Kremnos placed on the coffee table. Kopopo the Third immediately goes to sit next to it, ears lowered. “Is fake.”

One of Mydei’s eyebrows raises and says, dryly, “Really.”

“Really.” Khaslana replies, just as dryly. “It’s a good imitation, though.”

Mydei would be more inclined to believe him were his low, monotonous tone not suggest that he believes Mydei is being stupid, again, and were it not to have been one of his mother’s past belongings. She had spent a small fortune for it in an auction, and she had never been one to be given cat for hare.

“And what would you know?”

Khaslana opens his mouth, before a spark of something crosses his face, fleeting, but terribly, unmistakably alive, and he closes his mouth. Mydei wants to see more, but it’s gone before he can even think of the ways he could portray it, replaced by an almost disinterested, “Just a hunch.”

“And you expect me to believe you based on a hunch?”

“Want to bet on it?”

Distantly, an alarm bell starts ringing on the back of Mydei’s mind, but he can’t bring himself to listen to it over the fire licking at the back of his throat. He can be terribly, terribly competitive, push come to shove. “If I win?”

“I give you one more session.”

Tempting, but, “Do I look stupid?” He asks and immediately continues before Khaslana can answer, “I’m not falling for your poorly laid trap. I am not betting the last session.”

“I wasn’t asking you to.”

Mydei scoffs. “What do you get if I lose then?”

Khaslana’s head tilts.

“What do I get?”

Incomplete brushstrokes and rotting linen can’t even possibly begin to fathom how infuriating this man can be.

“I will cook you something.”

“Why in the hell would I want something you cooked?”

Mydei clicks his tongue and raises his chin, “I’m a very good cook.”

“You also said you could draw people pretty well.”

“Tomorrow,” Mydei bites instead of delving into that discussion again. Words and proclamations of could’s and can’s fall flat if he can’t prove them. It seems Khaslana knows this fact as well as he does, seems he’s keen to dig and dig deeper into it until a bruise forms, breaks and bleeds. “Nine in the morning, I will be waiting with the vase. Don’t be late.”

“Great,” Khaslana says. He turns the knob and pushes the door open. A wave of cold air rushes into the house as he does so, pushing unruly locks of white hair back. The dark, uncaring blacks of the night threaten to swallow him without a trace, leaving behind only soon fading memories. “It’s a date then.”

His exit would be a perfect recreation of an unfinished piece of a statue stepping out a room found amidst the smell of paper, wood and paint of an art store hanging on a cloth hanger like a dead man—were Mydei not see him place his feet on the wobbly stone step, stumble, and almost fall face first on the ground.

Oh, yeah, Mydei thinks with some amusement, he should fix it. It’s been loose for a while now.

Chapter End Notes

FOOTNOTES

1. There has been a moment of clarity before a brush dripping red raised where Mydei had set it aside to get the dusty old first kit-aid shoved away in some corner of his bathroom. Khaslana’s low “leave it” had been harsh and when Mydei had turned, it was to be met with the abyss looking up at him on derisive challenge. Mydei, not one to lose, had stayed—but, looking back, though, Mydei doubts there even was a way to win and he wonders if Khaslana knew. He doubts it, for some reason.Back

2. Sometimes, you just try to mug the wrong people, you know? Happens to the best of us—But was it his fault? No! How was Head Crusher 3000’s owner supposed to know that Mydei was the type of guy to bring his fists to a gunfight and win?Back

3. He thinks about it, sometimes. A board duster in this pocket. But Nous, shameful blood of his, wouldn’t care about lost knowledge— because they already know it.Back

4. It’s a terribly simple fact, terribly easy to forget.Back

5. He could get it fixed, quite easily, but Aglaea is a busy, busy woman, and Khaslana is of the opinion she shouldn’t waste the little free time she has on something as worthless as this. Not for him.Back

6. Once the session comes to an end and Khaslana leaves like smoke in the wind, Mydei will find the egregious colored pamphlet crumpled and thrown into the little plastic trashcan shoved in one corner of the art studio, hidden under empty tubes of paint.Back
