chapters.title: Chapter 4: Calm before the storm
chapters.html:
Question, where does humanity lie?

━━━━━━━━━━

On the middle of the seventh street of the tenth avenue of a place you don’t need to know the name of, in between the house of a man who only ever does cups without handles and teapots without spouts and the residence of kind old woman who bakes really nice cookies and most definitely killed her last three husbands; unassumingly enough, in warm terracotta reds and a wobbly step, Mydei’s home rests.

It can’t be described as a cozy little thing for the sake of flowery descriptions, for it is not exactly little. It’s certainly no palace, for he is no prince, and he has never had any intention nor wish to be someone else other than simply Mydeimos, Son of Gorgo. But it is big enough that he knows she would have undoubtedly asked if it wasn’t too big for only him and Kopopo the Third.

Solitude is no thing he struggles with. Yet, far away from the strife filled soil that had watched him be born, bleed and grow, far from the sharp vowels of his native tongue, far from all the people who he would go to war for, to her, and only to her, he would have admitted that those first months were—rough.

Lonely.

Mydei had endured, of course, a battle well won. He had stood with the temper of a warrior and the patience of a lion and, like water eroding rock, little by little, he quenched and conquered his unrest. He had come to know all the strange, strange idiosyncrasies this town has to offer, the nook and crannies, the streets and stories and, little by little, he had come to make this house a home.

It was built on top of a graveyard—or, at least, that’s what the kids playing along in the street like to tell everybody they might come across between laughter, scrapped knees, plastic balls, rope and chalk.

The day Mydei moved in, he remembers, they all had trailed after him like little ducks in a pond as he carried box after box from the back of his car to his new house. They told him that everyone around here walked on top of the dead, that the bricks of the houses were made out of tablets, and the soil at the bottom of the ravine at the other side of the block was filled with the bones of people that nobody loved and people that didn’t eat their veggies1.

It’s the sort of tale that abounds and arises whenever you are, wherever you go. Mydei doesn’t believe it, but the three knock-knock-knocks rattling at his bathroom door as he brushes his teeth make childish myths and boyish mirth come forth to the center of his mind.

People say you shouldn’t let a ghost in even if it knocks. Mydei has already invited one into his house twice.

He opens the door.

There’s nobody on the other side.

Because of course there wouldn’t be.

The clock on his night table reads eight thirty-six in red numbers, about half an hour earlier, and another knock, knock, knock resonates in his room, like the ba-thump-thump-thump’s of a bleeding heart heard from inside the organ. Mydei walks past his neatly made bed to the window that gives view into the street and slides the metal grid with a clack, clack, clack to the side before sticking his head out, mint foam still in his mouth.

He looks down. Khaslana looks up, his gloved hand raised to knock, knock, knock again on his door.

He bites onto the orange toothbrush and raises three of his fingers at him, indicating he will be down in three. Khaslana lifts his index back at him. Mydei’s eyebrow ticks and then lifts all of his fingers, now I will make it in five.

Khaslana stares at him, completely unimpressed, which is ridiculous considering he was the one that started it.

Mydei grabs the toothbrush again and waits a second before pulling his head back inside; lingering long enough to watch as the kids, let loose from school thanks to the Month of Freedom, slowly get close to Khaslana, spinning tops and chalk in their tiny little hands, before jumping at him like cats reaching for a canary.

He then continues to get ready, slower than usual—way slower. Khaslana is not the only one who gets to be petty.

He finishes brushing his teeth, passes dental floss through the gaps between. His hair is still a little damp from the shower after the gym. It’s not something he cares about, but he still takes the hair dryer from where it is buried way, way back in his closet and makes sure that it won’t spit a bunch of dust at him before thoroughly drying his hair. It puffs up like a lion’s mane before he fixes it. Then, very meticulously, and with very slow hands, he braids one long lock of hair and, very carefully, puts the golden aglet his mother gave him around it.

Once he’s done and the clock in his night desk reads eight fifty, Mydei puts on his shoes, grabs the vase, tells Kopopo the Third very firmly not to destroy the house while he’s out and steps outside, absentmindedly skipping the wobbly step2.

“The ravine is here, see? Right here.” One of the kids says, pointing at a blue line inside a square made with red chalk on the floor. Another two compete whose spinning tops can spin the longest at his back. “That’s where you will end up if you don’t eat your veggies.”

“Mm.” Khaslana, crouched at his side, in that ever-present distant muteness of his, replies, “Even if I really don’t like them?”

“Even if you really don’t like them!”

“I will make sure to always finish them, then, just like you.”

The kid lets out a nervous, “Um, uh, yeah! Like me, ha, yes. I really like broccoli.” At the same time, a little girl pokes Khaslana in the shoulder with a, “Mister, mister, look, it’s you.”

And the wind holds its breath, and the world stills, for there, on the street floor, made in crude strikes of yellow and blue chalk and traces of innocence, a little doodle of Khaslana smiling came to be.

Khaslana goes so, so very quiet.

“My little brother ate the white one, so you are blond now.” The little girl continues as if she hadn’t made life out of a corpse with mere chalk.

She starts another drawing, this time of a bird.

And then a bee.

And then what it looks like Godzilla.

And, after the time it takes a bridge to burn, Khaslana asks, “...Is it done?”

“Eh?” The little girl turns away from her drawing to him. She looks down at her little doodle on the floor, to Khaslana, and back to the doodle. She places the little piece of yellow chalk under her chin and hums. “Mm, I guess I could add a dinosaur.” She nods. “What’s your favorite dinosaur?”

“Uh.” Khaslana lets out, looking so very fickle as one of his hands goes up to pick at his lips, “...Triceratops?”

The girl nods. “That’s a good one.” Before she starts drawing it next to him.

A second tricks by, or maybe two, maybe three; tears slipped through the cracks of the hands of the Veil of Night.

Khaslana turns to see Mydei, then, who had been lingering on the edges of the conversation with sharp eyes and vase in hand. His face is set in marble, empty well eyes swirling by, but Mydei still gets the impression he looks unsure all of a sudden. Aware, perhaps, of this, Khaslana says, a little harshly, a little hastily, “About time.”

Mydei lets out a simple ‘hmph’ instead of dignifying him with an answer. He walks up to him with firm steps, coming to stand next to his crouched form. He does greet back the kids when they all let out small ‘hi’s’ and ‘hello’s’ and ‘what’s that in your hand?’ and ‘what’s your favorite dinosaur, Mister Painter?’ at him.

To that last one, he replies, “Velociraptor.”

“No, it’s not.” The little girl shuts down immediately, making a little triangle on the dinosaur’s nose. She sounds as fed up as one of Mydei’s math teachers back in school. “You only say that because of the movie, but those were more Utahraptors rather than Velociraptors, though they really weren’t Utahraptors either. Real Velociraptors aren’t that big, nu-uh, they were more the size of chickens, and had feathers, too!” She shakes her head, takes a long look at Mydei and adds, “You look more like an Ankylosaurus type of guy.”

She doesn’t wait for Mydei to answer before she nods, satisfied with herself, and starts drawing what he assumes is the dinosaur she just said, right next to the other one.

“Sure.” He says nevertheless and turns to Khaslana. “Let’s go.”

Khaslana does a little shrug of shoulder. “I don’t think I want to go out with someone who doesn’t know what real velociraptors look like.”

All four kids’ heads snap up at his words.

“Go out?” The one who doesn’t eat their veggies asks.

“You two are friends?” A girl with a purple spinning top asks.

“They are.” A boy with a green spinning top pipes. “I heard my grandmother tell my mom that she has seen him,” He points at Khaslana, who merely blinks. “Come into Mydei’s house. Twice.”

“Twice?”

“Twice!”

“Why have you gone into his house twice?” The kid who doesn’t eat their veggies demands of Khaslana. “You don’t look like one of Mydei’s friends. I saw you knock.”

“So what if he knocks?”

“Mydei’s friends don’t knock. They just break into his home.”

“They don’t break in.” Mydei corrects. “They just have spare keys.”

All the kids ignore him.

“Aren’t those just thiefs?”

“It’s thieves.”

“They can’t be thiefs.” The boy with the green spinning top says, ignoring him again. “The kind old woman would have already stripped them down in the middle of the street and drenched them in gasoline.”

“Oh!” The little girl with chalks brightens. “You must be his muse!”

“What’s a muse?” The girl with the purple spinning top asks.

“A person you draw because they are very pretty.”

“I’m not.” Khaslana cuts in, still picking at his lips; whether he means he’s not a person or a muse, Mydei doesn’t know. Maybe both, maybe neither, maybe it doesn’t matter, because all the kids ignore him too.

“Does that mean Mydei likes him?”

The boy with the green spinning top spins in his direction and asks, “Does that mean you like him?” At the same time, the kid who doesn’t eat their veggies questions, point blank, “Does that mean you kiss him?”

“I don’t—”

The girl with the purple spinning top gasps. “Are you going out on a date?”

This time, they wait for him to speak with waited breath.

Mydei opens his mouth to answer.

And pauses.

The thing is, Khaslana had called it a date, yesterday night, in that monotonously deadpan way of his. Does that make it one? Ha, no, probably not, he concludes in the exact same breath, feeling absurd to even have contemplated the thought. There isn’t anything particularly romantic about how all this came to be. If anything, all this seems more of an errand.

It’s a small pause, barely second and a half, but it’s more than enough for all the kids to latch on like sharks smelling blood.

“It is?” The boy with the green spinning top asks.

“It is!” The girl with the purple spinning top sings.

“So you do kiss him.” The kid who doesn’t eat their veggies accuses him.

“Mom!” The little girl with chalks yells, picking up all her colors before running towards her house. All rest of her friends following suit. “Mom! The painter you like is going out on a date!”

And just like that, with a ‘slam!’ and a loud ‘he’s what!?’, they are both left on their own in the middle of the street.

Mydei sighs, long-suffering, aware of the fact that, for the next few weeks, he will fall victim to prodding aunts, peeking grandmothers, nosy neighbors and invasive questions.

“Kids are so simple, uh.”

Mydei turns to Khaslana, just to find him staring at the image of his made on the street’s floor. One of his hands still picks, picks, picks at the edge of his thin rosy lips hard enough to draw blood. The vibrant reds would look nice smeared on them like lipstick, give them some shine, make him look more alive as much as it would make him look more dead.

His other hand hovers uncertainly over the little chalk doodle.

Mydei wonders, then, and “Khaslana.” He calls, for he is not one to disregard his wants.

The other blinks, long and paused. It takes a second for the words to dawn on him and another for him to make an inquisitive sound at the back of his throat, and even that is faint, as if he’s tethering on the edge of nonexistence. He doesn’t turn to see Mydei, eyes glued to the floor, and so he waits yet another second to make sure he’s here—as here as possible, either way. He doesn’t think Khaslana is ever fully present.

“Why did you start modeling?”

Khaslana doesn’t skip a beat. “To trick rich people into painting me and then robbing them blind.”

“Funny.”

“I know I am.”

The meaning is clear, albeit hidden, the glint of a fang peeking under closed lips.

None of your business.

Mydei is not the kind of man to disregard his wants, as he just said, but he’s also the kind of man that knows when to strike and when to wait. The hunter who lets go too early of the arrow only scares off the prey. So, he plays along, this time, taps the vase and the soft clink of his nail against the clay resonates like the crack of a mirror in a world come to pause. “Is that why you fixated on this?”

“As if that thing were worth a dime.”

“As far as you think.”

“Mm.”

He places his index finger on the face of the little chalk doodle and drags it to the side with such speed that the gravel must have sure burnt the pad of his finger. The strikes of yellow and blue chalk mix into green at the sides and the traces of innocence get lost. A man turned into a ghost, a blank slate, a haunting specter, a stranger met in dreams whose face you can never remember once you wake. Unreachable, unknowable, ephemeral.

The wind lets out a relieved breath when Khaslana ruins himself, rocking the leaves of the trees and the potted plants left on windows without glass as the world starts spinning once again.

As if a wrong had been rectified. Talanton’s scale in equilibrium once again.

He stands up. There’s a new tear on his lower lip, irregular and wobbly, burning red. It doesn’t bleed and Mydei half wishes it did in a desire he recognizes as not entirely his.

“Shall we?” He asks with that little tilt of his, the one that makes him look like a haunted doll, and he doesn’t wait for Mydei to answer before he starts to walk away. There’s chalk sticking to the pads of his fingers.

Mydei watches him go, takes one last look at the little chalk doodle without a face, then to the two dinosaurs drawn next to it3, and follows.

━━━━━━━━━━ It’s always a little bit strange, a little bit jarring, and, maybe, a little bit wonderful, the sudden realization a part of the life of someone you know edges and tethers ever so closely with yours. A tiny gap, merely a breath away, that goes unnoticed like a shell washed ashore, burrowed under the sands and the clear waters until you go looking for them.

The place Khaslana takes him with all so silent, unsynchronized steps, is a small little building at the side of the road that Mydei always passes by without spearing a glance when going from the gym to his home and from his home to the gym, barely thirty minutes away from the street where he lives.

It’s a small little thing, as it has been said, one of those things that look like they were built two or three decades ago and went forgotten by the modernization of times. The little spots of greenery in front have gone unkempt. Green, rich vines with tiny little white flowers extend through the quaint yellow walls and twist all the way inside through the edges of the windows and the door in the entrance, which an old man with wrinkled hands and a newsboy cap opens for them. He greets Khaslana with surprisingly warm eyes before telling Mydei to make time and go into the dinner on the last floor because the food his wife cooks is to die for and it’s not like none of them are getting any younger.

It’s quiet inside. A little bit empty in the way these sorts of places always seem to be, but not deserted. There's a small jewelry shop with a girl clutching her mother’s hand in a death grip as a woman with a dozen piercings brings a needle up to her ear; a bank with a few children running outside while they wait for their parents to be done with their boring adult stuff; and a movie shop with hundreds of old VHS and DVD’S in plastic sheets lining the walls, the owner inside watches a movie in blacks and whites, in one of those televisions that look like a box, as a group of friends argue which movies to take.

The stairs he is led to are placed right next to an elevator and Khaslana off-handedly mentions that it always gets stuck between floors as he starts climbing upwards.

“You come here often?” Mydei asks, though it is less than a question as it is an observation.

“You could say that.” Khaslana replies. His steps aren’t nearly as silent, this time, a little plap, plap arising as the ends of his untied shoes slip out of his heels every time he lifts his feet to climb another step—until one of them slips out of completely as they reach the second floor, rolling a few stairs down. “Ah.”

It lands right next to Mydei, who was walking a couple of steps after him.

He shifts to hold the vase with only one hand before grabbing it. He cuts the rest of the distance with long strides and places the shoe in front of Khaslana without a word, careful not to crush any of the little white flowers growing on the white tiles there.

Khaslana blinks at him but, nevertheless, accepts the little action with ease. He crushes the heel tab as he wiggles and slips his foot inside, not bothering to tie his shoelaces—stiff, gray things, full of dust and mud whose aglets have broken with how many times he has stepped on them.

At the sight, Mydei says, simply, “Tie your shoe.”

“When we are there.”

Mydei doubts he will, for some reason.

Not really knowing why but not really worrying why, Mydei hands the vase to Khaslana with an unceremonial ‘here’ before bending down. He grabs the shoelaces, scraps the pointed bits and sharp pieces of plastic still clinging to one before pulling them.

“That’s too tight.” Khaslana complains.

“It’s not.”

“It is. You are going to cut the circulation of my foot.”

Mydei pulls them tighter, ignoring Khaslana dry ouch, and ties it in neat, quick motions, making a double knot to make sure they won’t come loose. Once he’s done, he taps the foot and says, “Give me the other one.”

“I’m not a child.” Khaslana replies, flatly, but still gives him his other foot, and Mydei repeats the process. When he finishes, he stands up, wipes the dust off his knees and takes the vase from Khaslana’s hands, who lets out a quiet, “...Thanks.”

“Hm.”

They continue up one more floor, into a little shop with a sign at the top that reads in bold blacks against a brown background ‘Ancient Knick-Knacks’ and a piece of paper taped to the glass door that reads, in all caps, ‘NOT A CYBERCAFE ANYMORE. WE BEG OF YOU, STOP ASKING.’4

A little golden bell at the top of the door chimes with a melodious little ‘ding, ding’ as Khaslana pushes the door open into a place impregnated with the smell of paper and old coins. A bunch of wooden bookshelves filled with fragile-looking vases, elaborate clocks, wooden and metal statues, faded tapestry, obsidian knives, crystal eyes, jade jewelry and, true to its name, other knick-knacks, fill the space like pages of an old forgotten book.

At the far end, right in front of the door, like a book separator peeking under the paper, there lay a counter with a man inspecting pieces of chess carved out of marble and glass. His head lifts at the sound of the bell, and, upon settling eyes on Khaslana, he says, “I thought you weren’t going to come today.”

“Someone didn’t hurry-up,” Khaslana replies, walking up to him. “So, I ran late.”

The sheer audacity of his. It is baffling, truly.

“Be nice, Khas.” The man chastises, though, the words are more fond than anything. He throws Mydei an apologetic look. “What can I do for you today? We got a few amenities of Ancient Kremnos that might interest you.”

Mydei shakes his head, “I would like you to inspect a vase.” He says, settling it on the counter in front of him, careful of the other knick-knacks laying about.

He perks up. “A vase?”

“It’s fake.” Khaslana deadpans.

“He says it is fake,” Mydei explains, glaring at Khaslana through the corner of his eye. “But I am not inclined to believe a supposition based on a mere hunch.”

The man pauses.

“...A hunch?”

“We were hoping you could shed some light on this debacle,” Khaslana adds, and it is a little strange, a little uncanny, to hear him talk without any scalding insults nor derisive glances—but not particularly bad. “Considering you are the only one who knows about treasure appraisal here, Theodoros.”

A look of confusion passes through the man, Theodoros, that is quickly, almost immediately, replaced by one of realization, and he narrows his eyes up to Khaslana so hard his eyelids are practically closed.

Khaslana merely tilts his head.

“...Say, uh, sir?”

“Mydeimos—but just call me Mydei.”

“Mydei.” Theodoros nods, without taking his eyes for a single second out of Khaslana’s expressionless face. “You didn’t happen to bet anything over this, didn’t you?”

“What.”

“Nothing. Nothing, don’t worry about it.” He coughs, sighs, a little long-suffering. He settles with deep, deep care the glass tower in his hand on the table, next to the queen, and turns to the vase. “Let’s check this little thing of yours.”

First things first, Theodoros starts by going over the details. He asks for the time period the vase is supposed to belong to, he asks what image it is supposed to be depicting, he asks what it was used for and a hundred dozen things more.

Then, after Mydei has had to text Ptolemy with a dozen questions because half of the things he got asked are stuff only he remembers, Theodoros finally starts to check the vase. He looks at the material it is made, the thickness of it, the cracks spreading along the surface, the image of the last King of Castrum Kremnos in the middle, the art style it was painted on, the paint it was used—and a bunch of yet another hundred dozen things Mydei doesn’t quite care to catch nor worry about, because Theodoros goes over with the motions of a man that is as good as his job as he is passionate.

Slow, meticulous, thorough and careful.

And also boring to watch.

Very boring to watch—As in, watching paint dry ought to be more fun.

A couple minutes pass before Khaslana drifts away, like a small ship that wasn’t anchored properly to the coast, up to a nearby shelf to pick at a little something that has caught his eye.

Mydei watches him, and, after a pause where consideration mixes with curiosity, he unties his own anchor and drifts to his side in a way that feels almost natural.

“What’s that?”

“A doll.” Khaslana answers, tilting it towards him. It’s a little wooden thing, with fiery red hair, blue flowers for eyes and a little wooden sword in her tiny hand. It evokes as much security as it does kindness. Safety. “One of the Holy Maidens. The Protector.”

Hm. Mydei turns to the shelf, only to see mirrors, clocks and a moon. “Weren’t there supposed to be the other two?”

Khaslana hums an affirmative.

“We have them. They just like to play hide-and-seek.” Theodoros pipes in, voice both muffled as it is echo-y as he sticks his head inside the vase. “Check between the knick-knacks, you might find them there.”

They both turn to look down at the Protector’s doll held in Khaslana's hand.

It’s kind of sad to let her remain on her own.

Wordlessly, they walk further into the maze of bookshelves and little knick-knacks, picking at this and shifting through that. A candelabra here, a quill there. They walk through ladles, sails and goblets; through candles, books and tablet stones; through rings, bracelets and hammers; through glimpses of lives gone by, stories witnessed by the stars, scattered through the winds. None of them really mean to fall into step with each other, but it happens either way. Quietly, silently, tethering on comfortably, tethering on mundane.

The second doll, the Oracle, a little doll whose fiery red hair covers her flower eyes and evokes gentleness and calm, but the exact same kindness as the Protector—that one, they find hiding in between rolls of old, yellow parchments describing constellations.

Khaslana takes it with the same hand that holds the Protector, and then grabs a sword with a thin blade and an intricate blue handle lying on the shelf above the shelf of the parchments.

“This shouldn’t be placed with the rest of kremonan weapons.”

No, it shouldn’t. Kremonan swords are robust in nature, made with a thick blade and simple handles. A weapon is made to kill and die by, not parade around. On the battlefield, gems and elegance hold no value over blood. Though, on the rare occasions pretentiousness and decorations were valued, like in ceremonies, the colors used would either be red or orange, not blue. Judging by the looks of it, the sword in Khaslana’s hand “It’s from the Sky People.”

“Oh.”

Mydei's eyes shift to Khaslana's hand around the sword’s handle, and asks, “You know how to use it?”

“What gave it away?”

“The way you hold it.”

Khaslana looks down at the sword, the position he has placed it. “There are some habits you can’t really get rid of, uh.” He muses, more to himself, and twirls it around with a dexterous hand. “I did fencing for a little while.”

“Fencing?”

He nods, lets out a dry, “On guard," as he brings the hand holding the little dolls behind his back and the sword up, before, lightly, fleetingly, poking Mydei’s chest with the end of the blade, right where his heart beats5.

Mydei’s eyebrow lifts, amused, despite himself.

He grabs one of the other swords laid on the shelf and mirrors Khaslana’s action, but the other takes a step back, and Mydei misses.

“You suck.”

“I wasn’t even trying.” Mydei replies and repeats the action. This time, Khaslana brings the sword up, and a small little ‘clink!’ resonates as the metal of the swords meet.

For a second, something close to mirth swirls in Khaslana’s empty eyes without light.

“Mm. Still not trying?”

“Not one bit.”

A clink, clink, clink echoes and twists between the bookshelves of the store like smoke from a candle, surprisingly light, surprisingly gentle, for a clash of blades. But, maybe, that is to be expected. Both of their movements are light, small, and quiet, a little step forwards, a little step back, as Mydei attacks, clink, clink, clink, and Khaslana defends, clink, clink, clink.

Until a chastising ‘stop playing with the swords’ arises through the wooden bookshelves and both of them hastily place the swords back in place and all but dart to a far, far away shelf, away from the swords—as if they weren’t the only ones in the store.

The last doll, the Teacher, the guiding, soothing presence, with always the same kindness as the others, is inside a black teapot filled with dry, golden flowers shaped like butterflies. Khaslana takes it out with careful hands and places it, along the other two dolls, next to the teapot.

A big picture window rests on the far, far end of the hall, nestled in between the shelves like a secret whispered at night, letting green vines and little white flowers extend through the walls as the gentle rays of the morning sun filter into all the nooks and crannies and little knick-knacks of the store.

Mydei stares.

Khaslana looks impossibly, breathtakingly warm.

The filtering light makes Khaslana come to be shaded with oranges and yellows instead of the usual reds and golds he always thinks about when he sees Khaslana. It makes it easy to see that his hair is the same shade of white as the little flowers scattering about behind him, and his hands are gentle like the strokes of a brush against linen as he brings the little dolls together once again.

It’s all so very mundane, and, so, there’s a moment, a small little tender moment, held between bookshelves lined like pages of a book, where Mydei looks at Khaslana and doesn’t think of marble and porcelain nor statues and dolls, and much less corpses, because Khaslana looks painstakingly alive, if a little bit sad, a little bit lonely.

His fingers twitch and itch like never before. He half thinks the soft skin under his nails breaks and bleeds paint with the sheer, mere need that swells on him like water on a well.

I want, he thinks, I want, I want, I want.

“You are staring.” Khaslana mutters, a little quiet, a little weird.

“I can’t look away.” Mydei admits, freely, shamelessly. What’s the use of denying one’s desires, either way?

“Hm? What’s with you?”

“I don’t know.” Mydei exhales out and he wonders why he suddenly feels so out of breath. “It’s just that I found that I really want to paint you.”

Khaslana tilts his head, and turns to him, and there’s a moment, a small little tender moment, held between bookshelves lined like pages of a book, where Mydei looks at Khaslana and he almost looks human.

Almost6.

His eyes are so terribly empty, still.

━━━━━━━━━━

“It is fake.”

At his back, Khaslana lets out a cough.

Mydei’s eyebrow twitches.

“...Is that so?”

“Without a doubt.” Theodoros replies and Mydei doesn’t know whether he’s just rubbing salt in the wound at this point. “According to what you told me, this vase is supposed to come from the Golden Era of the Last King, and although the technique used to represent him is definitely of that era. The forging, the material, and shape of the vase are completely different.” He points at a picture of a vase in a book bigger than Mydei’s head settled on the counter. “See, vases of that era…”

Theodoros goes over step by step, pointing inaccuracies and little details, to the grand conclusion that—yes, Khaslana was right.

Infuriatingly right.

It’s a bit jarring, the knowledge that his mother was tricked, once upon a time. Though, looking back, he supposes it is the kind of story she would laugh and share about over lunch—right after beating the scammer half to death and taking back all of her money’s worth.

Maybe Mydei should do it in her stead.

“By the way, Khaslana,” Theodoros says, just, off-handedly, “Miss Demetria came by yesterday, said she found yet another batch of relics while she terrorised the tomatoes in her garden. Could you give it a look?”

“Sure.”

Mydei’s brain comes to a halt.

He turns to Khaslana.

“You work here?”

“I do.”

Mydei lets out a deep, deep breath and looks at the vase.

Theodoros gives him an apologetic look and a comforting, “He doesn’t. He just comes to help sometimes.” That, he realizes, isn’t comforting at all and instead offers him a discount on any knick-knack he might want.

A weight settles on the counter, next to him, and when he looks to Khaslana is to find him already looking back at him.

He tilts his head.

“I will see you on Saturday.”

What a prick.

━━━━━━━━━━

“He’s painting you. You are letting him paint you.”

“Don’t give me that.”

“I thought you stopped—”

“That I stopped?”

“That’s not—I just worry—”

“Don’t.”

“Khas—”

“Don’t.”

“Khaslana!”

“...”

“Khaslana, please—”

“It will be fine.”

“...You always say that.”

Sometimes, most times, Theodoros thinks, Khaslana is like cracked glass

just begging to be broken once and for all.

Chapter End Notes

FOOTNOTES

1. They had also told him things along the likes of the mother of the cousin of his sister said that the friend of the nephew of his great-great-great grandfather, that wasn’t pretty great despite having three great on his name, said that the youngest son of the friend of the woman of the store at the corner of the street was a ‘word-that-my-mom-told-me-not-to-say’ and Mydei, come aware of all the dirt of people he didn’t even know nor care of, had been hammered with questions after. When he told them he was from Castrum Kremnos, they all asked if he had any swords before starting searching for them through his boxes anyway. Back

2. He keeps saying he should fix that, but Mydei has adapted it into habit with a familiarity that suggests he probably won’t until he falls and loses a few teeth on the way down. Back

3. The rain will wipe them all out, either way, like sand castles next to the shore. The little girl with chalks is always a little bit sad when that happens, but it also means she never runs out of space to draw, and that’s pretty neat. Ah, isn’t it wonderful? To create in spite of destruction? Back

4. His pleas go unheard, of course, because people like to think they are just so damn funny. Khaslana says he should just take the paper off, Theodoros replies that it’s not him putting it up anymore. Back

5. Oh, and one wonders, one wonders! One simply has to wonder! If Mnestia was sly enough to tell Cupid to strike at that very same moment! Back

6. It’s always ‘almost’ with Khaslana, you see. Back
