chapters.title: Chapter 5: Sink! Sink! Sink!
chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

Trigger warning: Kind of (?) graphic depictions of (imagined) violence, though nothing bad actually happens to Khaslana. I don't go into that much detail, but there's mentions of Mydei wanting (curse influence) to slice Khaslana's chest open and, uh, stick his hands to check if there's something there. Better be safe than sorry, nevertheless, so if you don't want to read it, once you reach the sentence "The metal of the sharp, sharp scissors shines under the yellow light" skip all the way until a chorus of 'I want, I want, I want' in bold.

Also, emetophobia, if you don't want to read that, just skip one paragraph once you read 'Mydei’s stomach lurches'

This all sounds very omnious but don't worry guys, the fluff tag isn't there for decoration.

The answer is simple, of course.

━━━━━━━━━━

The strangest of sensations comes to befall over Mydei’s house as his last session with a statue fast approaches. Little by little, day by day, as slowly as eroding marble, decaying linen, as if everything tilted ever so slightly to

the right to dissimulate the fact the world turned upside down.

Did

you

know?

Time tock-tick-tock-tock-tock-tock-tocks like grind-grind-grinding rock, heavy, slow and appallingly grating. The dust gets under his tongue, into his

tear ducts and burns all the way into the back of his retinas—and when Saturday comes, ever so slow, and the always punctual three knock, knock, knocks dig into the terracotta bricks like cavity in a tooth, this time, they are

ever so close to striking nerve.

They say Strife’s brats are terribly prone to madness.

The red, red, red of the setting sun mixes at the far away edges with the last

vestiges of blue from the day, like watercolors running down a page, like

blood dyeing water. Yet the hands of the clock have barely reached three thirty-three. A sunset come to be far too early; as if the ever arrogant Eye of

Twilight was willing to yield time of his domain to the Veil of Night just to turn a blind eye to the silhouette of the Hand of Shadow hiding beneath the

folds of time’s dress as it looms over the horizon.

Khaslana’s face is set in marble, but his lips are picked bloody raw.

He’s much the same as last time, and the last time before that, standing at the edge of the same wobbly stone step that gives way to his house with the

same gloved hand, same empty, empty, empty, doll eyes, same all-

consuming, all-destructive allurement.

Unmoving, unchanging, eternally.

He’s all so, so still, all so empty, at the edge of Mydei’s house. His breathing is slow, his blink nonexistent, and his face doesn’t change.

Expressionless features carved out of marble.

He doesn’t offer anything, this time. No witty remarks, no cat hurting about,

not even an explanation as to why he’s so terribly late—or maybe there are,

all at once, but all the words he said were stolen by the wind, gone before

he could be heard.

It’s strange.

A second passes, and then a breath, not from Khaslana, and he says, or

more like snaps, really.

“Are you going to let me in, or what?”

What?

Mydei shakes his head, confused, willing for the static and the dust to leave

the deep crevices of his mind, and he steps aside. Khaslana walks in with steps so silent one might wonder if he’s actually walking instead of floating

as he makes his way into the art studio without even waiting for the door to

be shut.

His shoelaces are undone today, too.

Mydei says, “I told you to tie them.”

Khaslana doesn’t answer.

His brow furrows.

“...Khaslana.” Mydei calls, firmly. Khaslana halts, just so, tilts his head like a haunted doll without looking back at him, and only when Mydei is certain

the words will reach him. He—doubts, for a second, for some reason, but

still, he asks, “Are you alright?”

Khaslana doesn’t answer.

“Khaslana.”

He calls again.

Khaslana doesn’t answer.

He simply disappears around the corner of the art studio, into empty linen,

stale brushes and dripping paint.

It’s much like talking to a ghost, in that regard—or a moving statue,

perhaps.

And don’t you dare forget it.

Mydei sighs, shakes his head, again. His body feels as if submerged in water, eardrums about to burst under pressure, but he still closes the door

shut.

It closes like a casket’s lid.

Kopopo the Third gets in between his legs as Mydei follows an apparition

into his art studio, making him stumble a couple of steps, stopping him in

his tracks for barely a second and a half.

“What’s with you today?” Mydei asks him, softly, comfortingly, soothingly. Kopopo the Third lets out a mewl, long and plaintive, and he bends down to

pet him behind his ears. “It’s going to be alright.”

Another mewl. It tethers on desperate.

He has very well of an idea why. Waters lap at his throat and threaten to flood higher and higher, but Mydei has never been one to go down without

a fight—and he never once thought painting Khaslana would be easy.

He always knew it was dangerous.

“Don’t worry, I know how to swim.” He tells Kopopo the Third, scratching at the spot under his little fuzzy chin he knows his cat adores, who lets out a

purr. A little hesitant, a little dimmed, a little uncertain. “I won’t sink.”

Kopopo the Third follows after him, either way1.

Khaslana has already come to stand right in front of the easel in the middle

with the propped canvas with his image once Mydei enters the room. Silently, quietly, and it is hard to know whether to interpret his silence as

disdain or contemplation.

It still doesn’t make Mydei nervous, he’s still ever so confident in his talent,

but, for some reason, the silence makes the palms of his hands itch.

“I hate it.”

“What?”

“You heard me.”

Mydei isn’t sure what to answer, truth be told. Khaslana always gets as snippy as he gets snappy the second someone so much as thinks of painting

him. But there’s something different, this time, a little bit more pointed, a

little bit meaner.

“...Why?”

“I just do.”

Mm.

“It’s not finished yet.” Mydei reminds him.

“And will it ever?” Khaslana fires back, voice monotone.

He clicks his tongue.

“You talk as if I have already failed.”

“And you like failing is something that only happens to other people.”

“Ha! Only a fool would think they are above failure.” Mydei scoffs and

raises his chin. Khaslana tilts his head. “But, say, what kind of warrior

marches up to battle expecting nothing but defeat?”

Khaslana turns around. His empty eyes swirl and swirl by, like backwater on an empty well at night. Mydei can see his own reflection mirrored right

back at him, as if he was seeing him right past him.

“And did the warrior forget to check the time?”

“No, I remember.”

“Three sessions,” it said.

“I am not coming back.”

A pause.

“I know.”

“Ever.” Khaslana bites as he edges and tethers to disappear like smoke from

a burned bridge, like smoke from a cigarette, and, yet, in the little art room

that nestles within Mydei’s life like a heart in a ribcage, he doesn’t disappear fast enough for him not to start to rot away his lungs. “You won’t

ever see me again.”

What?

Mydei coughs.

“Why,” Another cough. The contractions of his chest feels like razor blades

slicing through his ribs up to his throat. “Why not?”

Khaslana doesn’t answer. Instead, he asks, “How do you want me?”

Mydei’s jaw tightens. “Khaslana—”

“How?”

“What’s with you today?” He snaps. “You are more…” And he halts, not exactly sure how to describe it. His arms hover in the air as if that might be enough to replace the meaning, but, when it doesn’t, he huffs and shakes his

head, almost in disbelief. “How do you say stuff like that and expect me not

to ask?”

“I expect you to paint.”

“And that’s what I will do.”

“Get it over with already then.”

“I asked you a question,” Mydei says, firmly. “And I expect an answer.”

“I will leave.” Khaslana replies, and there’s something weird in the way he

says it, kind of quiet, kind of harsh. Whether he means it as a threat or an

answer, he isn’t sure, but it shuts Mydei up immediately. “So, hurry up, Mydeimos, time hangs upon us like a guillotine—How do you want me?”

Mydei thinks about it.

“Same as last time?” The other asks.

“No.”

Khaslana’s fingers jerk, and, very pointedly, he does not look at the

painting.

“Finally decided to throw that thing away, uh.”

Mydei’s eyebrow lifts. “And when did I ever say that?” He huffs, and when

Khaslana doesn’t answer, he adds, “The pose you choose is clearly not working for me. I think it’s better to tackle this from a different angle.”

“And here I thought you were the kind of person to just bullhead through

it.”

I will show you bullheadedness, jackass, a part of Mydei itches to scoff. He

clicks his tongue instead, “Don’t change the subject.”

“Ha… How do you want me then?”

“You choose.”

Khaslana doesn’t skip a beat. “And if I choose the same pose?”

“I am painting a person, not a statue.” Mydei answers, even though the

words are not true—

A statue, a picture caught in time, a little porcelain doll to display about, a corpse.

The words taste like a lie in his mouth, rotten candy, drilling cavities.

Don’t

you

forget.

He forces himself to continue, nevertheless, forces himself to breathe.

“I am sure you can think of another position.”

“You say it as if I were stupid.” He sighs, more to himself than to Mydei, and he walks towards his place in the middle of the room. It’s only then he

realizes the other did not bring his little messenger bag with him this time.

The way Khaslana positions himself can not possibly be comfortable for him at all—In fact, it almost looks painful in nature. He sits right at the very

edge of the stool, legs extended out, making the long edges of his dark blue

gabardine fall onto the floor like tumbling cascades. He places both his hands on the leftover space behind, straining his arms to hold his weight

and not slide down onto the floor. It makes his hollow chest pop out.

Glassed doll eyes track every move, every shift, and every last breath Mydei takes like a noose about to tighten as he grabs Khaslana’s unfinished

painting from the easel with careful hands and places it gently next to a

painting of a simple bowl of ripe pomegranates.

Mydei shakes his head—It feels full of nails. The sharp edges ripping and

digging at the corners of his mind as they rattle and tremble with every

single thought he has.

He continues, nevertheless.

In one of the corners of his art studio lies a wooden bookshelf covered in little dots of different colors. On its different shelves, a dozen little teacups

without handles filled with crayons, pencils and pens, a palette knife, used brushes, scissors and paint-filled rags are scattered about. Mydei takes one of the less dirty rags and one of the few empty canvases placed on top. It

doesn’t smell new anymore.

Empty eyes bore into his back all the while.

Mydei doesn’t let it intimidate him. He places the empty canvas on the easel

and the rag on the black table next to it with practiced ease before placing

blues and whites onto the plastic palette.

He takes one of the brushes and turns to see the statue placed in his house.

Khaslana stops looking at him, then.

He throws his head back in a motion that seems almost crude, locks of snow

hair fall below his shoulders as he goes to stare at the cracks across the

ceiling that create grotesque shapes here and there.

The movement lowers the high black turtleneck he wears today down a

little, exposing the beginnings of his Adam’s apple at the center of his

throat along the edges of a bright golden sun2.

He isn’t wearing a choker today.

Mydei swallows.

He lifts the brush up to the canvas, eyes still fixated on Khaslana’s neck. It

stretches in an arc that lets him see a few lines of the faintest of blues extending like the ends of a river here and there. His skin is far too pale, is

the thing, like the rest of him is. White, nearly translucent. The gold of the

burning sun at the side contrasts nicely, but, hidden, as it is, is still not

enough, just—not enough.

Artistically, the absence of the little black band is felt, damning, maddening,

and Mydei thinks of adding colors like purple and yellow around his neck

with his bare hands to compensate.

A drop of paint falls to the floor.

Time hangs upon them like a guillotine.

And it falls at eight o’clock.

The blade comes to notice by the astringent sound of Khaslana’s phone alarm. It rings and rings and rings like a drill through the cold marble quiet

that has befallen the art studio—Yet, muffled, as it is, through the various folds of clothes, the sound seems ever so distant as Khaslana himself, as if

the ear-bleeding screech of the ring and rang was nothing but tiny, tiny

bubbles popping underwater.

Mydei doesn’t let go of the brush.

He can’t.

The painting on the easel is unfinished. All long shapes, sharp lines, and cold colors. It tethers, edges and flickers on a strange limbo between object and human, tilting slowly, ever so slowly, like a sinking boat, onto the latter.

But—

Time is the last thing he has.

Mydei breathes, breathes, and breathes again—but it doesn’t feel like any

air is quite enough to fill his lungs.

He doesn’t understand.

He just doesn’t understand.

Why can’t he paint it?

He shifts his eyes away from the ever unfinished painting of Khaslana to

the statue itself in the center of the room, just to find the depths of the black, black abyss boring into him already. Somehow, looking as if he’s

seeing past him at the same time he’s boring into his very soul.

The painting brush, with its stiff strands of dried, faded reds3, slips out of his fingers and clatters to the wooden floor with a deafening ‘clack, clack!’ that raises hauntingly above the ring and ring, ring and ring, ring and ring of the alarm. It rolls all the way down to Khaslana, colliding and stopping

against one of his untied shoes.

Khaslana’s eyes flick down to it.

When he moves from his position, a faint crack of multiple vertebrae arises,

and Mydei thinks of fissures spreading and chipping through marble. He bends down, like a puppet on strings, to pick it up. He then stands up. His

phone rings and rings, rings and rings, and he makes his way towards

Mydei.

Step

by

step

The brush is placed on the little black table at his side with a sharp ‘clack’ as the phone rings and rings, rings and rings, rings and rings, for the eternity

it takes a person to die, before it quiets down.

Silence lingers like a cavity about to strike nerve.

In the time it takes a bridge to burn, Khaslana says,

“This is the worst one yet.”

“It’s not finished.” Mydei replies. Repeats.

“I tried to warn you.” Khaslana continues, digging and digging fingers into

a bruise until it bleeds. “That there were easier ways to learn how to paint

people.”

“I know—”

“And it doesn’t mean you are any good at it.” He cuts in, cold as ice. The low yellow light of the art studio does nothing to warm his porcelain skin and his doll eyes flicker to the side, not quite looking at Mydei in the eye,

as he adds. “Especially in regard to the portraits.”

The words land like a rock in a motionless pond, shattering the tranquil surface like glass. It might have hit a fish and dyed the water red. The world

stills and time holds its breath as a loud, steady ba-thump, ba-thump, ba-

thump beats against his ears—for there is exactly only one portrait in

Mydei’s entire repertoire of work.

It is titled For Gorgo.

A portrait made for a late mother.

And, suddenly, Mydei is three again and picking up one of his mother’s brushes for the first time; and he’s fourteen and throwing all his brushes and

canvases to the trash after her death; and he’s sixteen and getting gifted a

little box of watercolors by his friends; and he’s seventeen walking away from home after his father, now mad with grief, tells him to either give up

painting or go; and he’s twenty-one moving out to Kremnos; and he’s standing in the middle of an art room failing and failing to do a statue; and

he’s both, he’s neither. He’s everything and he’s nothing, and he’s sinking,

sinking, sinking, deep underwater, not knowing how to swim from one

moment to the next.

The wooden easel tumbles down to the floor along with the painting when Mydei slams Khaslana against the wooden bookshelf. Crayons, pencils and

pens clatter to the ground as porcelain cups crash and crack and scatter in a

million little pieces down to the floor. He’s falling, and he’s drowning, and

he’s sinking, and he’s sinking, and he’s sinking. All the while, Khaslana

simply stands there.

Unmoving, unchanging, eternally.

He doesn’t even bother looking at him.

Mydei thinks of beating him raw.

The idea is stark, electrifying, far too visceral and far, far too overactive for

the situation at hand. It snaps him into realization at the same time it embraces him warmly like a second pair of teeth breaking and growing

through his gums and in the space under his tongue.

He breathes.

It’s hard to, but he breathes.

Mydei’s anger—is a sharp thing, truth be told. The sort that doesn’t exactly

go quiet but neither the sort that explodes and sweeps away everything in his path like a scorching sun. Controlled. The emotion flows, and he lets it,

but he doesn’t let it drive him. Closed fists that leave a bruise or a dozen, maybe even a scar, always towards those who deserve it, but certainly not a

corpse.

And he won’t start now.

He will.

He won’t.

The metal of the sharp, sharp scissors shines under the yellow light.

His hand tightens from where it is closed around the neck of Khaslana’s shirt; prickings of pain biting and arising from where his nails dig into his palm like teeth growing underneath his skin and he wonders if Khaslana’s own skin will yield like cloth under the blade or if it will chip like marble.

Both thoughts make his teeth, both sets, grind against each other, and he thinks he wants to drive the scissors into Khaslana’s neck and all the way

down, down, down to his stomach. The combination of bloody red and porcelain skin would complement each other nicely, he thinks, or maybe it is gold paint that would extend in the place of red like dying nebulas above

the constellations made by the little drops of paint in the floor of the art

studio.

Or maybe nothing would come out.

Khaslana’s eyes are so, so empty.

Mydei wants to rip him open in half like a ripe pomegranate and shove his hands deep inside him just to see if there’s something inside him. He wants

to slice Khaslana open all the way down to his stomach with rusty scissors and stick his own head inside the wound just to see if he even has guts and

lungs, a liver and a kidney, or if his eyes would only be met with nothing

but an empty abyss filled with dust.

And he wants to paint him like that.

I want, Mydei thinks, fingers twitching, metal shining. Khaslana is all so

distant still, I want, I want, I want.

I want, I want, I want, I want, I want, I want, I want, I want—

—To see what other things whispers and rumours fail to say about him.

That’s what drove him to wait for him on the skirts of a man-made pond in

the first place, wasn’t it?

Not the all-consuming, all-devouring, all-scorching allurement of a being

made out of incomplete strokes and rotting linen. Not the mind and bloodshot eyes gripped with the obsession of a man willing to throw himself to the sea following a siren’s song. Not the nail biting fear of a coward wishing to get rid of his obsession. But the simple sight of simple kindness gone unseen by artists that have forgotten they are no toy makers

nor morticians.

Mydei lets go of the other’s shirt to press his index and middle fingers at the

side of Khaslana’s neck, right in the center of the sun in his throat.

Ba-thump, goes his heart, ba-thump, ba-thump.

It didn’t even pick up.

“You…” Khaslana breathes out.

His exhalation is warm against Mydei’s wrist as his heart beats under his

skin.

Mydei’s stomach lurches—as if revolted by that fact.

The hand pressing gently above Khaslana’s pulse flies to clamp around his

mouth as Mydei runs away to avoid throwing up all over the floor. The heavy thump, thump, thump of his footsteps echo through the terracotta walls along the sound of the kitchen’s door being slammed open, but both

things are soon drowned by the gross, loud splat of bile mixed with half-

digested chicken spreading through the metal sink like thick petroleum

falling from his mouth.

He heaves, reaches, swallows, and breathes.

For a second, Mydei simply breathes.

The light of the kitchen flicks on with a quiet ‘click.’

Mydei breathes a couple of times more, sweat sliding down his face. He opens the water faucet and cleans his face, the coldness refreshing against

his heated skin, before he rinses his mouth once to get rid of the taste

lingering on the spaces where a second row of teeth used to be.

A minute passes.

Then two.

Then three.

Maybe even four.

“What are you?”

“...That which you see,” He replies, quietly. “Is me.”

He turns around. Khaslana lets his head fall like a man hanging from a

noose.

“What I see?”

“Nothing more and nothing less.” He says, and something about that answer

angers him, for some reason, but before Mydei can answer, he adds, “And it

seems what you see is nothing but defeat.”

Mydei’s eyes narrow. “Defeat?”

“It means is your loss, Mydeimos.”

“Ha…” Mydei exhales, jaw tightening. There’s still fire licking at the back of his throat and ants biting at the tips of his fingertips—and every single of

Khaslana’s words only serve to burn him hotter. “Fine. You win. I can’t

paint you. That’s what you wanted to hear?”

“It’s what I knew I would.”

He doesn’t even sound resigned.

“Would you stop,” Mydei bites out, turning around and slamming open one

of the cabinets to take out a notebook and a pen from in between the forks

and the knives. “Assuming you know how everything is going to be for

once?”

“What,” Khaslana starts, falters. “What are you even doing?”

“I’m drawing your stupid face.”

“...Come again?”

The sound of paper being ripped off is deafening. It even shuts up Kopopo’s

the Third low hiss that Mydei hadn’t registered until now. “Here,” He says,

sharply, walking up to Khaslana and extending what is probably the worst

doodle that Mydei has ever made in his life; all scruffy lines and unflattering lines with a big ‘STUPID’ written and underlined under it. It’s

simple, childish, and terribly petty—but he supposes is far better than smashing Khaslana’s head open against the counter. “This is how I see

you.”

“...Did you hit your head on the way—?”

“I sure wish I did.”

“What.”

“Just grab it!”

Khaslana stares.

Mydei shakes the paper impatiently.

Khaslana’s head turns to the side, as if debating whether to just go, before it

turns back to Mydei. Empty eyes flicker from his face, down to the paper, and to his face once again before a gloved hand, in almost hesitant motions,

plucks the paper from Mydei’s fingers without once breaking eye contact

with him.

There’s a pause before his eyes flicker down to the little doodle.

Humanity lies in mundanity.

And he laughs.

Khaslana laughs.

It’s not the quiet, refined laughter one might come to expect from someone like Khaslana, but a bright, loud thing, almost childish in its nature. The sort of sound that might very well light-up entire rooms with its presence even if there’s ash sticking to his tongue and cobwebs in his throat. He even does that little snort people always get embarrassed about—and Khaslana does too because one hand goes to cover his mouth once he lets it out.

Mydei’s heart feels as if it is about to burst out of his chest for some inexplicable, strange reason.

“This,” Khaslana says. There’s still remnants of laughter sticking into the corners of his tiny, tiny smile. “Might be your best work yet.”

“Yeah?” Mydei exhales, feeling as if he had just ran a marathon three times over and come out in first place. He clears his throat. “Yeah, well, I might just present that at tomorrow’s exposition, then.” He says and attempts to take the little doodle back. Khaslana moves it out of reach. “Give it back.”

“No.” Khaslana replies, lifting it higher. Mydei comes to the horrifying realization he’s a few centimeters shorter than the other. “You gave it to me, that means it’s mine.”

What a childish response. “Tsk, you are ridiculous.”

“I am ridiculous? You are the one that decided to do something like this after…” The smile falls. “Whatever, just draw another one if you like it so much.”

“You know what? Maybe I will.” Mydei raises his chin.

Khaslana huffs. “Really, now.” He says, not sounding as if he really believes him, as he turns around, doodle still in hand. “I suppose I might just drop in on the Irontomb’s exhibition on Monday, then4.”

Mydei watches him go, follows and stands at the edge of his home as Khaslana walks out the door without further word into a car with a green-haired man, who first inspects Khaslana head-to-toe and glowers at Mydei before driving off.

He closes the door. Then, he takes one step back, two, his heart thumps widely in his chest, laughter echoes in his ears and he all but runs back into the art studio. It’s a mess of scattered paint, scattered crayons and broken cups but he couldn’t care less about that right now.

Khaslana is alive.

Painstakingly, terrifyingly alive, with all the flaws and wonders that entails.

He doesn’t bother reassembling the easel back up. He simply grabs a bunch of colors and a bunch of brushes before he kneels down to paint on the canvas right there on the floor, feeling much like a child playing with chalks, as he starts painting the image of Khaslana laughing right over a statue. White skin blushed pink, white hair falling over his eyes, and his eyes are empty, empty, empty, still.

But,

Maybe that’s alright.

That’s alright.

The details of the image escape him. He doesn’t remember if Khaslana had any dimples or not, if his eyes crinkled at the sides, if his nose scrunched, if his teeth showed, and if, and if, and if—and it would be easy, frankly, to curse and hate the time-consuming nature of painting and drawing over the instant instance the snap of a photo provides.

But that’s the last thing on Mydei’s mind.

The things he doesn’t remember he simply fills with sentiments like yellows and oranges and warm, warm colors. It’s amazing, how every brush and every stroke and every pigment makes a picture slowly come together. There are butterflies coming out of his mouth with every breath he exhales and there are galaxies forming on the floor with every drop of paint that falls, and he’s having so, so much fun.

Because he likes painting.

He really, really likes painting.

His loss?

Ha!

Just you wait, Khaslana, just you wait.

Chapter End Notes

FOOTNOTES

1. He has plenty of trust in his owner, of course, but it is the strange entity that bleeds paint that he remains wary of. He is dan-ge-rous, like poisoned cheese he has seen little stupid mice fall for—Still, Kopopo the Third knows not everybody is as smart (and cute) as him; and he knows he’s but a little cat, so he can’t do much to stave off the water, but if his owner sinks, then down the well he goes too, no matter how much he might dislike bathing. Back

2. “The sun is set to die,” Is what the Ruin Author had answered once Khaslana demanded to know why he wanted to paint him, dipping a brush into gold. “Billions of years from now, it will run out of hydrogen and it will collapse in on itself—But it won’t go quietly. It will expand, and it will burn, and it will destroy everything close to it.” Their eyes settled on his neck, on the tattoo he had got to commemorate the sister he lost. Under their gaze, Khaslana had wanted to dig his nails into it and rip it right off. “Much like your whole existence does, Khaslana. You only exist to burn.” Back

3. Which is strange, because Mydei doesn’t remember ever putting red on the palette. Back

4. Khaslana knows better than to want, and much less hope, but there’s a tiny little part of him that needs to see what Mydei presents in that stupid art competition. Whether it be yet another empty stand, whether it be yet another grotesque rendition of his, he just—he just has to see it. Back

━━━━━━━━━━

EXTRA

Sometimes, most times, Khaslana is like cracked glass just pleading to be broken.

Theodoros can’t help but worry, yet, knowful of the fact his friend won’t listen to him, that day, he writes an e-mail starting with a polite good morning, Professor Anaxa, I hope this message finds you well— For he’s too intimidated to write to one Miss Aglaea and, he figures, if

there’s someone Khaslana ought to listen to, it must be the professor he so much respects.

It’s a tad bit too formal, a tad bit too nerve wracking, and a tad bit too stupid to write to a professor with far more doctorates than years Theodoros has about an ex-student of his who will go model for a painter, but he does so, anyways, because someone has to reach out when Khaslana won’t—Yet he still all but begs him not to shoot him with his gun. Anaxa replies with a simple ‘thank you for letting me know, also, it’s Anaxagoras’ and no promises about the shooting thing.

That day, Anaxa sends a text to that problematic student of his, uncaring that the last he sent went unanswered, that reads ‘call me if you need anything’ and nothing else. Khaslana ignores him for the whole week. Yet, when the day of the awaited third session arrives, he texts back a deceptively unassuming ‘I should be out by eight’ followed by a direction that, should Mydei been a lesser man, a weaker one, it might well have carried a life.

He regrets it immediately.

He deletes the messages but Anaxa replies with a simple ‘I’ll be there’ and, suddenly, Khaslana is both terribly young and terribly stupid once again—sitting on Hyacine’s kitchen with paint sticking to his hair, blood under his nails and purple bruises on his neck, half-wishing he had gone limp under that artist’s grip. Because, then, Anaxa wouldn’t have had to pick him up at two in the morning from a deserted bus stop. Then, he wouldn’t be bothering Hyacine on the night before her thesis. Then, they both wouldn’t be wasting time on rotten, incomplete work.

Again.

He texts back a ‘sorry’ before putting his phone in his pocket. A couple of years older he may be but he doesn’t love himself even a little bit more than he didn’t used to before and he knocks on Mydei’s door.

Like glass begging to be broken.

chapters.title: Chapter 6: Land in sight
chapters.html:
Khaslana’s painting comes to completion much the same way the change of Saturday to Sunday comes, quiet and unceremonial as the twenty-three fifty-nine in his phone changes to a cero cero cero cero while Mydei gives one last feather-light brush against Khaslana’s lips. All bitten and picked bloody raw. An ugly sight one would rather leave out for the sake of beauty, and yet, painted with a gentleness that would make you think Mydei was trying to soothe the faint ardor that must accompany the little self-inflicted wounds.

There’s no big shift in the world as he does so. No big burst of energy nor light. Time doesn’t start to go backwards before going forwards and then backwards once again. Neither is there a small shift. A mirror doesn’t shatter, a bracelet of pearl beads doesn’t break, a can of sardines doesn’t explode, a thread doesn’t snap.

Mydei simply looks at the painting in that strange space of time after yesterday is done but tomorrow hasn’t come, brush raised high and stares at the strokes of paint that compose a man laughing along the tiny little dots of colors that fell here and there like constellations, and before another drop can fall, he nods and places the wooden brush in the ceramic cup without a handle with a quiet ‘splash’.

And just like that, it is done.

His spine cracks with a bunch of little pops like plastic bubble wrap being stepped on as he stands up. He picks up the painting, careful not to touch the paint yet to dry, and puts it on the black table at his side. In familiar movements, he resembles back the easel, places Khaslana’s painting on it with care, and, after one last look and a prominent sense of victory, he flicks the light of the art studio off, closes the door and goes to his room.

In well-known motions, Mydei un-tucks the covers of his bed, takes off his shirt, but doesn’t bother to change into a set of pajama pants as he lets himself fall onto the soft mattress with a groan of satisfaction.

A little weight settles on his back, and Mydei hisses when tiny little claws dig into him as his skin is kneaded. His muffled reprimand of ‘stop that’ is dutifully noted but haughtily ignored until Kopopo the Third is satisfied by the now irritated hue of his skin and gives two circles before settling down. Like a tiny, silent protector.

Mydei sighs, a little fond, “You worry too much.”

Kopopo the Third mewls. A little long-suffering. Mydei twists an arm behind his back and pets him once before closing his eyes.

He sleeps1.

━━━━━━━━━━

A solid, healthy lifestyle must require a man to know that rest is as important as working and training.

On Sundays, Mydei doesn’t go to the gym, so when his internal clock honed through years upon years of routine and self-discipline wakes him up at exactly six in the morning, he lets his eyelids close again. He sleeps until the late, late hour of eight AM, not because he feels as if he particularly deserves it, but simply because he just feels like it—and sometimes that’s all the reasoning a person needs.

Once he wakes up, he stretches, goes to the bathroom and down to the kitchen. One of the hinges of the door is busted from where he slammed it open yesterday night, Mydei realizes, and makes a note to fix it later2. He serves Kopopo the Third his food and some water, tells him not to sink a paw into it, and sighs when his cat sinks both paws as he cooks breakfast. Something simple, really, some eggs with beans and two fried bananas with cream and sugar. He doesn’t drink coffee, so he makes himself a vegetable smoothie.

The strange, almost floaty sensation one gets after walking home after a concert or going to the movies late in the evening and coming out at night, waking through a mall that’s coming to a close, fills Mydei as he goes to the motions of his routine, almost uncanny in its mundanity; but he doesn’t let it unnerve him. He finishes breakfast, washes the dishes and the pan because if he doesn’t do it now, he then gets lazy. Afterwards, he goes back up to the bathroom to take a warm shower.

There are dots of paint scattered through his skin like freckles.

He showers, changes and doesn’t bother to dry his hair as he braids it. His mother would be livid. Throughout all this, the clock on his night table changes number by number from eight to nine. He’s not in any real hurry. Though, it was said for contestants to be there at nine thirty, so he will have to take the car instead of walking. He will have to pass by an ATM machine too, because the parking lot of the plaza only ever accepts cash for their overpriced space—But it’s either that or risking parking outside and having someone stealing your car or the police asking for a bribe if you don’t want a fine.

The painting is right where he left it, and just the same as he left it. Mydei grabs it with careful hands and, right before he leaves, he takes one look at the other painting of Khaslana he left leaning on the wall.

The difference is stark, almost sad, the image of a figure sitting on a stool like a lonely doll left sitting on a shelf contrasted to the laughing man in his arms.

Maybe he will fix it, later, or maybe he won’t. He certainly won’t throw it away because that just seems unnecessarily cruel.

So, he leaves it there, in the art studio nestled in his life like a heart in a ribcage as he closes the door. He tells Kopopo the Third very firmly not to destroy the house while he’s out and takes the keys of his car.

The plaza is as crowded as one would expect for a Sunday, families and friends and couples walking and laughing around lo and about, and it takes ten minutes for him to find a spot to park. Similarly, The Irontomb is crowded and full of people with canvases under their arms, like sardines in a can about to explode. The ambient is loud, voices overlapping one over another. The air is hot, humid and sweaty with way too many elbows digging into sides and shoulders bumping into each other.

Mydei takes one step inside, takes it all in, and immediately steps out.

What a nightmare, he breathes, and promptly decides to wait outside for the line to go down instead. Whether he gives his piece now or later doesn’t change much, maybe the chance to get a good spot in whatever place they shall put all the art.

But, that’s alright, there’s only one person Mydei is really looking forward to seeing his painting—and he isn’t even coming in today.

A few more people are of the same idea as him, laying and waiting on the outskirts of The Irontomb, which makes it difficult to find a good spot to sit that isn’t directly under the heated rays of the sun.

“Mydei?”

The call is soft, shy, almost lost in the hustle and bustle of the place. He stops walking, intent on maybe going to some cafe with air conditioning and coming back in an hour, and turns his head around in the direction of the voice, just to find a girl in a wheelchair under the shadow of a wall.

“Oh, Polyxia.” He greets back, walking up to her. “It’s good to see you. How have you been?”

Polyxia makes a motion for him to sit next to her, which Mydei complies with, laying the canvas on his lap. “Far better than last time, enough to— Oh, thank you.” She giggles, taking some peanuts with salt and lemon from the little plastic bag Mydei tilts towards her in silent offering. He bought them from the haggard old man who throws tomatoes at the cathedral. “Enough to pick a brush without trembling.”

Mydei smiles at her. “I’m glad to hear that. Who did you paint?”

“My sister.” She replies, taking the canvas reclined next to the wheel of her wheelchair and showing it to him. It’s a very pretty thing, gentle and elegant, showing a girl nearly identical to Polyxia tending with care to flowers in a garden in an array of watercolors. “She was the one who suggested that I participate.”

“A good suggestion—It’s beautiful.”

“Thank you.” Polyxia smiles, brimming with both shyness and pride. “What about you?”

Instead of answering, Mydei simply turns his painting over to her. Polyxia blinks, confused, before a look of realization passes through her face and she gapes. “Isn’t—Isn’t that Khaslana?”

“Mm.”

“That’s—That’s. Wasn’t it impossible?” Polyxia says, at a loss of words. She turns from the painting, to Mydei, to the painting and back to Mydei before blurting, “You don’t seem mad.” Before covering her mouth with a hand. “Ah, sorry, I didn’t mean… I just…”

“It’s fine, Polyxia.” He reassures her. Polyxia winces, nevertheless, so, he continues, “He is hard to paint, I won’t lie, and it certainly was,” He halts, searching for a word that might describe all that was and wasn’t with Khaslana, but coming up short, he settles on a rather lackluster, “Challenging.”

“...I think you are the only person who would describe painting Khaslana as merely challenging.”

“Maybe.”

“Are you alright? I have heard some stories…”

“I am, but thank you for worrying.”

Polyxia looks at him for a minute longer, probably weighing just how truthful he’s being, before she nods. Her lavender eyes go back to the painting, then, in almost childish wonder, she says, “He kind of looks like my sister’s friend.” She frowns. “No, wait, I think he is.”

“What?”

“My sister, Castorice, she has—or had? I am not entirely sure. She gets sad whenever someone mentions him.” She pauses, shakes her head, and continues. “She has this scrapbook with photos of her friends and he, well, I think Khaslana shows up in some of them.”

Mydei blinks, blinks, and blinks again. Not entirely sure what to say nor how to react. He opens his mouth, but the soft ‘clack, clack, clack’ of heels interrupts him, and he turns to see a girl nearly identical to Polyxia, Castorice, walking up to them with two bags of cotton candy, both lavender.

The purple gloves with butterflies in her hands are identical to the one Khaslana uses.

“Oh, hey, Cas, you are back.” Polyxia smiles, making a motion to him. “This is Mydei, from that coffee painting activity I told you about a while ago, remember?”

“I remember.” Castorice nods, extending one of the bags towards her, and turns to him. “Thank you for taking care of her. She can be a little shy, sometimes.” She says, and smiles at Polyxia’s grumbled ‘Don’t pretend you aren’t shy too’. “I’m Castorice. It’s a pleasure to meet you.”

“Likewise. Polyxia has spoken lots about you.”

“Only good things, I hope?”

“Only good things, yes. You seem like a very kind person.”

Castorice blinks, and flushes a little, “Hehe, is that so? Thank you.” She chuckles. “Polyxia has mentioned you are a very good artist. I would like to see what did you paint, if it’s not a bother.”

Mydei shakes his head and turns the painting towards her.

Castorice’s eyes widen and she lets out a breathless, almost shaky, “Oh.”

Gently, Polyxia asks, “…Isn’t that your friend?”

“My best friend.” Castorice replies, firmly, but her expression shatters like glass when she adds, “Though, I wonder if he even considers me as such anymore.”

“He still wears it.”

Castorice blinks. “What?”

“The glove.” Mydei adds, plucking his lips a little to point with his mouth at the ones in Castorice’s hands. Her eyes widen. “There hasn’t been a time that I haven’t seen him wear it.”

“...Oh.” She lets out, absentmindedly coming to toy with the hem of the purple fabric. She swallows. “Is it finished?” She asks, looking as if she’s dreading the answer.

“It is.”

“It is?”

“It is.”

Castorice stares at him as if she can’t quite believe what she’s hearing. Mydei holds her gaze, unshakeable and certain, leaving no room for doubt, and, after a long stretch where silence stretches, expands and melts, her eyes soften. Tension he hadn’t quite realized sweeping out of her like steam.

“What is it called?”

A name. Mydei hadn’t thought about a name, but the answer comes all too natural as he tells her, “Khaslana.”

“Just Khaslana?”

“Just Khaslana.”

Castorice blinks, and then smiles, relieved. “Fitting.” She says and turns to the painting, eyes trailing through the strokes of paint, the smile on Khaslana’s face and a quiet melancholy, more painful than outright sadness, washes over her eyes3. “...How is he?”

Mydei opens his mouth to answer—and hesitates.

Castorice’s eyes soften. “I see.” She doesn’t sound surprised. “I thought so.”

“...Cas.” Polyxia breathes, putting a hand on her sister’s arm, in silent support. Castorice puts a hand over hers, accepting, before shaking her head and turning back to Mydei once again.

“When,” Castorice starts, hesitates, and then amends, “If you ever see him again, whenever you think is right… could you please tell him that I’m glad he’s alive?”

━━━━━━━━━━

It takes about two hours and a half for the line inside The Irontomb to shorten and another half hour before they are able to give their paintings. Time Mydei spends chatting about simple little nothings that create an everything with both of the girls.

Castorice, turns out, is as pleasant company as Polyxia is, and every bit as kind, if not more, as her sister made her out to be. She’s a botanist, though most people first guess she’s an entomologist with her fascination towards butterflies, and she also writes as a side hobby. She’s a little embarrassed to admit that last part, but still promises to send him a copy of her last book The Princess and The Cat once she realizes he has already read a book of hers, a story about bugs with a name he can’t quite pronounce.

They go for lunch, afterwards, because none of them have anything to do and spending so much time under the sun is a good way to get an appetite; and, after they say their respective goodbyes, Mydei goes back to The Irontomb, simply out of curiosity towards the other paintings displayed.

He first goes through the children’s section, because there’s always so terribly charming about the innocence of crooked lines and disproportionate limbs. There are mothers and there are fathers, grandmothers and grandfathers, big sisters and little brothers, friends and superheroes, made in acrylics, pencils, crayons and a notable drawing of a long suffering woman shoved in a dinosaur costume made with chalks in a little black board called Dinosour Mum! whose author simply reads ‘Me’. He has a good idea of who the last one belongs to.

The adult section, in comparison, is a little less charming with all too realistic figures, but not less significant because of that, because here, too, are mothers and fathers, grandmothers and grandfathers, big sisters and little brothers, friends and lovers, with titles like Mother Dearest, Nagging Old Man, Half of My Soul, You Still Owe Me Twenty Dollars and For you, up in the clouds.

One particular sketch on paper, made with organic cycles and organic compounds like glutamine, proline, cysteine, asparagine and the like composing a woman with flowers in her hair and a needle on hand titled Unwanted Oxytocin4, catches his attention for its peculiarity and refuses to let it go for about twenty whole minutes.

Through it all, there’s no burning urge nor electrifying need to go see Thus Burns the Dawn, but there’s no aversion to it either. Mydei half-thinks of going, but it’s a decision that never comes to a head, for a piece of it follows him instead.

“Excuse me, Mydeimos, is it?”

For there’s an Antikytheran gazing upon Khaslana.

Mydei turns his head away from Polyxia’s On the Garden towards the other, standing a couple of paintings away from him. He debates, for a second, whether to answer him, but, ultimately, he answers, “It is.” Before asking, “And you are?”

“Lyugs. The Irontomb’s curator.” He says, and something about the name rings an ever so distant bell. He places a hand above the hollow space in his chest and bows. “It is a pleasure to make an acquaintance with you.”

“...Likewise.” Mydei replies, out of mere courtesy, and walks up next to him to not have to half-shout just to answer. “What do you want?”

“How straightforward, but rest assured I just wish to talk.” He chuckles. “After all, there’s only so many people that have managed to portray the impossible—and the Ruin Author is a terrible conversationalist.”

It clicks. “You are the one who painted Thus Burns the Dawn.”

Lygus smiles.

“Beautiful thing, isn’t it? My Magnum Opus. It took many months to finish and I must admit, I was a little preoccupied when I decided to put it on display. After all, how terribly pretentious of a curator to put their own work in their own gallery alongside artists like,” His lips curl. “Nous.” A pause. “But, in the end, I thought it would be a waste to let such masterpiece gather dust in some studio—Ah, but, of course, the credit can’t be all mine.” He continues and Mydei would think he’s fishing for compliments, were his pride not be evident in his voice. “It wouldn’t have come half as good as it did were it not for my muse.”

Lygus laughs, then, and doesn’t give a chance for Mydei to answer as he adds, a little fond, a little patronizing. “But, of course, he would throw a fit if he were to hear me call him that—He has always been terribly unpleasant to work with. Don’t you think?” He asks, but doesn’t let Mydei reply as he turns to Khaslana. “In fact, I am most surprised he let you paint him at all. I thought he had stopped ever since that fit of his from two years ago.”

Mydei frowns and, pointedly, refuses to use the word fit.

“What do you mean?”

“You know,” Lygus says, almost off-handedly, lifting his left hand, the same one Khaslana keeps covered with a glove at all times. “The whole Nanook thing.” He lowers his hand and taps his chin. “But, I suppose he just can’t help himself to go asking for it.”

Something churns in Mydei’s stomach at his words. “Ask for it? Do you seriously expect me to believe Khaslana sincerely wants to, what, be hurt, killed?”

“Ah, so you felt it, too—Yet, you still go and interpret him with such gentle strokes… It is certainly a choice.”

Mydei clicks his tongue. “I could say the same about your interpretation of his.”

“It’s not an interpretation. It’s, objectively, who he is.”

Broken, hollow and empty, goes unsaid.

“Objectively, you say.” Mydei’s eyes narrow. “Ha! How terribly pretentious.”

Lygus chuckles and shakes his head.

He doesn’t bother to refute Mydei’s claim, as if it was obvious why he was wrong.

Instead, he says, almost as if monologuing, “I am sure you have heard people compare Khaslana to a corpse in the ocean, with the wish to paint it sinking and swallowing you whole. I understand the appeal of such morbid descriptions, of course, but I disagree. The allure of Khaslana…” He sighs. “It’s like watching a dying star. Burning bright, dying bright—To not capture such beautiful, self-destructive end, it would only be a waste.” He turns to Khaslana. “Say, will he come?”

Tiny little ants bite and crawl under his skin with the way the curator’s tongue curls around the words, and a heavy, thick sensation spreads over him like viscous molasses trickling ever so agonizingly slow down his bare spine.

Cold, jarring and disgusting.

“No.” Mydei lies. “He won’t.”

“Hm, as I expected. He was never one for art.” He nods, and briefly, Mydei remembers a quiet, melancholic ‘why wouldn’t I?’ muttered like a secret not meant to be heard on that far, faraway first session. “Much less for creation.”

Mydei doesn’t reply.

He simply wonders, for the first time ever since he first saw it, if Thus Burns the Dawn is as complete as it presents itself to be.

━━━━━━━━━━

The Irontomb is quiet, Monday come, almost deserted if not for the few guards standing on the sides and the reception man who asks him for a synonym for warmth as he racks his brain upon yet another crossword. His steps against the porcelain floor bouncing off the metal walls with a plam, plam, plam.

The time on his phone reads ten eleven in the morning, a little early, maybe, for the beginning of the week, but when his eyes had opened at exactly six in the morning, a strange fluttering sensation on Mydei’s stomach5 had all but forced him to start to get ready early. Besides, Khaslana hadn’t said at what time he would drop by, and his reaction is not one Mydei wants to miss.

Plam, plam, plam echo his steps as he makes his way through the children’s section, before quieting down as he reaches the adult’s. Unwilling to disturb the silence of the big salon, unwilling to disturb whoever might be inside.

Unwilling to disturb Khaslana, standing all so very still, all so very motionless, as he stares at his painting placed at the far away end of the room.

Mydei watches him for a minute or two, maybe three, wonders how long he has been standing there, and when his stillness starts to reminisce far too much that of a statue, he walks towards him. Steps soft, but not silent, resounding in the big, empty room save for them too, but not heavy enough to echo, not heavy enough to disturb, until he is close enough to feel the warmth radiating off his skin.

A second passes.

Or maybe a lifetime.

Until Mydei turns to him and, as a mirror, a victory, a promise and a reassurance, all and neither at the same time, as something that edges on something unmistakable theirs, and only theirs, he simply says, “It’s your loss, Khaslana.”

Khaslana’s head turns to him before his eyes do, and the look on his face is nothing short of incredulous, maybe even awed. His mouth is parted and his blue lightless eyes are wide, wide open, and, for the first time ever since they met, he looks present—here, as if he had stepped out of that strange thread of nonexistence he always threatened to vanish like seafoam at night.

And, for the first time, for the very first time ever since they met, as his blue eyes meet golden ones, it doesn’t feel as if his gaze goes so very deep into his soul he misses the bigger picture, and neither does it feel as if he’s seeing right past him, but, instead, it feels as if Khaslana’s eyes settle to simply see Mydei.

He breathes out, and it’s a wonder how a million butterflies don’t come out.

“You…” Khaslana starts, halts and swallows. “You are so arrogant.” He tries, but it sounds as if he’s trying not to topple over, to take back lost ground. Mydei grins, and Khaslana’s nose scrunches. “I never once said I liked it, you know.”

“Didn’t you?” Mydei’s grin gets bigger. “Say it, then.”

“Say what?”

“That you don’t like it.”

“Have you ever been told just how arrogant you are?”

By Khaslana? Plenty. Even just now. But it’s not arrogance, not really, just an unshakable self-assurance as far as Mydei is concerned, though, he understands how that could be misinterpreted as any other thing—Not that he cares, and, besides, that’s not what he wants to hear.

“You are still not saying it.”

Khaslana’s eyes narrow.

“I—” He starts, tries, closes his eyes, and sighs. “I am not that unfair of a person.”

“You like it.” Mydei says, still grinning. Khaslana’s mouth presses. “Say it.”

Khaslana breathes, but, “...I like it.” He admits, almost defeated, and then, as if he can’t quite believe himself, “Kephale above, I like it. I really do.”

And Mydei can’t help but laugh and laugh and laugh with his whole chest while his heart ba-thump-thump-thump’s so widely and so frantically it feels as if it might burst out of him any second now and fall right into Khaslana’s hands.

“It’s not funny.” He mumbles, coming to cover his face with his hand. The tips of his ears are red. Mydei laughs harder. “Titans, you are the worst kind of winner.”

“Heh, won’t you allow a man to relinquish the spoils of his victory?”

“You look as if you will relinquish whether I let you or not.”

He’s not wrong, especially because, “You certainly didn’t make it easy.”

A pause.

“No.” Khaslana admits, breathes. “I did not, and, yet,” His hand falls and he turns back to the painting. “I don’t understand.”

“I just painted.”

“You make it sound so simple.”

“It is simple.”

“It’s not. I didn’t even know I could be seen this way anymore6, and you just… do.” His eyes shift to him. “How?”

How, he asks. How does one answer that? “I don’t know.” Khaslana’s lips press in a thin, thin line. “I just painted what I saw that night.” He repeats.

Khaslana scoffs.

“You looked like you wanted to hit me.”

“I wanted to do a lot worse.” He admits easily, because deflection is for cowards and repression a vice. “How’s your head?”

The other blinks. “My head?”

“I slammed you pretty hard against the bookshelf.”

Khaslana touches the back of it7 before he replies, “I’m fine.”

“Really?”

“Yes, tsk, I’m not made out of porcelain, you know.” Khaslana bites and immediately winces, as if he hadn’t meant to say that out loud.

Mydei’s eyebrows fly to his hair. So, that’s how it is. “Pisses you off, doesn’t it?”

“No.” He replies a tad too quickly. He’s an awful liar.

“Really.”

“It’s not like I can change how others see me.” He snaps. “What use is there in getting mad about it?”

“Sounds exhausting.”

“I’m used to it.”

Mydei stares at him for a while.

“Skin bleeds, though.”

“Is that your way of saying you worry you hurt me?” Khaslana asks, a little sardonic. But before Mydei can answer yes, he adds, firmly. “Don’t. It’s fine. I have had worse.”

“You do realize that’s not comforting in the slightest?”

He shrugs. “Not everybody has your self-restraint.”

“You do realize,” Mydei repeats, slowly. “That’s not comforting in the slightest?”

Khaslana doesn’t reply.

Mydei sighs.

“I’m sorry—for all it’s worth.”

Khaslana opens his mouth, closes it and swallows. “You are so very strange.”

The Irontomb is a building without any windows, so the light that envelops them it’s the wholly artificial yellows of the ostentatious chandelier on the very top of the room. It’s a wonder, then, just how much time passes between the growing silence. Hours, minutes, years, the day might have died and given way to the night over and over as their little bubble remains unperturbed—even when Khaslana speaks again, it doesn’t pop.

Because the words are only meant for Mydei to hear.

“Mydeimos,”

“Mydei.” He interrupts. There haven't been many instances of Khaslana using his name, if ever, he comes to realize. “Just Mydei.”

Khaslana pauses, and, almost hesitantly, he amends. “Mydei.” He turns to him. “...Now what?”

Now what, indeed.

He knows Khaslana never once thought there could even be an after, and Mydei, well, he’s not the type of person one would describe to live in the moment, because he always knows there’s a tomorrow, but he’s also not the sort of person not to forget there is a today, a now. So, he hadn’t come to stop to think what would happen after he painted Khaslana.

But, now, as he stops to dwell on it, the answer comes all too easy, because Mydei only paints what he wants.

“I would like to keep painting you.”

“...Even now?”

“Even now.”

“If I say no?”

“Then I won’t.”

Khaslana breathes, a little shaky—and he doesn’t look breakable, because he’s not made out of glass and he doesn’t look fickle, because he’s not a flame either. He looks vulnerable, just like any person would.

“Just like that?”

“Just like that.”

“I’m sure you could find any other model.”

“I don’t want another model.” Mydei replies, with a firmness that surprises even him. “It’s—Either you, or giving up the rest of the entries of the competition.”

Khaslana looks at him. “You don’t care about this competition, do you?”

“Neither do you.”

But it’s a good excuse as any, for both of them. Khaslana knows this as well as he does, because instead of answering to the accusation, he instead blurts, out of the blue, “Do you want my number?”

He gives it to him, and once Mydei’s phone has a new contact simply saved as ‘Khaslana’, he texts him a ‘hey’ for him to have his number too. It’s simple, innocuous, but his phone chimes immediately, and his eyes lower to see an equally simple ‘hi’ texted back at him.

Mydei breathes, butterflies don’t come out, but they sure feel stuck in his throat as he turns his eyes to Khaslana, who is watching him already, mouth hidden behind his phone.

“Hey.” Mydei calls.

“Hi.” Khaslana replies.

As if seeing each other for the first time.

Chapter End Notes

FOOTNOTES

1. Kopopo the Third, for his part, waits for about an hour, simply feeling the rise and fall of his owner’s chest, and only once he’s sure there’s no strange entities of paint attempting to sink his owner in his dreams is that he falls asleep—No, it’s not that he worries, he would tell, a little embarrassed, in the off-chance you spoke cat and were to ask him. It’s only that his mother, Kopopo the Second, Gorgo’s cat, would be livid from beyond the grave if he let anything happen to her human ward. Besides, who would give him pets and treats if something happens to him? But you don’t speak cat, so you can’t ask. Back

2. Much like he says he will fix the wobbly step. Back

3. She doesn’t quite remember what his laugh sounded like, she comes to realize. Back

4. Much like the little girl with chalks, the author is simply listed as ‘Me’, and it will be the first and last piece they give in the competition. Seeing that there’s no return address nor any way to contact the artist, the gallery sends the sketch to the residence of the woman depicted in the drawing. Aglaea scoffs at it, says something about ridiculousness and that fool of a man, but she’s all so gentle as she grabs it and keeps it—Tribios sends a text saying, ‘You could have just given it to her, you know’, to which she’s answered with a curt, ‘I don’t know what you are talking about.’ She laughs and asks if he doesn’t want to know if she liked it, he answers, ‘I know she did.’ Back

5. Once, he remembers being told, as one of those facts drawn on air to unnerve someone, that, on average, people eat about eight or six spiders in their sleep per year. He had never believed that, but that morning he couldn’t help but wonder if whoever told him that as a child got it wrong, and they meant to say butterflies, or moths, or bees —or any other winged insect that might explain the strange sensation bubbling in his stomach. Back

6. If you were to ask Khaslana—He wouldn’t answer you, not really, but in the quiet of his room, he would admit to the empty space he didn’t think he was even capable of laughing anymore. Back

7. It's a little tender. Back
