chapters.title: Chapter 7: Reaching shore
chapters.html:
The little grains that constitute the ever eternal and ever ephemeral sands of time fall, or maybe rise, one by one, in the hourglass that, pretentiously, humans call reality. Silent, as always, abstractly and tangibly, yet, inside the four terracotta walls that enclose dripping paint and colored linen, the slow, yet fast, trick-trick-trickle of time can almost be felt as Khaslana picks, picks, picks at his bottom lip.

For a while, brush in hand, Mydei simply watches.

It’s not obvious, at first glance. In fact, he is almost professional in how he tries not to let it show in his posture. But his back is held so upright it feels as if his spine might snap in two at any second now and he just can’t seem to stop pick-pick-picking at his bottom lip.

It’s strange, edging on uncanny, if for the way he always looked so dimmed, em—pty, in the earlier sessions.

Mydei thinks about it, for less than a second, and, before the other can dig so deep he tears at his skin, he sets the brush into the black table at his side with a faint ‘clack’.

Khaslana’s eyes shift to him.

“Let’s take a break.”

Khaslana’s brow furrows, in confusion, hand still hovering over his lips.

“It hasn’t even been thirty minutes.”

It hasn’t even been twenty.

Mydei shrugs.

“Have you eaten?” He asks. A shake of head is his reply. Mydei stands up. One of his vertebrae lets out a little ‘pop!’ as he stretches before making a motion for Khaslana to come with him. “Good. I still owe you a meal.”

Khaslana blinks, hesitates, a little, blue eyes shifting to the colors drying up in the plastic palette and the clean brush that hadn’t even been dunked in paint left on the table before he follows him out of the art studio.

Once he catches up, he asks, “Owe me?”

“Mm.”

Mydei makes a general motion to the coffee table in his living room, where the vase still sits.

Rather obviously, if you were to ask him, he hadn’t thrown it away once he was told it was fake. It still was his mother’s, at the end of the day, and Mydei finds that the worth people decide to assign to things always far, far exceeds the coin it is appraised for1.

“…Aren’t you taking this far too seriously?”

“A bet is a bet.”

“Even an unfair one? I essentially tricked you.” Khaslana must find it somewhat funny, because a tiny smidge of amusement arises as he says the last sentence, buried deep, deep under the soft cadence of his voice.

“Good you recognize that.” Mydei mutters. It comes out a little petulant— but not because he’s miffed about it, because he’s not, not one bit. That would only be childish. “But I lost, nevertheless. Trick or not—Do you like honeycakes?”

“For lunch?”

“Why not?” He asks. Khaslana lets out a little sound on the back of his throat, doubtful, maybe hesitant. “Yes or no, Khaslana.”

“...I do, yes.”

“Great,” Mydei hums, pushing the door of his kitchen open. A chewed-up brown rubber stopper is placed next to it, and he drags it with his foot into the space between the floor and the door to avoid it closing even though the busted hinge doesn’t let it move as smoothly as it once did. He will fix it, one day, he thinks and while he does this, he adds, half-joking: “Because I was going to make them, anyways.”

“Why in the world would you ask me, then?”

“Heh. If you answered no, then it would only be because you have never had mine.”

“You know,” Khaslana’s voice is dry when he replies. “This is exactly the kind of attitude that makes you so easy to trick.”

He doesn’t think so, personally, but instead of answering the accusation, Mydei simply lets out a simple ‘hmph’ as he delves deeper into the kitchen.

Like the rest of his house, the walls here are also built with the rich terracotta bricks, but the floor is carpeted with cream-colored ceramic tiles instead of the usual wood, because those are easier to clean. Its size is somewhere in the middle between little and big. The rectangular wooden table in the middle that, although it doesn’t wobble, he’s still pretty sure he built wrong all those years ago2, gives the impression that the room is more cramped than it actually is.

Reaching up to the ceiling, through the wall in front of the door to the right, a kitchen cabinet with a hundred drawers, doors and shelves is installed. A fridge with a grocery list he fills little by little and a few photos are held in place by little chimera magnets, an oven, a stove and a microwave are fitted throughout the empty spaces like little puzzle pieces painting the mundane evidence of a warm, clearly lived picture.

On the left wall, a door that gives way into a small backyard he mostly only uses to exercise when he can’t go to the gym is open, as always, but the mosquito door net is closed, as always, because the heat accumulates terribly in this room and those evil bloodsuckers seem to love Mydei’s blood. Kopopo the Third’s purple plate of food and water is placed next to it, along a fluffy cat bed he uses whenever he is pissed at Mydei. Hung on it, some little decorations he has been gifted over the years by nails, along a clock with a pendulum and a calendar.

He takes out a big red bowl he always uses to mix batter from one of the doors in the cabinet and places it on the counter with a quiet ‘tap’ before washing his hands in the sink. He mixes some yeast, sugar, water and flour with methodical, well-known motions and, as he waits for the yeast to activate, he goes to open the oven and rummage around for that one pan he reserves for making honeycakes.

After a second, Khaslana says, “Sorry.”

“For?”

A pause.

“Your door.”

Mydei blinks, frowns, the ‘clank, clank’ of metal against metal stopping for a second as he processes the words before he continues. “Why are you apologizing?” He asks, taking out a big pot with a dent on one side that’s getting in the way along some other dishes. Distantly, he wonders why that one pan is placed so far on the back considering how often he uses it. “It wasn’t your fault.”

“Wasn’t it?” Khaslana mutters.

“You weren’t the one that slammed it open, no.” Mydei replies, finally taking the pan out and placing it on top of the stove. He shifts his head to see Khaslana from the corner of his eye, just to find him looking at the busted hinge in the door while he shoves the other dishes on the floor back into the oven far less carefully. “It’s nothing I can’t fix, anyways.”

“If you say so.”

Khaslana hasn’t entered the kitchen.

He hadn’t entered last time either, choosing to linger instead on the very, very edge like an apparition about to dispel. Unsure—or unwilling, maybe, to disturb the quiet coziness that’s ever inherent to a kitchen, especially to one as well-loved as Mydei’s, with the all-consuming, all-devouring, ever-destructive allurement his sink-sink-sinking presence always seems to carry like a noose about to tighten.

“Don’t just stand there.” Mydei says with the same ease one unties a loose knot, adding more flour, vanilla extract and a little bit of salt in the batter now that the yeast has settled. He takes a whisk out of one of the drawers and starts to mix the batter. “Come in.”

Khaslana’s steps are ever silent, but Mydei doesn’t need to turn around to know that he does.

He expects him to take seat at the table in the middle. Instead, Khaslana pushes himself up to sit at an empty space on the kitchen’s counter, between the sink and the stove, right next to Mydei with a ‘bam!’ as the heels of his feet collide against the wooden cabinets. His shoes are untied, as always.

Mydei doesn’t stop in his motions, but he does raise an eyebrow at him, to which Khaslana merely tilts his head and offers no explanation whatsoever as he watches him cook. Mydei has never been fully comfortable with people doing that, for reasons he can’t quite pinpoint, but, nevertheless, he lets him stay there.

“Are you allergic to anything?”

“Cotton.” Khaslana replies, straightfaced. At the look Mydei gives him, he even adds, “Makes my skin itchy.”

“I will make sure not to add it, then.” Mydei replies, also straightfaced. “Do you want anything to drink?”

“Coffee?”

“I only have the instantaneous type.”

“That’s fine, thank you.”

“Alright. Here, mix.” He answers, shoving the bowl and the whisk into Khaslana’s hands without further ceremony. The other scrambles not to let it drop with a sound of surprise as Mydei walks out of the kitchen and back to the art studio.

The only coffee he has is the one he uses to paint, and so he has ended up treating it as merely another art supply, placed in between the tubes of paint. It’s perfectly drinkable despite that, though he does check the expiration date just in case.

When Mydei gets back to the kitchen, he finds Kopopo the Third sitting down on the table staring intently at Khaslana.

“I think,” He starts, speaking as slowly as he’s mixing the batter, not taking his eyes out of Kopopo the Third either. “Your cat is going to murder me.”

Mydei huffs. “He’s like this with everyone.” And he passes a hand through his little fuzzy back, lingering to pet his head. Kopopo the Third presses against it further with a face of satisfaction. Cute. “He will warm up to you, eventually.”

As soon as he stops petting him, his cat’s face immediately snaps back to stare at Khaslana.

“As my corpse eventually cools down, maybe.”

“Have you ever been told how dramatic you are?”

“Not as often as I used to.”

“Allow me to make up for it, then.” Mydei says, taking out a pot and filling it with water to boil. He then gives a sideway glance to the motions of Khaslana’s hands. “Faster.”

Khaslana’s face is wholly unimpressed as he stares at him, but he does start doing it faster. “When you said you were going to cook me a meal, I didn’t expect you to put me to make it.”

“I am just asking you to whisk it.”

“I am whisking it.”

“Badly.”

“No, I am not. See?” He tilts the bowl to him as he whisks it—badly, might Mydei add. “I am doing it faster.”

“And your technique sucks.”

“You do it, then.”

Mydei turns one of the knobs of the stove. A loud ‘ts! ts! ts!’ arises before the lighter catches with the gas coming out of one of the little black discs and a flame comes to life. He places the pot with water on top before he takes the bowl and the whisk Khaslana is extending back to him.

Then, looking at Khaslana straight in the eye, he whisks the batter with impeccable form. A fast clink, clink, clink, clink resonates through the kitchen as the metal collides against the bowl’s porcelain with the motions.

“Must you be good at everything you do?”

“Heh.” Mydei chuckles, a little smug. “You don’t bake much, do you?”

Khaslana shrugs. “Not as much as you do, apparently.” He answers, before doing that little tilt of head of his. “It’s a bit surprising, come to think of. You strike me more as the type of guy who would only subsist on a base of protein shakes and chicken breast.”

“That sounds like an actual nightmare.”

“You don’t care about calorie intake and all that?”

“I wouldn’t say I don’t care, seeing that I like keeping a good physique.” Mydei replies, eyeing the batter. It looks fine, so he settles the bowl down onto the counter to let it rest as he turns to the pot of water. Not boiling, but already hot. He turns off the stove. “However, I also really like sweets.”

Khaslana blinks.

“Sweets?”

“Sweets, yes.” Mydei nods, filling a blue cup, one of the few that does have a handle, with water before adding a teaspoonful of coffee. “How do you like it?”

“Just one sugar.” Mydei can’t help the expression of disgust that crosses his face even as he puts only a teaspoonful of sugar into the cup and stirs it with a clink, clink. “I gather you don’t like coffee, then.”

“Too bitter.”

“Just add more sugar, or milk.”

“It tastes like dirt water one way or another.”

He passes the cup to Khaslana, who stirs it a little bit more. “If you say so.” He replies before taking a sip.

Just to immediately spit it out in the sink.

The laugh Mydei lets out is sharp, near indistinguishable from the sound a choked cat would make. Khaslana glares daggers at him before turning to look down at the dark liquid in his hand. “What in the world did you just give me?”

“Coffee.” He answers, amused beyond belief. “I told you that thing tasted bad.”

“Not if you do it well—What brand is it?”

Mydei shrugs, making a general direction to the place he put the coffee in.

Ts! Ts! Ts! The stove lets out as a flame comes to life at the same time a little ‘pam!’ echoes in the kitchen when Khaslana comes down the counter. He comes to open the door he pointed at to check. While he puts some oil in the pan, Mydei watches as Khaslana finds and takes a little glass jar with chocolate chips.

He opens it, puts a handful in his palm before tilting his head back and shoving them into his mouth in one go. He closes it, puts it back, before immediately grabbing it again and grabbing another handful of chocolate chips.

Mydei’s chocolate chips, mind you.

It seems Khaslana remembers this a beat later, because he turns to him, looking wholly unapologetic, and tilts the little jar towards him in a silent offering.

A silent offering of, once again, Mydei’s chocolate chips.

The audacity.

Mydei sighs and extends his hand towards him, nevertheless.

A little handful is placed carefully on his palm, and Mydei copies Khaslana’s prior actions and tilts his head back before shoving them all into his mouth in one go. Then, he watches as lightless blue eyes trail away from his face to the red bowl with the batter. It’s not a silent petition, just a little second of want Khaslana doesn’t ask for. Mydei gives it to him, either way.

He grabs the bowl and places it closer to the other, and just like that, another little handful of chocolate chips is put in the batter.

He makes a note to write down that he needs to buy more.

Mydei stirs the batter a couple of times to spread the chocolate chips throughout before tilting the bowl into the pan until a little circle forms. The excess clinging to the edge and trailing down the bowl he swipes with a finger and licks it.

“Why in the world would you buy a brand of coffee named Dirt Water?”

“It’s cheap.”

“It’s a medical hazard, that’s what it is.” Khaslana replies, scanning through the contents of the label on the back.

“It’s not like I drink it.”

“But you will give it to your guests? Hmph. Buy a better one.” Khaslana says. Mydei wonders if he realizes how petulant he sounds. He then adds, “Unless, of course, this was all just a very complicated ploy to poison me ever since the beginning—In such case, I suppose I shall give you your flowers.”

Why would he give him flowers for that? Mydei wonders, absentmindedly3. But before he can question him, with all the naturalness in the world, Khaslana grabs the cup, tilts his head back and drinks it in one go.

He gags when he’s done and then goes to wash his cup in the sink.

“Why would you do that?” Mydei asks, a little incredulous, as he flips the honeycake.

“I don’t like wasting food.”

“Hm. There’s lemonade on the fridge.”

“...Thanks.”

━━━━━━━━━━

A couple minutes later, a neat, fluffy, and delicious-looking stack of honeycakes is placed in the middle of the table, along with a bottle of bee honey, and two plastic containers still cold with condensation. One with blueberries and the other with raspberries.

Kopopo the Third, now displaced from his position in the table, has recurred to chew into the rubber door stopper, though his eyes are still fixed in-tent-ly on Khaslana. If it bothers him, the aforementioned doesn’t let it show at all.

“Eat.”

Khaslana still looks sort of doubtful even as he stabs one honeycake with a fork and brings it over onto his own plate. He grabs some blueberries, adds some honey, cuts a little piece and, feeling the weight of Mydei’s gaze, looks him in the eye as he brings the little piece into his mouth.

Just to immediately freeze.

Khaslana blinks once, twice, eyes shifting from Mydei to the honeycake sitting innocently in front of him in a look close to wonder as he chews.

“Oh.”

He immediately stabs another honeycake from the stack and drags it to his plate.

Heh.

“Heh.” Mydei lets out, smiling like a well-satisfied cat as he serves himself two honeycakes from the stack too.

He has never had any doubt whatsoever about his abilities in the kitchen, but there’s always so undeniably warm in the sight of someone enjoying something you have made.

Effort, he had been taught, by both his mother and his father, back when he hadn’t gone mad with grief, is its own kind of care4.

Its own kind of devotion.

And, likewise, he knows, there’s trust in accepting.

Khaslana takes another bite of a honeycake.

“You are not subtle, you know.”

“I’m not trying to be.” Mydei replies.

Khaslana’s eyes lower.

“I’m sorry.”

“If this is about the door, I already told you it’s fine.”

He shakes his head. “I know we stopped the session only because of me.” He says, the edge of the fork catches onto his lower lip, and Khaslana winces as it digs into a space he must have hurt earlier with his picking.

“You needed a break. It’s fine.” Mydei reassures, grabbing the container with the raspberries and letting some fall onto his plate. “I don’t wish to paint you when you are uncomfortable, either way.”

Khaslana opens his mouth, closes it, and pushes the bottle of honey towards him instead.

A long, long beat of silence stretches, little grains of time coming into a halt, just for a moment, just in this room, just for them. A faint breeze comes in through the open door of his kitchen, refreshing and faint, and when it looks like Khaslana might not speak again, Mydei extends the container of raspberries to him.

He hesitates before he grabs one.

And, quietly, he admits, “I don’t know how to act around you now.”

“What a stupid thing to worry about.” Mydei tells him, upfront. Khaslana’s fingers around the raspberry in his hand tighten, a little trickle of juice sweeping between the gaps. “Just act like you always do.”

“If I acted like I always do, I wouldn’t have come back in the first place.”

“Then why did you do it?”

A pause.

“I don’t know.”

Mydei looks at him.

“Liar.”

Khaslana’s mouth presses into a thin, thin line, and he places the raspberry on his plate, cleaning his hand on his pants. He then stabs the raspberry with his fork and eats it along with a little piece of honeycake.

He does not answer.

And Mydei does not know what to say.

“It’s fine if you don’t know how to act.” He tries, nevertheless. A part of him knows he still comes up short, though. “You just have to be.”

Khaslana makes a face. “You always make things sound so simple. I don’t…” He halts, pushing with his fork a blueberry on his plate from right to left and left to right. Empty blue eyes shift fleetingly to the broken door before going back to Mydei’s face. “What if I ‘am’ and you don’t like what you see?5 ”

Mydei tilts his head. “If I do?”

“How could you know that?”

“I don’t, and that’s why I won’t make any empty promises, but both of us will never know the answer if you don’t let me.”

Khaslana stabs the blueberry.

“And how would you go about it, mm?”

Leave it to him not to make things easier from the get-go. But that’s fine, he should have already learned by now Mydei can’t resist a good challenge.

“For starters,” Mydei thinks for a second. “Tell me what’s your favorite color.”

The look Khaslana sends him is nothing short of incredulous. Briefly, Mydei wonders, how did he not notice just how expressive the other could be. “What are you, five?”

“Answer the question.”

“Gold.”

“As in coin?”

“As in wheat.”

“Why?”

“...It reminds me of home.” Khaslana shrugs, but it looks a little bit too mechanical, as if he’s trying not to let whatever emotions accompany his statement show. Maybe, that’s why he asks immediately, “What’s yours?”

In the past, he remembers, back in school when Mydei came with his hundred dozen crayons of different colors in his purple droma’s case, he always struggled with that question. And, even now, even to this day, it is still somewhat hard, because, as an artist, it is hard to place one tone over the other when all of them can be valuable to form this picture or the other.

Still, he finds, today, and maybe from this day on, the answer comes to him with terrible ease.

“Blue.”

“Is there a reason for that?”

Mydei looks at Khaslana’s eyes.

“No, not particularly.” He replies, chewing on a piece of a honeycake, deciding to keep that little secret for himself for no particular reason. “Now, what do you like doing?”

“...How many of these are you going to do?” Khaslana mutters, still looking unconvinced. “Bird watching, I guess.”

“Bird watching?”

“I like birds.”

An idea comes into Mydei’s mind with a little ‘pop!’ like a corn kernel exploding into a little white popcorn and, a little impulsively, a little too much spontaneously in the way he often doesn’t tend to be, he asks, “Would you like to go watch them, then?”

Khaslana blinks at him.

“You mean right now?”

━━━━━━━━━━

The ravine on the other side of the block is more a little forest than it is a ravine. A little lush of greenery in between houses of brick and concrete colored in an array of artificial tones, that goes down, down, down into a little creek with cold, cold water in which it isn’t strange to see the kids waist deep when the weather is hot or whenever they simply wish to catch fish with their hands.

It’s humid, in the way these sorts of environments always are, with dirt that’s always a little muddy and slippery and trees that reach high, high into the sky. Big green leaves cast shadows that shift as the wind pushes them side to side.

They cling onto Khaslana, dig into the edges of his skin and wrap around him like thorned vines, in the way they always do, and, maybe, will always do, because Mydei’s shift in perspective doesn’t mean the world has stopped seeing Khaslana much more like a ghost or a broken wind-up doll.

It doesn’t mean Khaslana has stopped regarding himself as such either. But, that’s fine, Mydei is a patient, patient man. Tenacious in his perseverance.

Now, close to the edge of the creek, there stands a gray pillbox reclaimed by the greenery that the kids have now turned into a secret base everybody pretends not to know about until it is time for dinner. Mydei places the white canvas he brought with him in the top of it, along with the black box with the ugly-looking chimeras where his art supplies rest, and hauls himself upwards.

He turns around, intent on helping Khaslana up, just to find him lifting himself upwards with the same ease as Mydei’s.

It’s not surprising, not really. Khaslana’s build isn’t as bulky as his own, but it is certainly athletic. Enough that it is easy to see he could certainly carry himself well in a fight and more than enough that it is easy to know he would be able to push back were he to be slammed into a bookshelf.

I suppose, the curator’s smile flashes in Mydei’s mind, he just can’t help himself.

Mydei scrunches his nose and shakes his head, trying to dispel the image— which comes to be all too easy when Khaslana lets out a dry ‘ah’ that is followed by a loud 'splash!'

His shoe came off6.

“I did tell you to tie them.”

“Yeah, yeah.” Khaslana waves off, sitting at the edge of the pillbox. He pulls his leg up and ties the remaining shoe. “There, happy?”

“That thing is so loose you might as well leave them undone.”

“It’s not loose. You—Why are you untying my shoe?”

“Because it’s loose.” Mydei replies, sitting down in a more comfortable position next to Khaslana as he tightens the knot. He’s about to say something else, when a glimpse of brown mixed with neon yellows and greens catches his eye and he blurts out, “What in the hell is that thing on your foot?”

“...My shoe?”

“No, not that.”

Mydei lifts the leg of his pants, enough for the abomination the other is wearing as socks to be put on full, shameful display.

Khaslana pins him with the sort of dead look that only someone who has been told the exact same thing many times over could have.

“I like them.” He defends, flatly.

“You do?”

“I think they are fun.”

“To laugh at.”

Khaslana scoffs. “You are just jealous.”

“Jealous of the person I was before seeing them, yes.” Mydei replies as he finishes tying Khaslana’s shoe.

“I’m going to shove you into the creek.” Khaslana threatens, looking as if he means each and every word he’s saying, as he points at the water—until a little bird comes to rest on his extended finger with a joyful chirp.

Mydei blinks at it. Khaslana doesn’t look the least bit surprised.

“They like to do that.”

“Every time?”

“Since I was a child, yes.” Khaslana replies, looking down at the little bird on his finger. “I used to think it was only because they liked the music, but they continued to come even after I stopped playing.”

In quiet movements, as to not scare off the bird, Mydei drags the white canvas into his lap and starts to put greens and browns in the plastic palette.

“What did you play?”

“The ocarina.”

Mydei hums. “I used to play the piano.”

Khaslana tilts his head. The little bird in his finger also tilts its little head.

“Really?”

“Is it so surprising?”

“Maybe.” He shrugs. “If anything, I would have expected you to play the lyre.”

“Why is that?”

“You just have very kind hands, that's all.”

“Kind?” Mydei blinks, caught more than a little off-guard at Khaslana’s words.

He turns his eyes down to see the array of calluses littering his fingertips and the ever-perpetual bruise on his middle finger, in the skin under his nail where the wood of his painting brushes always digs, digs and digs in.

His hands aren’t the type one would usually associate with kindness, not really. They aren’t small, nor smooth, and much less delicate. They are big, and gruff, and more than a little rough. The type of hands far, far more fitting to that of a fighter than that of a painter, he knows, and, he thinks, would always know even if he hadn’t been told time and time again.

And yet.

“...I see.”

Khaslana seems them as kind.

How strange.

Mydei can’t quite help the smile that blooms and spreads over his face.

He doesn't finish the painting that day, for there is no threat of that moment in between the creek and the trees to slip away through the gaps of his fingers like grains of sand as there was with the image of Khaslana laughing.

So, they come back, again and again, to talk of little important nothings as Mydei paints, and, at the end of the month, when the second round of the art competition arrives, a painting titled Of Conversations and Birds comes to hang on the Irontomb’s walls like a little star.

Chapter End Notes

FOOTNOTES

1. Even then, first and foremost, Mydei is his mother’s son. So, he still had made the time to take a little impetus trip to Castrum Kremnos to meet with old friends, and even though none of them will delve into the details of their fun little escapade, especially without a lawyer in the room, they will say that the scammer will think thrice the next time they decide to pull off something like that. Back

2. There’s no word for ‘reading the instruction manual’ in the Kremonan Language. Back

3. Sometimes, Mydei has a hard time understanding little turns of phrase. It’s fine, but it makes it so that, later in this story, much, much later, hidden somewhere somewhen in between the lines, he asks Khaslana when will he give him the flowers he said. Khaslana looks at him weirdly before explaining it wasn’t literal. Still, he asks, “Did you want some?” To which, Mydei replies, “I was expecting some, that’s all.” He believes that’s the end of that, but, a month later, he is given a little bouquet of pink and blue hydrangeas tied with a ribbon from where a little bag of silk with a hundred pressed forget-me-nots hangs. “So that they last longer,” Khaslana says. The hydrangeas wither after some time, for such is the cycle of life, and a new painting comes to appear in Mydei’s art studio the day after it happens—as for the forget-me-nots, those, he keeps on a glass box in his night desk. Back

4. This, Mydei won’t ever know, for grief withered Eurypon into a coward, but, even now, even though it pains him terribly to see his wife’s strokes in his son’s paintings, he still makes an effort to go into each exposition he knows one of Mydei’s works shall be presented. It’s not enough, it will never be, especially after his actions forced Mydei out of his house, but, it sure makes you wonder. Back

5. Once, in a book Khaslana really liked but could never come up with the energy to finish reading, it said than an overexposure to mirrors could chip away bits and pieces of a person, for the fragment of a mirror could contain both a piece of the universe and a piece of soul. Khaslana has never really liked mirrors, and he has come to not like being painted either, and a part of him wonders if the statement the book said about mirrors applies the same to paintings. If, maybe, he has been chip-chip-chipped so much by brushes instead of chisels, that there’s nothing left for him to be. Back

6. They never manage to find it. So, that day, Khaslana walks back to his apartment with a pair of Mydei’s shoes. Back

━━━━━━━━━━

A couple of notes on the footnotes, lol. The book Khaslana is referring to actually exists, is 'Witches Abroad' by Terry Pratchett, which I love and has irreparably changed my writing style. It's pretty good, I do recommend it.

On the flowers, hydrangeas can have lots of meanings depending who you ask. The pink ones, I have found, tend to mean things along the lines of love and sincere emotions, while the blue ones tend to mean apology, forgiveness, gratitude and understanding. If you wonder, Khaslana focused on the ‘sincere emotions’ and ‘gratitude’ meaning, and so, he’s practically telling Mydei, ‘Thank you (for understanding/seeing me)’

The forget-me-nots are self-explanatory.

chapters.title: Chapter 8: Stable ground
chapters.html:
“And where are we going today?”

Khaslana asks that day.

Mydei blinks once, twice, and then thrice at the question.

Khaslana blinks back at him with the sort of quiet, almost gentle, tranquility he always seems to carry with him, standing expectantly at the edge of the ever-wobbly stone step that Mydei will definitely fix later. He’s much the same as ever, the same three knock-knock-knocks, the same messenger bag, same glove, same sharp tongue, same blue, deep ocean eyes, and even his inquiry is much the same as it has been for the past weeks, maybe even months.

Still, he finds himself surprised, like coming aware of the fact you are in a dream, maybe, or like coming to notice the dirt path in the middle of the grass that slowly, gradually, formed unnoticed under the weight of your steps.

When, Mydei wonders, suddenly overly aware of the way Khaslana tucks a lock of his hair behind his ear, did things change?

He thinks about it, for a second. Time coming to a halt.

It would be a complete, utter lie, not to say terribly unfair, to say that things started to change once the last brush of Of Conversations and Birds was given and Khaslana, ever so disbelieving, asked a faint ‘is it done?’ at the side of the creek with about five canaries in his lap and his ugly socks, as if still unsure Mydei had actually finished painting him, not once, but twice, because, the truth is, things had started to change long, long ago.

Change, it’s the thing, it’s just the nature of things, as melancholic as it might be.

The oceans turn to sand and the sands to ocean. Day turns to night and day to night. Metal rusts, rock erodes, dust settles, and vines grow. The blanket you used to sleep with unravels thread by thread, the plastic toys gain a hundred little white scratches, and that shirt you liked doesn’t quite fit you anymore. One day, you look at your mother’s face and come to notice the wrinkles and creases on her old face and can't quite remember if she always looked like that, and you realize flowers bloom just to die; and maybe there’s some sort of tragic beauty in that, such is life, alas1.

Things had already started to change long, long ago, ever since the moment Mydei ever laid eyes on Thus Burns the Dawn, maybe. Khaslana had changed from an urban legend, a whisper in between the linen and the paint, a mere concept, to an apparition, and from an apparition to something in-between a challenge and a muse, and then to a proper muse with how he had fulled and ignited Mydei’s passion for art before it could die a slow, painful death.

But, now, as the question changed from an empty, monotone ‘how do you want me?’ to a light, almost expectant ‘and where are we going today? 2’ he isn’t exactly sure what exactly Khaslana changed into, much less what exactly he became to Mydei.

But that’s alright, maybe, he thinks. Some things in this world don’t need a name.

They just need to be.

“I don’t know,” Mydei replies, easily. He passes the blank canvas to Khaslana to carry, and the action comes with a strange sort of naturalness, a little mundanity between them. “Where are we going?”

Khaslana blinks again, this time surprised. The winds of change can be felt.

He brings his phone out of his back pocket in his white pants and taps it once to check the hour. It’s two o’clock of a day that will probably be forgotten in history because the events and affairs that happen that day aren’t particularly worthwhile. If that makes it matter less or more, Mydei doesn’t particularly care, he’s no romanticist.

He just knows he will remember, nevertheless—even if sometime in the future he won’t be sure if it happened either on a Monday or a Wednesday, maybe even a Thursday.

“Have you eaten?” Khaslana asks. “Lunch, I mean.”

“No.”

“Do you want to go to the diner?”

“You mean the one on the last floor of where you work?”

“Mm-hm.”

“Hm.”

Khaslana shuts down his phone and shoves it carelessly into his messenger bag through a little gap left by the flap, and says, “They have really good desserts, you know.”

Mydei arches an eyebrow.

“Bribery doesn’t work on me.”

Khaslana tilts his head. “Pomegranates ones.”

Ah, maybe it does work, just a little bit—but it’s not like he was ever actually going to say no to Khaslana’s choice of place. He didn’t give much warning that he was going to be the one choosing their destination today, anyway.

Mydei turns his head around. “Don’t destroy the house while I am out.” He tells Kopopo The Third, firmly, who is laying on the floor tummy-up, with that little smile dogs and cats always seem to have when they are very, very comfy. He meows non-comitally at him. Hmph, little fuzzy bastard. He’s lucky Mydei loves him.

“You always say that to him.” Khaslana points out as Mydei steps outside, skipping absentmindedly the wobbly step, and closing the door behind him.

He lets the keys of his house fall unceremoniously into the messenger bag through the little gap left by the flap as he answers, “He’s a menace,” and they start to walk towards the diner. “As you must be aware.”

“I think he’s cute.”

He is, but, also, “He has attempted to kill you at least three times now.”

“Four.”

“Mm? When was the fourth one?”

Khaslana hums, also non-comitally.

A part of Mydei wonders if he should be glad Kopopo The Third doesn’t get along with him.

They reach the building a little after, as untouched by the modernization of times as it ever is. The green, rich vines have extended further and further up to the top, and the tiny little white flowers have grown in numbers and bloomed beautifully, covering completely the quaint yellow walls. It’s the season, he believes, somewhere in between the Month of Reaping and the Month of Weaving. Soon they will dye red in the Month of Strife before they wither and fall in the Month of Mourning, and who knows what will happen in the Month of Fortune. Maybe Zagreus will make strawberries grow, Mydei says. Better than potatoes again, Khaslana replies.

The same old man with wrinkled hands and a newsboy cap from last time opens the door for them once again. He’s delighted to hear they are going to his wife’s diner. Upon hearing he likes sweets, he laughs and recommends the carrot cake she makes before patting him hard on the back hard enough to knock the air out of Mydei’s lungs. Apparently, he used to be a very good wrestler.

It’s as quiet and a little bit empty as last time, in the sort of way places like this always seem to be. In a little corner of the first floor, colorful linens on wooden easels held together with adhesive tape stand in place of people. A small art exhibition of the works belonging to the art class given up in the diner on the weekends. Charming things, as always, some better than the others, little pieces of dreams put into reality with watercolors and oils, though, the painting of a drowned man with hair dipped in gore and spider lilies for blood is a stark, gruesome contrast to the rest. Khaslana’s eyes flicker in something like melancholic recognition at the image before they continue towards the stairs next to the elevator that always gets stuck between floors 3.

Khaslana walks a couple of steps ahead of him, climbing upwards in fast strides that echo with a little plap, plap, plap, as the ends of his ever untied shoes slip out of his heels every time he lifts his feet.

“You would think that after losing one shoe more than once you would have learned to tie them by now.”

“Don’t speak to me as if I were five.” Khaslana replies, giving a little wave of hand to Theodoros, who is ripping yet another sheet of paper taped to the glass door of his store. “I know how to—Ah.”

His shoe slips off.

It lands a couple of steps behind Mydei.

He goes to fetch with an ‘I told you so’ or some other witty comment already at the tip of his tongue that he doesn’t get to utter as Khaslana says, monotonously, “Race you.” And before Mydei knows it, he has already disappeared onto the next floor.

“That’s cheating!” Mydei yells at him, voice bouncing in the walls. He picks up Khaslana’s shoe and scrambles to reach the diner first, skipping steps four at a time with fast, long strides. The painting utensils in his box clatter around loudly with the movements.

Still, “You lost.” Khaslana not so kindly tells him once he reaches the diner merely seconds later after he arrived. His face is impassive. “That means you are paying.”

Mydei, unimpressed, lets the shoe fall to the ground with a ‘plap!’

Khaslana doesn’t look the least bit surprised at the fact Mydei still got it for him. He half wonders if he’s that predictable as he watches him wiggle his foot into it. “Thank you,” He says, holding onto Mydei’s shoulder to maintain balance before he lifts his leg to straighten the heel tab he crushed against his feet. “You are still paying, though.”

“For my own food, yes.”

“Penny pincher.”

“Says the freeloader.”

Khaslana lets out a little ‘hmph’ sound in the back of his throat, pushing open the diner’s wooden door. The hinges, old rusted things, grinds and creaks as if they were getting murdered.

He lets Mydei pass first.

“Shouldn’t the winner get something?”

“You never once said the loser had to pay.”

“It was implied.”

“No, it wasn’t.”

“Mm, I knew you were a bad winner, but I didn’t expect you to be a bad loser, too.”

“I’m the bad winner? You are the one always starting competitions where I am at a disadvantage.”

“What you are saying it’s that you are slow.”

Mydei steps on the back of his shoe, just to be petty. It comes off Khaslana’s feet swiftly and, before he can put it back, he kicks it to the side.

A beat.

“...And a bully.” He adds, dryly, walking to it.

“Hm-hm.” Mydei lets out. The sound edges on the side of indulgent.

His shoe landed under a table with two grannies on a little date. One of them pushes it towards him with her long walking stick that has a skull on the top, looking amused as Khaslana thanks her. The other says something to him as he bends down to tie it. He shakes his head and replies with another thing that makes both grannies laugh. One of them even pinches his cheek.

“What did they tell you?” Mydei asks, a little curious, after Khaslana comes back.

“That you are being very mean.”

“Hm-hm.”

The face Khaslana makes is close to a pout, but not quite. Were he to be more childish, or younger, maybe, Mydei suspects he would have stuck his tongue out at him.

He sighs.

“Fine,” He concedes, for some strange reason, yet, not one to yield, he adds, “But you are paying next time.”

Khaslana’s face doesn’t twitch nor change one bit, no quick turn of lips, no crinkled eyes, but he still manages to look unbearably smug, somehow.

Mydei clicks his tongue and attempts to step on the back of his shoe again. Khaslana kicks him in the shin.

The diner is a quaint little thing, shoved into a corner thanks to a big saloon occupying the majority of the last floor that’s used for this activity or the other, like Zumba classes on Fridays or haunted houses where the most terrifying thing is the price to enter. A bunch of metal tables and metal chairs that you have to get on your tiptoes to get onto stand across the checkered floors. The end wall is covered with childish paper drawings hung with red tacks.

It is quiet, although not silent, with the clinks of cutlery and the clatter of the kitchen resonating like distant notes in the back of a song. Lyrics made out of fragments and pieces of conversations floating around. Tiny glimpses of a million lives that seem so far away and, at the same time, so close. ‘She told me not to tell anybody, so you better not tell this!’, ‘...I texted him again.’, ‘Oh, come on. It’s five o’clock somewhere.’, ‘So, what if it has more than a thousand episodes? I swear you are going to like it!’, ‘No, no, I can still pass the class. I need fifteen points and there’s still six from activities and ten from the test. He’s also giving extra points if you come dressed as a fruit on the examination day. I will go as a carrot—What do you mean that’s a vegetable?’ Unfamiliar in their familiarity, familiar in their unfamiliarity. The distinction might not matter.

They sit at a table next to a window filled with faded stickers of princesses and transformers, placing both the canvas and his box with the ugly-looking chimeras on the sides below the table. And, after they order and the waiter takes away the cheap, laminated menus that Mydei has always hated the sensation of with him, he opens the blue cardboard box of clay crayons in the middle.

It only has four colors.

He takes out the blue one as he says, “Whoever makes the better drawing pays.”

“You are already paying.”

“Not if I win.”

“This is unfair.” Khaslana replies, looking unamused. It’s almost funny. “You are the painter here.”

“What I am hearing is that you can’t.”

He points a finger at him. “Don’t use my own tactics against me.”

“Why, is it working?”

“No.”

“So, you lose then.”

Khaslana’s finger twitches.

It’s a little bit curious, Mydei thinks, how terribly, almost pettily, prideful he can be in the most inconsequential of things. Then again, it’s not like Mydei has much room to talk. He has come to realize he’s much the same ever since he met Khaslana.

“Art is subjective.” He replies.

“Hmph.” Mydei lets out. “Don’t you think I know that?”

“I wouldn’t be surprised if you didn’t.”

Mydei’s eyebrow twitches. Instead of replying and giving Khaslana more ammunition to shoot back, he sends a pointed look at the blank sheet of paper the diner uses as placemats in front of him before starting to make a sketch on his.

Khaslana clicks his tongue.

From the corner of his eye, Mydei watches with a sense of victory as a gloved hand takes out the green crayon from the box.

“Heh.” Mydei chuckles, smug.

Khaslana throws the crayon at his head. Mydei throws the one in his hand right back at him.

Now they only have two crayons.

━━━━━━━━━━

The food arrives soon after, and they eat it between meaningless chatter and little banter. The old man with the wrinkled hands and a newsboy cap hadn’t been lying when he said his wife’s cooking was to die for, because saying that it tastes amazing is an understatement. A part of him can’t help but compare the explosion of flavor on his tongue to the feeling of placing cold hands around a warm cup despite him being no romanticist. He even ends up asking if he can have the carrot cake recipe4.

Once they are done, Mydei makes a motion of writing in air in the direction of the waiter, who nods and disappears into the kitchen to get the tab before he turns to face the other, expectantly.

Khaslana covers his mouth with the paper with the drawing.

“...Why do I have to go first?”

“You have seen my art plenty of times already.” Mydei replies, easily. “I want to see yours.”

Khaslana brings the sheet of paper a little higher, now covering his nose along with his mouth, leaving only his deep blue eyes uncovered, staring accusingly at him.

It’s a little endearing, for reasons he can’t quite put a finger on.

“Ha! Don’t tell me you are getting shy.”

“I’m not shy.” He replies immediately. “It’s just not very good.”

Mydei extends his hand in a silent request. “I will be the judge of that.”

“You are going to laugh.”

“I will try my best not to.”

Blue eyes narrow. “Try?”

“I don’t make promises I can’t keep.” He replies, earnestly, and perhaps a little too solemn for the situation at hand. But Mydei has always been a rather solemn person, a sincere one, in all aspects of his life, and he has never seen the point in either pretending or hiding who he is. “It can’t be that bad.”

Khaslana’s gaze flickers across his face before he lowers the drawing from his face. He looks at it once, mouth pressing before it goes back to his usual lack of expression. “I don’t really like it, but,” He sucks in his upper lip, scraping his teeth against it as if he wanted to draw blood before he lets it go. He extends the paper to him. “I tried.”

Mydei’s eyes flicker down.

A hundred thousand little butterflies catch in his throat.

Despite the fact the world does not change nor care, not one bit, it still feels as if the winds have changed from south to north. Time, ever present, ever important, ever going, tick-tock-tick, fading far, far away, as if eternity took grace and allowed him to stay watching the little drawing made with pinks and reds as long as Mydei desired.

Still, eternity would get lonely, he thinks, and Mydei would rather live the moment he’s in, so, he says, a little redundantly, for the butterflies seem eager to steal all words and all air, “You drew me.” And the gears of time start grinding forward again, or maybe backwards. It doesn’t matter.

“Why do you sound so surprised?” Khaslana mumbles, letting go of the drawing once Mydei grabs it. “You paint me all the time.”

He’s not wrong, but, also, somehow, someway, this, “Is different.”

Khaslana rests his chin on his hand. “Maybe.” He replies, and then hums, looking contemplative. “Maybe not. I do think you would do far better as a muse than I do, though.”

“Really now?”

The words come out like little butterflies.

“Hm? You have never been painted before?”

Mydei huffs. “Of course I have.” By his mother, when she lived, and then by a bunch of people back when he started getting into art again after her death and when he went into art school.

He’s no fool either, much less blind. Mydei knows he’s attractive with certainty, not vanity, enough that he knows he is appealing to capture in art.

And yet,

Nobody has drawn him the way Khaslana did.

Arguably, it’s also the worst, lacking the finesse and technique a skilled artist has. Khaslana has a good sense of perception, he will give that, but he does not know how to calculate proportions. He drew his head a little too big, his upper body a little too small. Arms a little wonky, and both his tattoos and his braid look like wavelengths. The traces aren’t firm, but he absolutely nails his face, golden eyes made with pink that look both piercing, ferocious and kind.

It’s strange.

There’s a certain innocence to it, almost. The him in the sketch gives off a firm sense of tranquility, or safety, maybe, despite the roughness of the lines —but that’s fine. Mydei wouldn’t be who he is if he weren’t more than a little rough, if he lacked the sharp lines Khaslana used.

Is this, a part of Mydei wants to ask, how you see me?

He doesn’t ask.

The drawing is enough of an answer.

“You are smiling.” Khaslana says, quietly. Mydei hadn’t realized. “You can laugh if you want. It’s fine.”

He shakes his head. “I like it.”

“Uh.”

“It’s nice.” He says, and it’s true. It may be the worst way he has been painted, but there’s still a certain skill peeking through the wobbly pinks and the shaky red. Not quite talent, but technique that went uncared, unnurtured, like vines in a garden that overtook the flowers. He wonders, shifts his eyes to him, and asks, “Did you used to draw?”

Khaslana’s eyes flicker down. “I never liked it.”

“Why did you start, then?”

A pause.

“...I like taking photos.” He admits, so quietly that Mydei has to lean on the table to hear him. “I had a camera, back when I was a kid, but I dropped it into the river. I didn’t want to bother my parents to buy me another one, so,” He shrugs, making a motion to the drawing. “People told me I was good— for my age, that is, so I kept doing it. I even tried to get into art school, you know.”

Mydei’s eyebrows fly to his hair.

“Did you get in?”

“No, thank Kephale. Being in a place full of artists sounds like a living nightmare.” He says, and a shudder climbs up his spine that he tries hard to dissimulate. Mydei has enough grace not to mention it. “My portfolio got accepted, though. But there was a test where you had to go into the school and draw what the examiner tells you that I didn’t pass.”

“What were you supposed to draw?”

Khaslana’s eyes drift to the side. “I don’t remember5.”

Another pause.

“I would like to keep it, though.” Mydei speaks after it comes to be obvious Khaslana won’t say anything else on the subject.

“Why?”

“As I said, I like it.” He answers without a trace of doubt. “It’s as simple as that.”

He huffs, a little incredulous, but says, “Do what you want.” Before he asks, “What did you draw, anyways?”

With care, Mydei settles the sketch of him down on the table before he takes his own drawing and lifts it.

“Chimeras?”

“Us as chimeras, yes.”

“...Uh.”

“This” He points at one of the chimeras, the one made in pink. “Is Beagle Coconut,” He points at Khaslana, who looks very confused, “That’s you. Now this,” He points at the other chimera, the one made in red. “Is Fig Stew—”

“Why do I look like the incarnation of the devil?” Khaslana interrupts.

Mydei shifts the paper and cranes his neck to see his drawing. “You don’t look like the incarnation of the devil.” He picks up the red crayon and makes two horns on Beagle Coconut’s little fuzzy head. “Now you do.”

Khaslana looks terribly unimpressed.

“This is defamation.”

“No, it’s not.”

“Yes, it is. You made me look bad in comparison to you—And why in the world did you draw Fig Stew so cute?”

Mydei sets his drawing on the table and, in what is probably the blandest tone ever, replies, “I’m adorable.”

Khaslana blinks, slowly, eyes flickering up and down, gauging just how serious Mydei is before he hums. “I don’t see it.” He says, tilting his head in the way Mydei is quickly coming to associate with trouble. “Maybe if you made a cute face, I would.”

A what.

“A what.”

“A cute face.” He repeats. “You know,” Khaslana tilts his head again and winks at him.

It’s ridiculous, frankly, his face doesn’t even change one bit while he does so, remaining in its quiet, gentle impassiveness of always, not even a turn of lips. Ridiculous, he tells you, utterly, terribly, ridiculous—

“You are blushing, Mydei.”

“No, I am not.”

“Yes, you are.”

“There’s no word for ‘blushing’ in the Kremnoan language.”

Khaslana lets out a little ‘oh’.

“Well, your face is very red, Mydei.”

“Out of anger.”

“Because I am cute and you are not?” He asks, mirroring Mydei’s bland tone from earlier. He can’t tell if he’s being serious or not, either. “Or is it because you can’t do it?”

“Who says I can’t?” He snaps.

He can make a cute face—cuter than whatever Khaslana’s very poor attempt that definitely didn’t make him blush could be.

Distantly, a part of him wonders why he is getting so riled up by all this, before Khaslana makes a motion for him to prove it and the thought dissipates like sea-foam.

Tsk.

Mydei thinks for a second, takes a breath to shove the surge of embarrassment that threatens to overcome him, and plucks out his lips while closing his eyes.

Click!

Makes the phone camera.

Mydei goes very, very serious. “Delete that.”

“No.”

“Khaslana.”

“No.”

“Khaslana, I’m warning you.”

He locks his phone and presses it against his chest. “No.”

When the waiter finally comes back with their tab, it’s only to find Mydei trying to forcefully lift Khaslana from where he has pressed his upper body flat into the table, phone and hands tightly kept and secured under his chest like a turtle.

Mydei doesn’t ever get to delete the photo, but he does manage to lock the phone for more than an hour trying to guess the password.

This, he won’t know, but Theodoros catches Khaslana looking at it more than once.

Chapter End Notes

FOOTNOTES

1. Much more of a tragedy is to not be witness to such sight, though. Gorgo died young, very young, to the point that a wave of bittersweet sadness will hit Mydei the day, far, far away into the future, in which he starts to catch grays in his own hair and wrinkles around his eyes. Back

2. It wasn’t on purpose, not really. It’s just that Khaslana always seems to shut down the second he steps inside the art studio, like a wind-up doll running out of cord, dim and em—pty. Too many bad memories, Mydei thought, and he had adapted easily to such revelation. It is not much of a bother. Mydei has come to find he much prefers to paint Khaslana doing inane things, like stealing his fries next to a random food stand, than sitting still. Back

3. Once, Khaslana met a corpse. A ghost from the Xianzhou. He had ink for hair, rubies for eyes, linen for skin, and paint for blood. He smelled of flowers and death. He saw him some night staring at a painting of a vase with spider lilies dripping blood, hung like a dead man in an art store that was most definitely a mafia front. Khaslana had bought it for him, not exactly sure why, and watched him burn it right after. Apparently, long, long ago, the ghost had fallen in love, and the man he loved cursed him in return. “My Yingxing?” He had said his lover once said with a smile, right before his head fell, “No. As long as my art lives, he will live too.” He has been searching death ever since, but new paintings of him keep appearing. His lover reincarnates. Khaslana had told him his own story, then, in that self-destructive way that makes you want to bleed in front of someone knowing they won’t do anything to save you. In the end, the ghost had asked, “What do you want, then?” and Khaslana replied, “Nothing.” The corpse said, “Only dead men don’t want for anything, and even I

wish for death.” Struck, Khaslana admitted something, that night, next to a burning painting, but his confession isn’t meant for you. Back

4. The old woman proceeds to drag Mydei into the kitchen nearly by the hair and doesn’t let him leave until he gets it right, because she will be damned first before she lets anybody botch her recipes. Mydei gets it right on the second try. The old woman starts calling him ‘grandson’ from that day on. He’s strangely touched. Back

5. That’s a lie. It was a self-portrait. The second the word left the examiner’s lips, Khaslana set down the pencil, stood up, and left, because he only ever drew things he loved. Back

chapters.title: Chapter 9: Planting seeds
chapters.html:
“Kites?”

“You don’t want to?”

“No, it’s not that.” Mydei replies, watching the colorful slips of color paper tissue peeking from the top of the black plastic bag loosely held by Khaslana’s middle finger. There are blues, purples, yellows and greens; pinks, reds, oranges and a little bit of whites and blacks. A faded blue wallet with frayed ends rests atop, thrown carelessly along with the rest of the things. “I just didn’t expect it, that's all.”

Khaslana shrugs. The brown paper bag pressed against his chest crinkles with the movement. “The theme is wind.”

Soon after the first pieces to the art competition had been submitted, an e-mail had been sent to the participants filled with meaningless chatter and hollow congratulations of this and that before having the pleasure of informing that, from now on, to incentive and prod at the limits of creativity and something else Mydei had skimmed past, themes would be introduced, before the word ‘Wind’, in big curved red letters, declared the concept to more-or-less follow for the next installment.

After reading it, Mydei had sent a screenshot of the e-mail to Khaslana, who had replied at three in the morning with a simple, ‘I think I know what we can do.’ Mydei, when he had woken up, had replied with a simple ‘sure’ and a question of what on earth was he doing awake at that hour.

Khaslana hadn’t answered that and instead sent a photo of a lizard he found in his sink1.

“Does it get messy?”

“Making them? A little, I guess. Depends.”

Mydei’s eyes shift to the coffee table in his living room, where Kopopo The Third has settled onto, not watching Khaslana for once but the paper bag pressed against his chest.

He hums, “Outside?”

“Sure.”

Mydei drags the chewed-up brown rubber stopper from the kitchen and places it in the space between the floor and the door to stop it from slamming closed.

It’s a little windy outside. It’s always a little windy this time of the year, when the Month of Weaving edges to its end and the winds of love start to shift to the winds of war distinctive of the Month of Strife.

Khaslana has settled onto the last stone step of Mydei’s house. The black plastic bag placed between his legs as he absentmindedly chews a little strawberry pastry. When the ‘tap, tap, tap’ of Mydei’s footsteps he shifts his head upwards before extending the brown paper bag to him.

Mydei peeks inside to find another little pastry there. Chocolate, judging by the smell, and he takes it with a, “Thanks.”

“They were on discount.” Khaslana waves off2.

“Mm-hm.”

The stone steps aren’t particularly big, so Mydei sits on the floor, crosses his legs and pulls the black plastic bag into the gap between his legs. He takes a bite of the pastry, settles it onto his leg, and cleans his fingertips before starting to rummage inside. Color tissue papers, a spool of black thread, ribbons, a bag of wooden dowel rods, liquid glue and little blue scissors with drawings of stars still on its package.

Out of curiosity, Mydei takes the wallet on the top and opens it. There’s ten bucks, little white slips of paper bills and expired coupons that he takes out to throw in the trash. The plastic edge of the identification card peeks out, and Mydei pulls it out. Khaslana looks a little bit funny in the photo of it, in the way everybody always seems to come out in these sorts of things. His signature is rather nice, although simple, and his birthday was two weeks ago.

Mydei doesn’t comment on it, although some distant corner of his mind makes note of it. Instead, he looks at the year and says, a little smugly, “I’m older than you.” Although not by much. A year or so.

“And I’m taller.” Is Khaslana’s immediate reply.

“...Tsk.”

“Heh.”

“I’m stealing your ten bucks.” Mydei replies, closing the wallet and throwing it back onto the bag. “Where do we start?”

“The skeleton.” Khaslana replies, placing his half-eaten pastry on the discarded paper bag and leaning forward to take out one of the bags of wooden rods and the spool of black thread. He smells of clean laundry and linen painted on. Unfinished work, wet paint.

Mydei wonders how long will it be before Khaslana lets it dry.

Khaslana opens the bag and passes him four rods, explains and shows to him how to tie them with the thread to form an octagon before he cuts the thread off from the spool with his own teeth.

Mydei goes along with the motions, notably a little less smoothly and more haltingly than him, and he points out, “You have done this before.”

Khaslana hums an affirmative, bringing a gloved hand to hold one of the wooden rods in place as Mydei ties them. “Not for a long time.” He says.

“Why is that?”

“Wasn’t much of a reason.”

“And there was before?”

“I suppose.” He shrugs, taking his hand away when the wooden rod is set tight. There’s a little pause as Mydei goes to tie the last one, almost as if he’s dwelling on continuing, before he adds, “There used to be a festival close to where I lived. Something about the dead, I think. Evil spirits bothered the good ones, and the sound of the paper against the wind drove away the bad ones.” He makes a vague gesture to the skeleton’s kite in Mydei’s hands. “So, they made these big, beautiful kites that would cover the whole expanse of the sky—It always reminded me of a kaleidoscope, you know.”

“You used to go help, I gather.”

“Just with the little ones. I wasn’t that good. I always used too much glue, so they always ended up a bit soggy.” Another pause. “I haven’t gone back3.”

Mydei’s eyes flicker to him before he returns to his work.

“Why is that?” He asks yet again.

And, “No reason.” He replies. When Mydei turns to him, blue eyes drift away from his gaze. Then, almost casually, “Does Kremnos have anything like that?”

Hm.

“You aren’t particularly subtle.” Not to mention a very bad liar, as always, but Mydei has already told him that before, and he isn’t one to repeat himself if it is not needed, and he suspects Khaslana is very much aware of the fact. “But, no, Kremnos does not have any tradition like that. The dead recognized are the ones deemed strong in life, so the idea we would have to do something to protect them is laughable at best.”

“What of the weak ones?”

“Forgotten.”

Mydei frees the little blue scissors with drawings of stars from the package and cuts the thread from the spool and finishes tying it.

Khaslana’s eyes are low, and he is absentmindedly dragging one of his feet back and forwards, back and forwards, back and forwards, on the ground with a ‘crish, crish’, dragging dirt and dirtying the tip of his red basketball shoes—The ones that Mydei gave him that time he lost one in the creek4. Laces tied up, for once, without Mydei’s prompting, and he can see a peek of purple and yellow under it, no doubt yet another pair of ugly socks.

He seems a little bit distant, almost, as if…

One of Mydei’s eyebrows raises.

“Does the notion sadden you?”

Khaslana scoffs, “It is a sad notion.”

“That’s a way to put it.”

“How would you put it, then?”

Mydei blinks, a little taken aback at the question, though, maybe, it is one he should have been expecting.

He has never given it much thought before, truth be told.

“Harsh,” He replies after a beat. “But so is life.”

The wind blows, chilly, gentle, and a little bit wild. The end of love, the beginnings of war. It lifts dead leaves off the ground into a dance, whistling through windows without glass, bags crinkling and shifting with a soft sound, raised dirt. It steals the little breath Khaslana lets out, ever-intent, ever-bent, on taking him with him, like yet another dead leaf, but his presence is warm at his side, undoubtedly alive, undoubtedly present, and so the wind fails to steal his words away.

Maybe, just maybe, that’s the reason why world does not still, and neither does Mydei, when Khaslana says, quietly, certainly, melancholic, “I would remember you,” while he takes a sheet of color paper tissue as orange as Mydei’s hair from the bag, “If you died.”

He lifts an eyebrow, and, dryly, asks, “Are you calling me weak?”

Khaslana lets out a sound that could very well be a chuckle—as if the mere idea was ridiculous.

“No, not at all. If anything, you are the strongest person I know. But,” His eyes shift. The deep, deep depths of the blue, blue sea swirling as he looks directly at him. “You wouldn’t need to be for me to remember you.”

Mydei laughs.

No, the world doesn’t still, and neither does he; if anything, his heart beats. He wouldn’t be alive, otherwise.

“You are so very sentimental,” He answers. It’s even a bit surprising, Mydei thinks, how much Khaslana’s heart bleeds, perhaps even foolish. “I’m not dying anytime soon.”

Khaslana does not reply.

The ‘snip’ of the unpacked scissors cuts that trail of conversation as effectively as it starts to cut the sheet of orange paper in his cold, pale hands.

━━━━━━━━━━

The process of putting the color paper tissue on the skeleton of the kite is rather simple enough, Khaslana explains. It’s basically putting glue on the wooden dowel rods and on the thread and placing the paper there. The hard part is actually making it look good.

Mydei opted for making a lion’s face with reds and yellows, along with a wild mane made out of different colored ribbons because there aren't enough orange ribbons while Khaslana simply puts different colors in every gap, like a kaleidoscope of sorts, little triangles made with pinks, greens, oranges, reds, purples, yellows and grays.

It’s in the middle of Mydei attempting to make an eye with white and black paper that Kopopo the Third attempts to steal his half-eaten chocolate pastry.

“No.” Mydei says, firmly, raising both the kite and the pastry up into the sky. Kopopo the Third, from his position on his lap where he ended up falling, yowls as if he was being murdered. “Chocolate is bad for you.”

Kopopo the Third yowls again.

Movement from the corner of his eye catches his eye, and he shifts his head to see Khaslana breaking in half the little piece of strawberry pastry he has left before placing it on the floor.

“Don’t indulge him.”

“It’s not for him. It’s for the ants.”

“And what if he takes it?”

“Strawberries aren’t bad for cats in small quantities. Nothing bad would happen to him.” Khaslana replies, pauses, and adds, a little haltingly, “If he were to steal it from the ants, that is.”

“Sure.”

“It’s just a little bit.”

“And he’s already fat.”

Kopopo the Third mewls, indignat.

“Don’t call him fat. He’s cute.”

Kopopo the Third scrunches his little nose, as if being in agreement with Khaslana disgusted him.

Slowly, he pushes himself off Mydei’s lap and lands gently on the floor with his ears flattened back, as if ready to pounce and attack, as his little fuzzy face goes from Khaslana’s impassive face to the little piece of pastry left for him.

One minute passes, two, maybe even three.

Haltingly, his cat starts to walk up to the piece of food, step by step, fuzzy paws soundless against the floor before his face lowers and he sniffs it a couple of times.

Then, he sits.

Khaslana blinks.

Kopopo the Third mewls at him, sharply5.

Khaslana tilts his head.

Kopopo the Third also tilts his head.

“...It’s for you.” Khaslana admits.

Kopopo the Third lets out a sound that resembles a scoff, which is a little bit weird to hear coming from a cat.

And then, as fast as a light, his cat grabs the little piece of strawberry pastry left for him off the ground before darting back into his house. He stops at the door, twists his head to see him, hisses loudly, and disappears into the kitchen6.

Khaslana lets out a hum. “I didn’t think he would actually accept it.” He says, and even though his face is still impassive, he sounds strangely pleased.

It’s a little bit funny.

A little ‘crack’ of a branch being stepped on comes from behind him, and a chilling, ruthless sense of foreboding crawls up like a hundred thousand spiders in Mydei’s back. When he turns around, it is to find the kids with plastic balls, rope and chalk standing a couple of steps behind him.

The kid who doesn’t eat their veggies narrows his eyes at them while the girl with the purple spinning top tilts her head and asks, “Whatcha doing?”

Ever so slowly, as if movement might get them pouncing on them like a cat towards a mouse, Mydei turns his head around yet again to face Khaslana. Discreetly, he takes the rest of his chocolate pastry and eats it in one go to keep them from stealing it.

Khaslana’s lips twitch, and he coughs to dissimulate a laugh.

“Kites.” He tells them while Mydei tries not to choke on the pastry. A faint rustle of paper arises as he lifts his own to show them.

The kids’ eyes light up.

The little girl with chalks sprints first and plops down next to Mydei, letting all her chalks fall and clatter to the floor, leaving tiny dots of color in the concrete like little stars or distant galaxies. “I want to make kites, too!” She demands. The rest of her friends follow suit.

One of them steals the last bit of Khaslana’s strawberry pastry.

━━━━━━━━━━

“So,” The little girl with chalks starts, hands full of dried glue as she places a sheet of pink paper above the skeleton of her kite. She’s making Godzilla, but pink. “When is the wedding?”

Mydei, helping the boy with the green spinning top cut purple paper for his own, blinks once, twice and then thrice, not fully registering the words. “What?”

“The wedding.” She repeats. “That’s what people who date do. They marry and then they kill their husband.”

“Uh.”

“I want to be the flower boy.” The boy with the green spinning top pipes at his side.

Mydei opens his mouth, but the girl with the purple spinning top chimes from where Khaslana is helping her tie the wooden rods for her kite, “Not fair! I wanted to be the flower girl!”

Khaslana blinks. “Um.”

“Nu-uh! I already said I would be! You can be the ring girl.”

“But I wanted to be the ring boy.” The kid who doesn’t eat their veggies scoffs.

“You can’t be the ring boy.” The little girl with chalks interrupts. “You already were the ring boy for the kind old woman’s wedding last week.7”

“But—!”

“We are not getting married.” Mydei cuts in with a sigh.

All the kids go silent, incredulous, almost.

The little girl with chalks settles his pink kite on the floor, turns to him and, with the sort of dead, lifeless tone only a person who has worked a nine to five every day for the last thirty-four years could have, asks, “Do I look stupid to you, Mister Painter?”

Mydei opens his mouth, closes it, but before he can muster a semblance of an answer, the girl with the purple spinning top says, “That’s not very nice to tell the person you are dating.”

“We are not dating.” Khaslana replies.

“But you guys go on dates all the time?”

“They are not dates.”

She stares at Khaslana before turning to her friends.

“They may be stupid.”

“Very stupid.” The boy with the green spinning top agrees.

The kid who doesn’t eat their veggies stands up abruptly, kite left discarded, and walks up to Mydei with the certainty of a war general.

“Does this mean,” He demands, crossing his little arms. “You haven’t kissed him?”

“No.” Mydei replies.

“Wimp.”

“Wimp?”

“Wimp!” Khaslana repeats as he breaks into a fit of laughter, loud and bright, like the chime of a bell, picked, dry lips stretched wide into a smile as his shoulders shake.

It’s as breathtaking as the first time he heard it, perhaps more, because the cobwebs have un-stuck from his throat and his tongue dusted off ash. Mydei’s fingers twitch, half-regretting he didn’t bring out something to paint him, sketch him, empty linen or empty pages to fill with warm, bright colors; although, the emotion is dampened, a little, by the knowledge Khaslana is laughing at him.

It pisses Mydei so much his heart skips a beat or two, maybe even three.

He opens his mouth, but the kid who doesn’t eat their veggies beats him to it, turning his head around like an owl and, rather eerily, saying, “Don’t think I have forgotten about you.”

Khaslana’s mouth shuts with a sharp ‘click!’.

All the kids, smelling weakness, cats to a canary, sharks smelling blood, turn their little heads towards him and stare with their piercing little eyes.

“That’s—”

“Why haven’t you kissed him?”

Khaslana’s eyes flicker to him in a silent plea for help. Mydei ignores it. Ha, that’s what you get for laughing, jackass.

“...Can we go back to making fun of Mydei?”

“No.” The kid who doesn’t eat their veggies replies immediately.

“We are making fun of you now.” The boy with the green spinning top says.

“Now, answer.” The girl with the purple spinning top demands.

“I already said we aren’t dating—”

“Because you haven’t kissed.”

“It’s not like that—”

“But you are his muse!” The little girl with chalks pipes in. “All artists kiss their muses.”

“No, they don’t.”

“Yes, they do.”

“...I think I would know.”

The little girl with chalks scoffs, as if she thought he was being dumb.

Khaslana looks mildly offended at the notion.

Suddenly, “You don’t like him?” The kid who doesn’t eat their veggies, and who also seems terribly invested in their love life, asks, looking scandalized. “Is that it? You don’t like him?”

“Is that why you don’t break into his house?” The boy with the green spinning top continues, and, ignoring Mydei’s ‘For the last time, they don’t break in. They just have spare keys’ the girl with the purple one gasps with a, “Is that why you knock?”

The lips of the little girl with chalks wobbles, as if she were about to cry. Khaslana makes a sound akin to that of a strangled cat at the sight.

“Ah, don’t cry—”

“But you don’t like him!” She hiccups.

“I like him.” Khaslana replies, gently. It’s stupid, but it makes something in Mydei’s chest feel warm. “He’s, ah, a very nice person and—”

“But you haven’t kissed him.”

“And you don’t break into his house.” The boy with the green spinning top interrupts. He seems oddly hell-bent on it, for some weird, weird reason.

Khaslana answers, “Because we are only friends.”

All the kids go silent, quiet, eyes flickering from him to Mydei, who nods in confirmation.

They all turn to each other.

“Adults are so dumb, aren’t they?” The kid who doesn’t eat their veggies asks.

They all nod in unison and, unceremoniously, go back to making kites.

A pause.

“Kids are so strange.” Khaslana sighs.

Mydei makes a faint sound of agreement at his side.

━━━━━━━━━━

They finish their kites as Aquila up in the sky begins to doze off, the blues high above bleeding into warm oranges and rich reds like watercolors diluting in water. Some of the light posts have turned on as Khaslana ties a long piece of thread in the center of every kite so that they can rise high, high up and not lose.

It’s a little bit cold by now. The frigid exhales of Oronyx sweeping into the world. Some of the kids run into their houses for a sweater to wear before running back outside, leaving trails of mud and dust in the ceramic tiles of their houses as the wind picked up; mischievous gusts of air that rustle the leaves of the tall, tall trees. It makes it so that the kites rise high with little to no prompting, but the kids still run between laugh and laugh to lift them up, either way.

“I’m a little worried they might run them into one of the electric cables, electrocute and then die.” Khaslana says as he moves his hand side to side, making his kaleidoscope kite swish this or that way in the sky.

Mydei lets out a startled chuckle, watching as the wind pushes the colorful ribbons of the mane of his lion kite. It’s fun. “They won’t die.” He tells him. “At most, they will feel a little electric shock—I am more worried they might cause a blackout in the block.”

“Oh, well,” Khaslana shrugs, making his kite bump into Mydei’s. “I don’t live here, so I don’t have to worry about that.”

“Ah!” One of the kids cries at their back. Both of them jump and turn their heads around sharply. “My kite!”

Khaslana lets go of his kite and runs to catch the kid’s.

Mydei scrambles to catch Khaslana’s. His whole arm snapping up towards the thin line of black thread floating in the air, swaying side to side, almost in mockery when the tips of his fingertips graze it before the wind picks up and pushes the kite far, far up in the sky, out of his reach, like grains of sand slipping past the gaps of his hands.

The kids cheer behind.

He turns his head back to see that Khaslana has caught the kid’s kite and bent down to tie the black thread around their wrist, securing it, and the rest of the bunch crowd around him with extended arms so that he can tie their kites to them too.

The kaleidoscope dances above, all on its own, swaying side to side.

Khaslana is a rather lonely person, isn’t he?

Mydei stares at the kite, drifting away. He’s no romanticist, has never been, will never be, but he can’t help but think that, eventually, the wind will die down, and Khaslana’s little multicolored thing will fall somewhere. Forgotten and alone, and the color paper will tear and the wooden rods break.

Khaslana won’t be sad about it, he thinks, knows, but Mydei is, a little bit, inexplicably so.

Golden eyes shift from the kaleidoscope kite and shift to his lion kite with its wild, multicolored mane and round eyes, and, rather impulsively, Mydei lets it go.

He watches it fly after the other one for a second before turning around and walking up to the rest in quiet steps as the other finishes tying strings of black threads around little wrists.

“Mm?” He lets out as Mydei appears, standing up and turning to him. “Where’s your kite?”

Mydei points at the sky.

“Oh.”

The lion kite flies high, high up and bumps into the kaleidoscope kite, making them tumble and spin around in the sky. The black threads of each twist and loop around, tangling together until they start to drift side to side.

Click!

Makes the phone camera at his side.

The painting Mydei creates is rather simple, truth be told, a plain orange background with two kites flying together high in the sky, as Khaslana watches them from behind, phone held loosely in his hand.

It’s nothing big, just a little memory preserved in paint, titled Two Kites.

Chapter End Notes

FOOTNOTES

1. He does that a lot. He also likes taking pictures of Mydei whenever they agree to meet somewhere else and sending them to him along with a simple ‘see you’ instead of walking up to him and saying ‘hi’ like a normal person. He seems to get a kick out of seeing him search for him even if he doesn’t show it. A part of Mydei thinks he just likes to be found. Back

2. They weren’t. Back

3. Not since Cyrene died and his home burned, either way. A little bit contradictory, maybe, seeing the purpose of the festivities, but the only thing Khaslana can think about when he looks at the big, kaleidoscope kites is that Cyrene hadn’t had a hand in making them yet again, never again. Back

4. Khaslana had tried to give them back the next day, but Mydei had waved him off and told them to keep it. They were always a bit too big on his feet, anyways. Back

5. He means to say, “Hmph! You think you can bribe my affections, strange entity that bleeds paint?” But, contrary to popular belief,

Khaslana doesn’t speak cat, so he doesn’t understand him. Back

6. “This doesn’t mean anything, you hear me?” He means to say. Khaslana still doesn’t speak cat. Back

7. Her husband disappears mysteriously the following month. Back

━━━━━━━━━━

I do love the trope of characters being good with kids, but I love more kids bullying the absolute hell of adults. It's fun.

Anyways, I read through the comments (and you are all so kind ;_;) and, after some consideration, I decided to break the following chapter into two. One of them said that it would make the little dates stand out their own and I agree!! So, 14 chapters it will be, really really this time.
