chapters.title: Chapter 10: Growing plants in burnt soil
chapters.html:
The sound of the slap echoes and resonates through the silent industrialized walls of The Irontomb like the furious rumbling of thunder before lighting that gives way to a forest fire, engulfing, devouring and burning down the trees and the flowers to nothing but cinders and ash; blackened earth, smoke in the air.

A bunch of gasps from the two or three people littering about the halls of an art gallery on a Monday afternoon arise as Lygus’ head snaps crudely to the side and the breath Khaslana lets out seems to crackle.

“Your opinion is as misguided as it is unwanted, not to mention repetitive and uninspired.” In the quiet that has frozen the space in place, Khaslana’s voice thunders, incinerates, and razors, hell on earth, even though it doesn’t rise. “We, unfortunately, have had this conversation a thousand times before, and your view of art1 is still as flawed as the first time I ever had the displeasure of hearing it—It’s a complete waste of talent, I dare say.”

Melting heat irradiates in the air, burnt earth, but when Mydei exhales, steadily, calmly, sparks don’t come out of his breath.

Somewhere along the way, without none of them knowing, silently, intrinsically, intimately, they had fallen into a routine, of sorts. All Mondays without fail, following a new entry to the art competition and The Irontomb is near deserted, Khaslana will come to see the painting he presented, and, all Mondays without fail, Mydei will meet him there. Afterwards, depending on the hour, they either go for breakfast or lunch.

He had run late, today, for no particular reasons worth lingering on about, the sort of innocuous little things from day-to-day life that pile up here and there and made it so that he hadn’t even had the chance to change out of his gym clothes.

The faint smell of sweat clings faintly to him.

There were a couple of things Mydei was expecting when he entered The Irontomb. The little mundanities of a routine. The few guards standing on the sides, the reception man asking him for a synonym for some word as he taps, taps, taps the chewed pencil on the counter while doing yet another crossword2, and Khaslana, either lingering on the children’s section of the art competition or near the space of the painting Mydei had made; toying with his phone, maybe, and a demand for him to pay that day for making him wait so long.

He was not expecting, however, to turn the corner and be met with the immediate sight of the curator finishing saying something or another to Khaslana with a razor-sharp smile before the man whirled around and slapped him so hard that Lygus nearly collapsed onto the floor.

Mydei’s hand closes into a fist.

He can feel the phantom sensation of the sting.

Khaslana lets out another breath, sparks coming out, a lighter lit up, and he burns, burns, burns inside out and inside in as he spits, “Don’t ever talk to me again, Lycurgus.”

Having said that, he turns around, and walks away towards the door on the other side of the room. He’s not running. He is much too valiant for that, a part of Mydei believes, and, perhaps, much too proud, though, that may not be the right word. It’s fine. He’s a painter, not a writer, and much less a poet. He only knows that Khaslana’s steps, firm, but ever silent, seem to scorch the floor beneath him.

Mydei’s footsteps aren’t silent as he walks after him, but no less firm because of that, although they certainly don’t burn.

Two Kites hangs next to Polyxia’s Petals In The Sky, and Mydei’s eyes shift to his own painting, almost absentmindedly, before the ‘plam, plam, plam’ of his steps slowly comes to a halt.

For a second, just one second, a brief, fleeting instance of time under Oronyx’s melancholic sighs, Two Kites seems no different from the rest of the paintings displayed at The Irontomb. Beautiful, in its own way, but thriving on destruction of some kind, rejoicing in it, because the soft oranges of the warmth of the sunset start to resemble more the warmth of the burn—ing fire.

“Unfitting, isn’t it?” Lygus says, the beginnings of madness, the end of humanity, “Such gentle strokes don’t fit a thing like Khaslana.”

His fist tightens, nails digging into the palm of his hand.

What a rotten belief.

Mydei shakes his head and looks at the painting again. Madness is alluring, and sinking is easy, and, yet, “No,” He answers, because he remembers the warmth of that day. The taste of a chocolate pastry on his tongue, the child’s rambunctious laughter, the sound of the paper tissue fluttering against the wind, warding off bad spirits as a lion kite entangled with a kaleidoscope one. “They fit him just fine.”

Lygus chuckles, soft, a little condescending.

Mydei doesn’t know how Antikytheran’s work, truth be told, so he’s not sure what exactly is the dark, dark liquid that slowly starts to trickle down Lygus’ mechanical nose. Oil instead of blood, maybe. It falls down onto the porcelain floor with a drip-drip-dripping sound, staining the ornate designs made in gold.

How hard must Khaslana have had to hit for him to hurt a being solely made of metal?

In practiced motions, Lygus retrieves a silk handkerchief out of his pocket. It’s white, with an owl embroidered in the corner, and it’s covered in washed-out black stains that now look gray.

Mydei’s eyes narrow.

“What did you say to him?”

Lygus smiles. “Nothing he doesn’t know already.”

He opens his mouth to reply before he notices Khaslana isn’t in the room anymore. With a click of tongue and a scoff, he moves past Lygus to chase after the other.

He catches up to him as he is exiting The Irontomb, long legs walking along with long strides, making quick work of the few steps outside the entrance.

“Khaslana.”

He does not reply.

“Khaslana.” Mydei calls again, a tad bit louder, a tad bit harsher.

He does not reply.

Mydei scoffs, picking up his pace a little bit. One of his hands goes to catch Khaslana’s wrist to stop him, his name already on the tip of his tongue, but before he can even form the first syllable, Khaslana yanks his arm out of his hold and keeps walking.

A beat.

He grits his teeth and grabs his wrist once again, “Khaslana.” Mydei demands, this time, his hold tightening when the man attempts to yank himself free again. “Where are you going?”

Khaslana stops.

Silence trickles drip by drip into the space like water flooding a ship before it stretches like bubblegum held between teeth. The outskirts of The Irontomb are empty, save for them two, and the world stutters from where it spins, as if unsure whether to halt, for a second, for them, or to continue.

It doesn’t stop, though, for it could not care less about the insignificant occurrences and happenings in their lives, and silence remains as the sun shines bright, burns bright.

As a mercy, or maybe a cruelty, up above, a long, big cloud slowly comes to cover it, like a ship left adrift, covering the unbearingly hot light of the star, casting long, dark shadows over them as the faint sound of the wind howls like the crackle of firewood burning down.

“Let go.” Khaslana says.

“Where are you going?” Mydei asks again.

“Away.”

“Hmph,” He lets out. “And where is that?”

Khaslana turns his head around to see him, locks of white hair bouncing with the movement like tumbling snow in an avalanche, and a lesser man would have probably cowered at the rage burning like a million stars in his blue, lightless eyes, spreading like a wildfire, consuming, devouring, burning.

Mydei, who grew in between honor and strife, where everyone is adjacent, intimate, well-prepared, to the concept of conquest, war, thinks Khaslana would do well in one.

It would break him, irreparably, he’s much too kind for that, much too sensitive, but he would do well, probably even use the little broken parts of himself as ammunition; and a part of him wonders if, back, back then, he should have been more worried about him burning down to ash instead of the wind chipping marble into dust.

He shakes his head.

Khaslana raises his chin, defiant, angry, and Mydei doesn't cower one bit, meeting the fire burning and crackling head on.

“Don’t make me repeat myself, Mydeimos,” He demands, yanking again. “Let go.”

He tightens his grip around his wrist, not enough to bruise, but certainly not scared to do so if it means that Khaslana won’t disappear like mist in the night, sea foam in water, wood in the pyre, ash in the wind.

“Mydei—”

“Have you eaten?” He interrupts, not exactly sure of what to say but very well-knowing he has to say something, anything.

Khaslana’s anger doesn’t recede, and neither does it soften, but the tension in his shoulders falls slightly, and he stops trying to yank himself free as he lets out a dumbfounded, “...What?” That all but echoes in the empty, empty space.

━━━━━━━━━━

He hasn’t, turns out.

The maze of paths and streets that surround the plaza has no shortage of restaurants and diners, cafes and holes in the wall, food stands and carts moving along the cobblestone with a ‘racka, racka, racka’ filled with candy, a cooler with ice cream, or sliced bits of fruit. It means there’s much to pick and choose.

Khaslana does not choose, though, and a part of Mydei, a foolish one, maybe, probably, ridiculous in its softness, honest in its care, half-wishes to just take Khaslana to his home and cook him something himself.

Still, he didn’t bring his car today, and the walk from the plaza to his house on foot is far, far too long.

There isn’t really a place Mydei has in mind to take the other for that very reason. Though, he doesn’t worry too much about it, opting to walk around the place, eyeing the different options there are as Khaslana walks silently at his side.

The cathedral, with its colorful stained glass of long-forgotten saints and paint-stained balcony, rises in the distance, not as tall as The Irontomb, but imposing enough to draw attention. The bell tolls, marking the pass of yet another hour, the sound echoing through the streets.

A stray dog without an ear eating the scraps of rice somebody threw in the trash growls at Khaslana once it sees him while a black dog licking the mouth of a drunkard passed out between a police commissary and a casino whose bets are most surely illegal stares at him with its red eyes before tilting its head.

They take a detour before the stray dog starts chasing them, turning into a street without a number where an old lady with a glass eye and a golden tooth sitting at the feet of a morgue that used to be a school scams a bunch of tourists with plastic trinkets and cheap imitations of this painting or the other. One of them pays for an overpriced wooden butterfly while another looks between copies of A Chess Master’s Last Piece and Spectator of Life. An unfinished imitation of Mydei’s Khaslana3 peeks under the edges of Missing Heart.

They keep walking. They get lost.

None of them worry, though, in between this maze of paths and streets, it is not strange for one to find themselves lost. Sometimes, people say, it’s as if the locations of certain shops, houses and restaurants changed places from one moment to the other.

Eventually, as they turn onto another street with its number upside down, at the very end, a modest hotel without a name rests. Mydei had stayed there, once, when he first came to this city and was searching for a place to move into. The room had been too cramped, the bathroom probably haunted, and the outdoor pool on the last floor so cold that Hephaestion had gotten hypothermia.

The food in the restaurant below had been pretty nice, though.

Mydei doesn’t particularly bother asking Khaslana if he wants to eat there, and Khaslana doesn’t particularly bother asking where they are going. Mydei walks, and he follows.

If it is out of trust or out of lack of care, he isn’t particularly sure. Nevertheless, he tries to be responsible with whatever is that he’s been given.

The inside of the place is dim lit. A hard attempt to appear classy that, in reality, only serves for the place to resemble more a stereotypical tavern where pirates of old would sing lo and about. The wooden tables, wooden chairs, wooden floors, wooden ceiling and wooden counter at the back only serve to drive further the point.

Khaslana grimaces at the cramped space. Mydei has to resist the urge to chuckle at it, though the glare sent his way tells him his amusement does not go unnoticed. He asks him what he wants, Khaslana says that whatever is fine, and when Mydei tells him to go pick a table, he immediately makes a beeline to the ones set outside on a little balcony that resembles more of a dock.

The restaurant does not have any waiters, mostly because they all get lost, and so Mydei spends about fifteen minutes in the queue to order something. Once he reaches the counter, he makes quick work to ask for the steak, for him, and a salad with a bowl of fruit, because Khaslana’s appetite varies widely between eating thrice his weight in one sitting or taking one or two little bites before he pushes his plate towards Mydei, and he doesn’t look much hungry right now.

He also orders two milkshakes, vanilla and pomegranate4, mostly because he just feels like having one, though, distantly, he remembers his mother once saying everything is better with a little bit of ice cream. He’s given both and then shooed away with a disgruntled ‘come back in twenty minutes for your food’.

Outside, the wind is dead. The airs of war, the drums of battle, and the cries for glory proper of the Month of Strife settled down like the death-filled quiet that follows the aftermath of a battle. The cloud engulfing the burning light of the sun has yet to go, and instead of dead bodies littering the ground, the balcony is filled with wooden tables with big black umbrellas in the middle.

It’s empty, today, save for the man in far too polished of a suit with a fedora reading the newspaper as a black case rests at his side, a girl tapping something or another into her phone and Khaslana, seated at the far edge of the balcony with a cigarette on hand, staring down emptily at a piece of paper as a person with graphite smudges on their palms and a sketchbook under their arm fidgets nervously at his side.

Mydei’s eyes narrow.

He walks towards the table with firm steps. The plam, plam, plam of his feet against the wood resonates and vibrates, unfaltering, but the person seems so enthralled by Khaslana they hardly even notice, body swaying side to side like a ship left adrift, about to sink, sink, sink.

“—You are not going to convince anybody,” Khaslana’s voice drifts as he gets closer. Monotonous, flat, a little distant. Em–pty. His hand taps the paper on the table with his gloved hand. “To model for you if what you present them is an unfinished product.”

The artist flinches at the words, even when the tone isn’t even particularly harsh. The sketchbook under their arm falls to the floor with a fluttering noise. A hundred thousand loose sheets of paper with doodles and sketches scatter through the balcony like dismembered limbs.

More than half of them are of Khaslana.

All incomplete. All unfinished.

The artist scrambles to pick them all up with apologies and shaking hands, shoving them all under the black covers of the sketchbook carelessly, folding, crumpling, shredding and breaking the sketches.

Mydei, who certainly isn’t a bleeding heart but certainly isn’t cruel and much less indifferent, would be much more inclined to help them pick all of their drawings if not for the way Khaslana’s hand, the one holding the cigarette, comes to pick-pick-pick at his bitten lips.

Instead, he sidesteps the loose sheets of paper scattered across the floor and places both milkshakes on the table with a loud ‘tap’.

“I didn’t know you smoked.”

Khaslana’s head turns to him, swirling eyes blinking once, twice, before he registers the words, and he scoffs, some life returning to him as he bites, “If you are going to tell me it’s bad for my health, then zip it, Mydei. I don’t want to hear it.”

Mydei’s eyebrow raises, and he takes seat in the empty chair between the artist and Khaslana.

“I am not one to tell you the ways in which you should or should not accelerate your own death.” He replies, plainly. “You can make your own decisions.”

The glare sent his way is entirely unimpressed.

“You say it as if I smoked five packs a day.”

“Mm.”

Khaslana sighs, takes a drag, and the smoke filters through the gaps of his teeth like rot as he speaks.

“I only do it when I’m stressed.”

Mydei’s eyes flicker from his face to the piece of paper settled like a sentence on the wooden table. It’s a simple sketch, made in pencil, all long, elegant lines that constitute Khaslana’s rather lonely-looking figure. The face’s area is smudged, almost crumpled, and a hundred dozen lines, the imprint of a hundred thousand empty eyes, that the eraser couldn’t remove remain.

An orange, almost red dot burns in the middle of the page, the edge of a cigarette.

His eyes go further down, then, past the sketch, past the table, to the floor. Two cigarette ends lay extinguished next to two red basketball shoes. One tied, another untied. Another sheet of paper rests there, too, but before Mydei can make out the lines and forms, a graphite-smudged hand snatches it.

With a jump, the artist stands up again. The sketchbook now tightly pressed against their chest, pages peeking from under the hard covers.

They clear their throat, embarrassed. “So, uh,” They shift, not even acknowledging Mydei. “You really won’t let me draw you…?”

“You can do whatever you want. I can’t stop you.” Khaslana replies, flatly. “But, if you are asking whether I will model for you or not. Then, I’m afraid my answer hasn’t changed.”

“Why not?”

“I’m not interested.”

“That’s not an answer.” They reply immediately. Khalsana’s eye twitches, almost irritated, and the hand holding the cigarette flexes and tightens. “I have seen you in The Irontomb—The paintings made of you, I mean, and Thus Burns the Dawn is simply…” They sigh, dreamlike, and when they look at Khaslana, it’s as if they were seeing something ethereal, indescribable, unreal. “You are clearly not opposed to being someone’s muse, why can’t you be mine?”

Khaslana takes another drag of his cigarette.

They frown.

“What’s so different between them and me?”

“It’s not about y—”

“Is my art not good enough for you?”

Their fingers are knuckle-white around the sketchbook.

Khaslana lets out a low, deliberate breath and, wordlessly, Mydei shifts in his seat so that his body comes to shield most of him. It’s a rather futile endeavour, truth be told, Khaslana is no small man, he’s even a little bit taller than Mydei, but it is enough so that the artist’s eyes snap towards him instead, fleetingly, almost annoyed before they go back to the other.

“You are not impossible to draw.” They continue. The words are pleading, but the tone is demanding. “You have been painted more than once in only a few months by that Mydeimos—”

“You mean me?” Mydei interrupts.

The artist flinches as if they had been slapped, and their eyes are wide as they turn towards him, looking as if his presence hadn’t actually fully registered to them before, only Khaslana’s, always Khaslana’s. “You?” They ask, incredulous. “What did you do to make him pose for you?”

Mydei’s nose scrunches, disgusted at the implications.

“I asked.” He replies.

“I am asking.” They bite, and turn back to Khaslana. “I could finish drawing you too. He’s nothing special.”

Khaslana scoffs. “And that’s why you gave me an unfinished sketch?”

“That’s—!”

“And none of the others seemed completed, either.”

“Because I didn’t have good enough of a reference!” They snap. “If you just let me—!”

One of their hands shoots forward to grab Khaslana’s.

The wooden table scratches and digs against the floor with an ear-grating sound, nails on a board, scissors cut-cut-cutting through skin and bone, and the salt container tumbles down, scattering little white crystals through the brown surface like falling, dying stars. The milkshakes wobble precariously, like old pillars about to collapse.

Mydei’s hand closes around their wrist before they can even so much as graze Khaslana.

The whole balcony seems to freeze at the action.

A low, long inhale comes from behind him, and Mydei’s head shifts just enough to watch as Khaslana exhales a cloud of gray, gray smoke. His face is impassive, but the hand that had been resting on the table has come to rest on his lap.

“As I said,” Khaslana says, monotone, tight, a little distant. Some ash falls from the cigarette down onto his white, clean pants, and his eyes, glassy blue things, latch onto the gray stain. His eyebrow twitches. “I’m not interested.”

The artist’s hand jerks, and he tightens his hold around their wrist. He turns towards them, watching as they open their mouth to say something probably more biting than the last. But, there must be something in Mydei’s gaze as he stares at the artist, because they shut his mouth with a ‘click!’

Their hand jerks yet again.

Mydei lets it go, this time, and watches pointedly as the artist brings it towards their chest.

They look at Mydei, then to Khaslana, and back to Mydei once again before they swallow, taking one step back, two, three, and halting at four.

Mydei raises an eyebrow at them.

The artist all but scrambles out of the balcony.

The door closes with enough force to rattle the whole wooden structure under their feet. The cloud above them stretches and expands above them, like cotton pulled too far, letting some of the bright rays of sun filter down to earth like little fish in a big net. The girl who was tapping something or another on her phone looks rattled, eyes flickering anxiously to them and the door while the man in far too polished of a suit with a fedora keeps reading the newspaper.

Mydei, once again, turns to Khaslana, who is still watching the gray ash stain.

“I brought you a milkshake.”

The words are firm, certain, as Mydei always is, but they still come out more gently than he intended.

Khaslana’s eyes flicker towards the milkshakes in the table and instead of taking one, he takes a drag of his cigarette.

Mydei waits, and, after a couple more minutes, Khaslana sighs, “You are ridiculous.” He says, but, nevertheless, grabs the pomegranate one, takes a sip, and makes a face at it.

Despite the situation, Mydei still finds it in himself to be amused at the reaction, “What is it?”

“...I thought it was strawberry.”

“You didn’t like it.”

“No, it’s fine.” He replies, taking another sip. He doesn’t make a face, this time, though he still doesn’t look as if he liked it. Mydei does not grab the vanilla one and Khasana repeats , sounding exhausted, “You truly are ridiculous.”

“For the milkshakes?”

“For this,” He waves a hand in the general direction of the table before picking up the salt container again. “It was unnecessary.”

“Unnecessary.” Mydei repeats, flatly.

Khaslana shrugs, brushing the salt crystals off the table. The little things fall and snake their way into the gaps left by the wood, like sugar drilling cavities.

Mydei looks at him.

“How often does this happen?”

He picks up the sketch, looks at it, eyes drifting through the desperate strokes. “I have told you before, haven’t I? Not everybody has your self-restraint.”

“Khaslana.”

“It’s fine.”

“Fine.” Mydei scoffs. Khaslana’s eye twitches. “You looked like you were about to put out the cigarette on them.”

His head jerks upwards. “I wasn’t.”

“I never said you would. I am saying you looked like you wanted to.”

Khaslana’s mouth opens, closes, and takes a long, slow drag of his cigarette instead of answering him.

“It pisses you off, doesn’t it?”

“You already asked me that question before.”

“And you didn’t answer.” Mydei replies, plucking the paper from Khaslana’s hand and settling it down on the table in a way the sketch isn’t seen. “Not concretely, at least.”

“I said there’s no use getting mad about it.”

“So, you do get mad about it.”

“I didn’t say that.”

“Didn’t you?”

“Maybe.” He all but spits, admits. He takes another drag and, as the smoke curls around every syllable he speaks, Mydei imagines him setting fire to his own heart. “But what does it matter? How people see me won’t change.”

“I changed.” Mydei replies easily.

“That doesn’t count.”

“Why not?”

“Because it’s you.”

Mydei’s eyes flicker from one place of Khaslana’s face to another, and he watches the drawn eyebrows, the tight jaw, the fire burning, crackling, consuming inside his eyes, and something occurs to him, and he asks, blurts out, almost, “Did it piss you off?” And at Khaslana’s look of confusion, he adds, “When I first asked if I could paint you at the side of the pond. Were you angry?”

For a moment, Khaslana looks so, so terribly lost. It’s almost painful to see.

“I—I don’t—” He starts, tries, and breaks, “It’s not—”

“Yes or no, Khaslana.”

“Yes—No. I mean, no. Maybe.” A pause, a wince and then, in a whisper, “...A little bit, I think.”

“A little bit?”

“I don’t know, alright?” He snaps, then sighs, as if the energy physically drained out of him. “I don’t know. It’s—always there, underneath it all, the anger,” He turns to the cigarette in his hand, watches as the flame on top consumes the white slips of paper around the tobacco, leaving only ash and smoke behind. “It’s rather ugly, if you ask me.”

Mydei breathes, but the answer is simple, “Isn’t that just human, though?”

Khaslana’s head whips to him so fast that Mydei can actually hear something in his neck snap.

“Don’t.” He spits, begs. “Don’t say that. Not to me.”

Mydei looks at him.

“Why not?”

Khaslana’s does not reply.

Getting answers out of Khaslana is like pulling teeth. Mydei has no intention of hurting him, but he has no intention of letting him keep burying himself alive either.

“Why not?” Silence. Mydei’s fist clenches. “Why not, Khaslana?”

“Because I might believe it!”

The words land like a rock into a frozen lake, crashing and cracking the ice before sinking deep into the cold waters, creating ripples and a hundred million jagged ends. Khaslana’s hand jerks as he says it, slamming onto the table, and the pomegranate milkshake tumbles down onto the table, pink spreading through the table and being absorbed by the paper like blood.

Khaslana’s expression flickers, and he brings his hand onto his lap.

Wordlessly, Mydei plucks a couple of brown napkins from the holder in the middle. He picks up the pomegranate milkshake, cleans the liquid clinging to the side of the plastic glass before moving to clean the table.

A couple minutes pass in muted silence, fallen like a thick blanket on a hot summer day onto the space between them. The girl taping away something or another on her phone went away some time ago, and there’s another man dressed identically to the one with far too polished of a suit and a fedora watching as the other bangs his head repeatedly on the table with a guilty expression. In his hand, a case that would be identical to the other, save for the fact that one is bright red, shines under the few rays of the sun.

Once it is cleaned, Mydei picks up the soggy napkins, stands up, throws them in a nearby trashcan and comes back to sit right back at Khaslana’s side.

“...Sorry.”

Mydei sighs. “You are so terribly stupid.”

“And you are so terribly cruel.”

He blinks, once, twice, eyes going to Khaslana. Silently, he watches as he finishes the cigarette, throws it on the ground and squashes the flame with his shoe. Then, immediately, he picks up the messenger bag he had placed on the floor. He opens it, takes a cigarette box with a dead dove on the front and a red lighter.

He places the end in his mouth.

“Another one?”

“Shut up, Mydeimos.” He mumbles. The lighter lits up with a silent ‘click!’ and a ‘ts!’ and, with stark, sad ease, he lights the cigarette.

For a man like Khaslana, maybe care is just another form of cruelty.

A necessary one, in Mydei’s opinion.

Carelessly, Khaslana throws the lighter and the box of cigarettes back into his messenger bag. A black pen rests on top of a copy of The Princess and the Cat, and Mydei takes it before the flap closes.

He takes another napkin, places it on the table, and draws a game of tic-tac-toe. He places an ‘x’ and extends it towards Khaslana.

Haltingly, he grabs it, and, haltingly, he places a ‘o’ on the top right corner.

He extends it back to Mydei.

Mydei takes it.

“...You are not asking.”

Mydei blinks, draws another ‘x’ on the bottom right corner, and passes the pen back. There are a lot of things he could be asking, truth be told, but, somehow, someway, he knows exactly what Khaslana is referring to.

“You are not talking.”

Khaslana breathes.

A dozen rounds of tic-tac-toe replace the tick-tock-tick of time where none of them win.

It’s anticlimactic, almost.

“Do you know the process of pinning butterflies?” Khaslana asks, drawing another board on the napkin. “To kill them, you put them in a freezer so that the wings won’t be damaged, and then you unfreeze them. Afterwards, you put a pin right in the middle of their body and there’s—this little thing,” He puts two fingers side to side, leaving a gap in the middle. “Where you put them, and then you put some type of paper onto the wings, to keep them down and in place.”

A ‘x’ in the middle right, none of them wins.

Mydei draws another board.

“It’s hard, frankly, more often than not, you end up taking one if not all of the butterfly’s legs in the process, and the wings are so delicate they break as you try to make them look symmetrical and pretty.”

A ‘o’ in the top left, none of them wins.

Khaslana draws another board.

“...I dream about it, sometimes.”

Mydei’s eyes shift to Khaslana.

He doesn’t look at him as he places another ‘o’ in the napkin. “More often than not, Lycurgus is the one pinning me in place.” A pause. “That’s all you need to know.”

A hundred million things said and a billion hundred more left unsaid.

Mydei draws another board. The strength with which he does it tears the little napkin with the same ease butterfly wings are torn.

My Magnum Opus, Lygus had said.

Something hot bubbles up in Mydei’s stomach, and his teeth clench. To lament and sigh at how life has turned out is a fantastic way to drive yourself insane and drown in sorrow, and, as such, Mydei does not. Yet, there’s a small part of him, a small part of his heart, that still wishes he could have met Khaslana earlier.

He does not know how to reply.

“I—” He starts.

“Don’t.”

So, he doesn’t.

Khaslana takes another napkin, places it on the table.

Mydei obliges and draws another board, and a couple of ‘x’s’ and ‘o’s’ pass in place of words.

“I met Castorice,” He replies instead. Khaslana halts. “A couple months ago. She asked me to tell you that she’s glad you are alive.”

The cigarette slips out of Khaslana’s fingers.

The breath he lets out is shaky, though his eyes are dry as ever. His hand hovers in the air, uncertain, for what seems to be a lifetime, before grabbing the pen instead of the cigarette.

Mydei takes the cigarette as Khaslana writes an ‘o’ on the middle right. He throws it to the ground and squashes it under his foot. As he said before, he’s not one to tell Khaslana what or what not to do, but that does not mean he wants to see him indulge in little deaths like this one.

“And, if it matters,” Mydei continues, placing an ‘x’ on the bottom right and drawing a diagonal line. He wins. “I’m glad you are alive, too.”

Khaslana turns to him. Something indescribable, almost incredulous, but all too vulnerable crosses his expression, and Mydei meets his gaze head on. It’s all too easy to do so. He’s not ashamed, much less embarrassed, of his words, not when each and every one is rooted in sincerity.

Mydei cares, is the thing, and he cares deeply, devotedly, ferociously.

Khaslana laughs. It’s a little bit sad. “You are so dramatic.” He breathes. “I don’t want to die5.”

“I still want you to hear it.” Mydei admits.

Khaslana lays his arms on the table and rests his head on top of them.

“I will leave, though, one day.”

“...Why?”

“I don’t know.” He replies, closing his eyes. “But I always do.”

“I will go with you, then.”

“You don’t even know where we would be going.”

“It doesn’t matter.”

Khaslana cracks one eye open. “And if you can’t find me?”

“Then, I will wait for you.” He replies, unflinchingly. “As long as it takes for you to come back.”

“Sounds exhausting.” Khaslana replies. His voice nothing but a whisper. A part of Mydei wonders if he’s falling asleep as they talk. “You should spend that energy waiting for someone worthy. A savior, a hero, certainly not someone like me.”

“But you are worth it.”

Khaslana opens both eyes.

“Why?”

Ha! What sort of question is that? Hasn’t Mydei made it obvious?

“Because I care about you.”

Khaslana opens his mouth to reply, but nothing comes out. Instead, his eyebrows furrow as Mydei pushes the vanilla milkshake towards him and takes the pomegranate one.

“That’s—”

“I prefer the pomegranate one.” Mydei replies, and takes a sip. “I will ask for the strawberry one for you, next time, but I think you might like this one.”

Khaslana stares, breathes, and, after a beat, takes a sip of the other one.

“...It’s sweet.”

“That a complaint?”

“No.” He says, softly. “I like it.”

A pause.

"Thank you."

Chapter End Notes

FOOTNOTES

1. Ergo, Khaslana. Back

2. Many have told Mister Reception Man to quit the crosswords and instead just stick to the cheap gossip magazines, seeing he sucks so bad at it. He’s intent on finishing one for this very reason. Back

3. That Khaslana pretends not to see. Back

4. The restaurant, nicknamed fondly as Not a Tavern, does not usually have pomegranates, much less milkshakes made of it. If you were to ask the owner, he would tell you it’s the season. In reality, though, the old man who throws tomatoes at the cathedral had wondered if pomegranates would be harder to clean off. When he found that, no, they weren’t, he had already cultivated a ton. In a show of goodwill, he proceeded to dump all of them here and, kindly, threaten them to either keep the fruit or be pelted to death with rocks. Back

5. Make no mistake, this is no lie. Though, it would be a lie to say he hadn’t thought about it, in the same way a soldier thinks about his death. All-too close, all-too tangibly, all-too present. Would his body be left to rot at the side of an art studio? Will it be kept like a doll in a glass showcase? What of the mortician preparing his body? Will they, too, obsess over him? No, Khaslana does not want to die, if anything, he always wanted to find a reason to live, but he thinks that if he were to die, he would not want it to leave him pretty, and he certainly would not want to be found. Back

━━━━━━━━━━

EXTRA

The last message on the chat is a defeated ‘I am here if you ever need anything’ sent by Castorice three and a half years ago.

Khaslana stares at it for what seems to be an eternity, fingers hovering over the keyboard as guilt eats away his guts like termites eat away wood.

He does not know how to reply.

He scrolls far, far up to his chat, and something bitter claws up to his mouth when he sees the ease in which he used to talk, in which he used to be, and a part of him wonders if he should just copy one of those texts, but, no matter how much tries, it all comes a little too stiff.

She’s glad you are alive, repeats in his head like a mantra and, in a surge of courage, he sends her a simple ‘still alive’.

‘I’m glad’, is the immediate response, and Khaslana flings his phone to the other side of the room. Heart beating in his eardrums like a war chant, bile crawling up to his throat and he wants to throw up.

His phone buzzes. Once, twice.

He could not answer.

He picks up the phone. The screen is cracked.

‘There’s a book fair happening in a week,’ reads the first. ‘Do you want to come with me?’ reads the second.

A part of him does not want to answer, wants to cut the connection before it even has the chance to re-grow, take the flowers and keep the weeds, because misery is easy, happiness all-too terrifying, and vulnerability feels like ripping the nails out of his hands.

She’s glad you are alive.

Khaslana breathes, happiness is hard, but, he thinks, now that he has remembered the beginnings of its taste, he’s willing to fight for it. So, he takes out a few nails and, with bleeding fingers, answers ‘yes’.

It’s funny, almost, he didn’t know how much he missed her until he saw her again.

chapters.title: Chapter 11: Budding flowers
chapters.html:
Pitter-patter, goes the world outside, pitter-patter, pitter-patter, as rain falls down from the skies. A wide sheet of water pulled over the dark veil of the night like the closing curtains of a theater play, quickly gaining intensity like thundering applause. It’s the last day of the Month of Strife, and the clouds have already started to cry as seconds pass and the Month of Mourning approaches.

A little 'clack, clack, clack', accompanies the sound of falling rain. Specks of ice bounce on the floor as it hails. One last battle, one last war, one last attack before the last soldier falls to the ground to be buried alive. Under the dim yellow lights of the light posts outside, the little white dots of frozen tears look more like little pieces of broken stars, soon to be pulled into the crude rectangular holes at the side of the road that leads into the sewers by the running water.

There’s a certain tranquility to the sound despite the growing violence of the grief, a certain beauty, maybe, and, for a minute or two, both of them simply stare out at the rain. A faint breeze of cold air filters deep into the crevices of the terracotta bricks through the open door as they both linger at the entrance. It’s way past eight. Nine ten, maybe, or nine fifteen.

“I didn’t bring an umbrella.”

Khaslana’s voice is soft at his side, calm in the same way staring out into the rain is.

“I have one.” Mydei replies, watching the trunks of the faraway trees tilt to the right and the leaves blow out like manes of wild hair. “But I don’t think it is going to serve you much with the wind. You are going to get drenched, either way.”

“Yeah.” Khaslana breathes out, sounding resigned. “I guess I should make a run for it, then.”

“You are going to get sick.”

“Probably.”

Little specks of ice bounce off his red car parked outside with a dull, metallic 'clang, clang, clang', nearly lost under the cries of the sky. Mydei stares at it, feeling the way that the raindrops that fall onto the stone steps in front of him break and sprinkle onto the hem of his pants, before he turns his head to the side to see Khaslana. The key of his car, resting next to his mother’s vase on the coffee table in his living room, glints damningly from the corner of his eye.

Mydei stares at it with distant consideration before his eyes shift back to Khaslana.

Selfishly, or foolishly, maybe, though Mydei does not particularly care about the nature of his sudden, almost childish, impulse, instead of offering him a ride, he asks, “Do you want to stay the night?”

Khaslana blinks. Once, twice, before he turns towards him. A stray lock of white hair falls into his face as he tilts his head and, without permission, Mydei’s eyes can’t help but track the way long, pale fingers go to tuck it behind his ear.

Pitter-patter, goes the rain, pitter-patter, pitter-patter.

“I don’t exactly have another set of clothes.”

It’s not a no. It’s not a yes, either. Mydei shrugs. “I can lend you some.”

“Will they even fit?”

Mydei sighs, annoyed, this time. Khaslana’s mouth twitches.

“You keep talking as if I barely reached your waist when there’s barely any difference in our height, you know.”

“But there is a difference.”

Mydei clicks his tongue.

“I’m going to kick you out into the street.”

“No, you won’t.” He replies, instantly, with a certainty that surprises even Khaslana, if the way he blinks and falters right after is any indication. The funny part is that he’s not even wrong. Not one bit.

Still, “Don’t try me.” Mydei threatens without any real heat, waving his hand in the general direction of the empty street.

Bottom-deep ocean eyes shift from one side of his face to another. Searching for something held between the planes of his expression that he seems to find after a beat or two, and he goes to watch the rain once again.

Pitter-patter, it cries, pitter-patter, pitter-patter.

“Ha.” He sighs, laughs. Only once. “I wouldn’t dare.”

“Mm-hm.” He lets out, not convinced before he, too, goes back to watch the rain. A layer of thick, white fog has started to raise, meandering through the space like a snake in between the grass. It’s getting colder. “Does that mean you will stay?”

“...Maybe.” Khaslana concedes faintly, uncertain. “If it isn’t much of a bother.”

“I wouldn’t be offering if it were.”

There’s a long, long pause.

Movement from the corner of his eye catches his attention, and Mydei’s eyes flicker to the side to find Khaslana’s gloved hand going up and down, up and down, up and down, through the strap of his messenger back, before they flicker back to the rain.

“I will just drive you home if you don’t want to.”

“No, it’s not that. I—” He starts, breaks, and breathes. “I will stay,” Another pause. “For tonight.”

The corner of Mydei’s mouth twitches upwards. “For tonight.” He repeats and closes the door with a soft ‘click’. The cold from the pit-pat rain still lingers inside the nooks and crannies of his house, but his chest feels warm, for some strange, strange reason.

━━━━━━━━━━

Mydei’s house does not have a guest room. The expanse of the second floor of his home is occupied by his bedroom, a closet room and a bathroom. Khaslana protests rather vehemently when Mydei says he will take the couch and, effectively, shuts down any protest by threatening to fill his shoes with paint and entering the bathroom to take a shower before Mydei even has the chance to reply1.

In the meantime, Mydei changes into a set of pajamas, which is a very generous description, considering it consists solely of a pair of loose sweatpants and a rather pronounced lack of shirt. He also leaves a pair of fuzzy red pajama pants, a pair of socks, and well-worn, well-loved black hoodie with the logo of a rock band he used to be really into a couple of years ago2 outside the bathroom for Khaslana to change into before he goes to rummage around his closet for some blankets.

He is not the kind of person to get cold easily, truth be told, and the second floor is considerably warmer than the first one. So, it takes him some time to pull those from the very top, which is, apparently, enough time for Khaslana to get out of the shower and the low rumble and guttural groan of the washing machine that Mydei is pretty sure will just explode on him one day to filter through the floors.

Ultimately, he manages to take out a heavy, green blanket that faintly smells like dust, and he’s already halfway through the door before he catches sight of the little white label sewn in a corner that reads in thick black letters ‘100% cotton’.

A distant recollection of a conversation scratches at the back of his mind at the sight. He frowns, places the thing on his bed before going back into the closet. He rummages some more and finds a thick white wool blanket that he had forgotten he owned. He barely uses it, too much of a sensory nightmare, but it had been a gift, so he had never thrown it out.

He picks one of the pillows on his bed and makes his way halfway down the stairs. The low humming of the probably soon to explode washing machine arises is muted, nearly drowned by the ever-distant pitter-patter from the rain outside. He cranes his head to the end of the hallway, where the laundry room is placed, just to find it closed.

“Khaslana?” A distant, half-shouted ‘what?’ comes from the direction of the kitchen, and Mydei asks, “Is wool alright?”

"Is what alright?”

“Wool.” Mydei repeats, louder.

“...Uh?”

“Just come here.”

A few seconds pass before Khaslana pops out of the kitchen, idly scrolling through his phone and finishing eating a cookie from the batch the kind old lady next door had given him yesterday3. His hair is still wet from the shower, water darkening the fabric of the hoodie around his neck. Mydei’s hoodie. It fits him nicely, Mydei notes with a distant sense of satisfaction, though the fuzzy red pants, on the other hand, do end awkwardly around his shins.

He has also put the purple glove back on.

Mydei stares at it for a second too long. He has long realized its presence is not exactly merely a fashion choice on his part, and he thinks it would be rather naïve to attribute it only to sentimentality. It’s much too deliberate, much too present, to be that.

Still, instead of hounding him with questions he’s more than sure will only serve to make Khaslana bite, his eyes go down to the fluffy chimera slippers the man hijacked and asks, “Did you go through my closet?”

Not looking up from his phone, he replies, “Your cat would have snapped my neck if I so much dared to look at your room, Mydei.”

“Hm.” He lets out, blandly, already accustomed to Khaslana’s random surges of dramatism. “With his fuzzy little paws?”

“With his deadly fuzzy little paws, yes.”

“Where did you find my slippers, then?”

“Dryer.”

“Ah.”

“Do you want them back?”

“Will you actually give them back to me if I say yes?”

“No. They are comfy.”

“Thought so.”

“Be nice to me.” He says, dryly.

“I’m being more than nice.”

“Hmph.” Khaslana lets out. He turns to him, the beginning of an answer forming in his mouth before he cuts himself abruptly and blurts out, “You— Why are you naked?

Mydei blinks, looks down at himself, raises an eyebrow and turns to face Khaslana again, who is staring at the expanse of his naked chest with a blank expression.

“I’m not naked.” Mydei replies, lifting the blanket so that he can see the loose sweatpants he’s using. Khaslana does not look away from his chest. “And my eyes are up here.”

A beat of silence passes as Khaslana registers the words and, once he does, he goes bright red, much to Mydei’s amusement. He coughs once into his hand to dissimulate his embarrassment. “Sorry. It’s just—” His eyes flick down, up. “It’s a little bit distracting.” He mumbles out.

“Distracting.” Mydei repeats, slowly and, out of curiosity, flexes one of his pecs.

Khaslana goes even redder, if possible.

Heh.

“Heh.”

That does snap him out of it. “Show off.” He accuses.

“Jealousy is an ugly sight on you, Khaslana.” Mydei shoots back immediately. Khaslana scoffs. It’s a little funny, truth be told, but he’s still mindful enough to add, “I can put on a shirt if it makes you uncomfortable, though."

Khaslana opens his mouth, closes it, and, ultimately, sighs, “You don’t have to change your habits just because I’m here, you know. It’s still your house…”

“So, you don’t want me to put on a shirt?” Mydei says. Khaslana doesn’t go red this time. Shame. But the look he sends his way is still amusing, nonetheless. He shakes his head and jostles the blanket in his hands. “Nevermind. Is wool alright?”

Khaslana tilts his head to the side, confused.

Mydei raises an eyebrow. “Aren’t you allergic to cotton?”

“...I am, yes.” He frowns. “How did you know?”

“You told me.”

“I did?”

Mydei nods.

“Oh.”

A pause.

“I’m surprised you even remember that.”

“I remember everything you tell me.” Mydei replies easily, naturally, and entirely unaware of the immeasurable weight his words carry, because such fact it’s not a weight to him, neither a deep secret, just a simple, straightforward truth.

The same can’t be said about Khaslana, though, who blinks once, twice, before the words and their implications sink deep into him and his eyes widen.

Pitter patter, goes the rain, pitter-patter, pitter-patter. The noise may be washing away all the sound right out of Khaslana’s vocal cords, drowning out the syllables underwater as Mydei watches him mouth an answer without being able to let out a single word.

One of his hands goes to his neck, long fingers going to toy with the straps of the black choker around it before Khaslana realizes he already took it off for the night, and instead he presses his palm against his mouth.

A second passes, then two, three. Tick-tock-tick. Time stolen by the mischievous winds of Zagreus outside, dancing in between strife and death.

“You—” He starts, tries, and breaks, voice muffled. “You really are—” A pause, and his eyes lower, and maybe the light-footed, time-stealing jester snuck in between the crevices of the terracotta bricks uninvited and came to sway and hide Khaslana’s little bleeding, childish heart, for what he says instead is, “...Must be pretty empty up there if that’s the case.”

Mydei blinks, looking up at the ceiling. “Up there?” He repeats just to immediately catch on and sigh. “Must you keep finding clever ways to call me stupid?”

“Why, does it piss you off?”

“Immensely so.”

Khaslana’s smiles are a rather precious thing, truth be told. Mydei does not know if he would admit it if asked, not out of shyness, and much less greediness, selfishness, perhaps; but he does know he would not be able to deny it, not then, not after, not now—Especially not now, not when Khaslana’s hand falls from his mouth to reveal pale, chapped lips curved upwards. Soft, small, a little mischievous, this time. They come easier to him now, the smiles, but they still feel as wondrous as the first rays of light at dawn after a long night.

Though, right now, it does not make it any less infuriating because of that.

Mydei feels the weight of the wool blanket in his hands. Heavy, but not overly so, and asks again, “Is wool fine, then?”

Khaslana nods, still smiling. “Wool is fine.”

“Great.” He says and immediately throws the blanket towards Khaslana’s head, who yelps and, pulled down by its weight, falls down to the floor with a loud ‘blam!’.

He resurfaces slowly from under it, shaking his head before he turns to glare at him. As soon as he does so, Mydei throws the pillow directly at his face like a seasoned pitcher would throw a baseball.

“Ha.” Mydei chuckles. “Jackass.”

The pillow slides off Khaslana’s face and down to the floor with a dull ‘plaff’, revealing a very disgruntled expression underneath.

Approximately five seconds pass before Mydei bolts onto the second floor as Khaslana chases him to hit him with the pillow, and, approximately, another ten pass before it is Khaslana the one darting off onto the first floor as Mydei chases him with two.

Pitter-patter, goes the rain, but Mydei can’t hear it over the wild ba-thump-thump of his beat–ing heart.

━━━━━━━━━━

Truth be told, truth be said, there isn’t any particularly interesting event worth the waste of flowery words and redundant descriptions that happens over the course of the night. The rain pitter-patters, the ice hails, and an admittedly late dinner stretches for hours upon hours as they talk of this and that, here and there, did-you-know’s and no-I-did-not’s, before Morpheus’ arms come to rest upon weary shoulders.

And, then, morning comes, as all mornings often do, rather unceremoniously. Aquila’s eyes crack open bit by bit as he, too, struggles to escape the throes of late sleep, the throes of early death, until he shakes himself awake and the skies clear and the stars disappear, for the Eye of Twilight has always been much too proud to resign his half of the day to the Veil of Night.

Mydei follows soon after. The clock on his nightstand shifts from eight cero cero to eight cero six in the time it takes him to muster enough strength to get out of the warm comfort of his bed with lazy movements before he goes down. Some of the steps creak and grind under his weight, up until he sees a little white cloud of hair peeking from the side of his couch and he stops.

Khaslana is still asleep.

Still here.

…

He wants to look at him.

The thought comes unbidden, unannounced. It surges all the way from the tips of his fingers to the confines of his chest, running along his veins like blood. It’s not an unfamiliar want, not really, nor a strange desire, and it is not unusual, not really, for him to do so, whether he’s painting or not.

But, it’s different, this time, for reasons he can’t quite pinpoint, and, Mydei, rather foolishly, he himself will admit, can’t help but feel like a thief sneaking under the cover of the night about to steal the most precious of treasures as his steps turn careful, silent, avoiding loud noises and abrupt awakenings while he makes his way towards Khaslana.

One step, two, and then three. Four, five, and then six.

And then he bends over the couch’s headrest.

There’s nothing particularly noteworthy in Khaslana’s sleeping expression, if he's being honest. Not in the way pale pink lips, bitten and chapped, part slightly as his cheek squashes on the pillow, not in the way the tip of his nose has gained a faint reddened hue thanks to the cold, nor in the tranquil softness of his face, and much less in the way a stray strand of white hair curls on his cheek.

Mydei is mesmerized, nevertheless.

Vulnerability, is the thing, is a strange sight on Khaslana.

His hand moves out of its own volition, out of pure, unadulterated emotion, and Mydei is still so captivated that he barely manages to catch himself just as his fingers come close to graze the man’s cheek.

There’s a second of hesitation, almost, encapsulated, contained and witnessed by the walls of his house. A second where Mydei almost, just almost, wishes to not have the kind of self-awareness and restraint that he does, because, now, he can not say that tucking the strand stray of hair behind Khaslana’s ear is anything other than a conscious decision.

Khaslana’s eyes twitch, long lashes fluttering like the wings of a butterfly as his head shifts towards him.

It would be terribly, deceivingly easy to say Mydei’s heart stutters in his chest. A beat, beat, be–at too long, a be–at skipped. A rug pulled out his feet. A bucket of cold water splashing over him. Hand flying as if it had been burnt. Easy, yes, but untrue. Love is terrifying and love is wonderful, and there’s an inherent fear, maybe, of it being caught so blatantly, so mundanely. But there’s nothing of the sort as the deep blue of Khaslana’s eyes peeks and peers up at him, as it is, Mydei doesn’t even move his hand away from where it is now pressed against the side of Khaslana’s face, and a part of him wonders what does that mean.

“Mydei?” Khaslana mumbles out. His voice is rough, and he’s eyes aren’t opened fully, almost as if he’s debating whether to shake himself awake or simply burrow himself deeper in the blanket. He does not ask what he’s doing, for some reason, and instead asks, “What hour is it?”

Mydei’s fingers card through his hair. And that, too, is a conscious decision. “Early,” He replies, quietly. His hair is soft. “Go back to sleep.”

Khaslana blinks once, twice and, wordlessly, closes his eyes once again.

It’s such a small action, but it undoes him.

Whatever butterflies might have been pullulating in Mydei’s stomach and fluttering on the crevices of his throat fall and fly out of his mouth with each exhalation he gives. He can feel the pulsations of his heart spreading like wildfire all the way from his chest to the end of his fingertips, and he all but has to hold himself on the couch’s headrest to avoid falling.

“I…” Mydei starts, stops. He’s not sure what to say, not sure how to convey the enormity of what he’s feeling, not even sure of what he’s feeling, just knowing that it feels as if he’s being pulled around by the seams only to reveal the raw of his insides. “Can I paint you?”

“Why are you asking?” Khaslana doesn’t open his eyes. “You paint me all the time.”

Mydei breathes. Flip-flap, make the butterflies. “Still.”

He sighs as he burrows himself deeper into the blankets. “You are so very strange, did you know that?” He mumbles before cracking an eye open. “Catch me drooling and I am tossing my shoes into your washing machine.”

Mydei’s mouth twitches upwards.

His fluffy chimera slippers rest neatly at the side of the couch, and Mydei hijacks them back before walking to his art studio to retrieve a white canvas and his paint case with his ugly chimeras painted at the sides. He finds a stack of brushes held by a stretched-out white hair tie on top of one of the shelves of the bookshelf there, and he takes it out and uses it to tie his hair into a high ponytail.

When he goes back to the living room, Khaslana is already fast asleep, still in his home, still on his couch, still here.

It’s, well, not strange, Mydei thinks as he sits down a couple of steps away from the couch and props the canvas in between his legs, not quite, they are already far past that point, but there’s something about it that is making him heady, maybe. He’s overly-aware, from one moment to the other, that, were this situation have happened earlier, much, much earlier, when skin resembled marble and emptiness proved to be much more alluring than the blatant humanity held in between bottomless eyes, Khaslana would not have hesitated once in stepping outside even if the rain and the hail were nails and daggers; wouldn’t even have given Mydei the chance to offer his umbrella.

And now he’s here.

━━━━━━━━━━

Time passes slowly, bit by bit, tick by tick, grains of sand falling one by one. The ‘clack, clack, clack’ of the hail outside has long stopped, and the rain outside no longer pitter-patters, but it has not yet stopped. A faint drizzle bathes the streets today. The beginning of the Month of Mourning is silent, but heavy.

The low fwish and swish of the brush pressing and dragging on the linen, however, isn’t mournful—if anything, is almost reverent, gentle, as he goes over the soft strokes of the planes of Khaslana’s expression.

Mydei is not yet done by the time Khaslana awakes. He’s painting with loose swirls the strands and curls of his hair splayed across the pillow when his eyes flutter open.

“Morning.”

He blinks a couple of times, shaking off the drowsiness before replying, belatedly, “Morning.” And he yawns. “Did you finish?”

“How fast do you think I paint? It’s barely even been,” Mydei pauses. He places the brush on the table with a little ‘clack’ and turns around. Khaslana’s phone is a couple of steps behind him, left charging through the night. He stretches, practically laying on the floor and manages to tap it once with his middle finger. The time reads ten twenty4. “Two hours.”

Mydei sits down once again. He picks up a new brush and mixes some colors in the plastic palette placed on the coffee table to match the wool blanket crumpled around Khaslana as he hums.

“What’s the theme?”

“None.” Mydei replies. “This isn’t for the competition.”

“It isn’t…?”

There’s a long beat before the rustle of fabric arises. Mydei’s eyes shift upwards and sees Khaslana lifting the top of his body as he cranes his neck to try and catch sight of the canvas on his lap. His eyes aren’t wide, but there’s certainly an undertone of incredulousness around him.

Mydei drags himself towards him, twisting so that his back is against the couch and Khaslana has a clear view of the canvas as he goes over the repetitive patterns that create the blanket with his brush.

One, two, three strokes. He dips the brush in paint and does another three.

The silence isn’t heavy, but it is charged with an unvoiced question in the air. Mydei already knows which one is it, and, so, he answers simply, “I wanted to.”

“...Yes.” Khaslana replies, quietly. Slowly, he lays back down. “I had a feeling you would say that.”

Mydei’s fingers twitch around the brush. He shifts his head sideways, and, this close, he can smell the scent of his own shampoo in Khaslana’s hair, and it hits him all at once, the underlying intimacy of this moment, this everything. Khaslana in his home, in his clothes, in his life.

His, a treacherous part of his mind thinks. Mine.

He swallows. “You know me well, then.”

Khaslana gives a half-hearted shrug. His left hand, ever gloved, sneaks from under the warmth of the blanket to pull lightly at a strand from his ponytail and, wordlessly, Mydei scoots closer. There’s a pause, followed by a faint rustle before Mydei feels his hair tie being pulled off.

The brush nearly slips out of his hands.

“What are you doing?”

“It’s weird seeing you without a braid.” It’s his excuse as he divides his hair into three sections. “Though, I can make you pigtails if you want.”

“...The braid is fine.” He breathes out and wonders if Khaslana understands just how significant what he’s doing is.

Hair, in general, is important in kremonan tradition. It’s a warrior’s pride. A symbol of strength. A point of honor.

In the past, he had been taught, his people used to braid a section of their hair and only cut it whenever they lost in battle. Having it cut, not in between the strife and bloodshed, but in between deception and treachery, became the worst kind of humiliation. As a result, touching a person’s hair, doing a person’s hair, became something akin to a ritual, reserved only to family, confidants, close friends and only very close friends, and—

Equals5.

Ha! Oh, how far has Mydei fallen, to contemplate such thoughts, and he thinks of telling Khaslana this—laugh about it, even. But the laughter gets stuck in his throat, suffocated by fluttering butterflies, because he knows that, flighty, as Khaslana can be, he would stop immediately.

Love, if what he’s feeling truly is that, makes you stupid, Mydei concludes, as the treacherous part of him that whispered mine, also whispers, yours.

“Mydei.”

Flip-flap, make the butterflies. “What is it?”

“Why,” He starts, stops. “Why do you paint?”

A blink.

“Right now?”

“In general, I mean.”

Mydei thinks about it for a minute or two, maybe even three. Khaslana lets him. His hands are gentle as he twists the strands of his hair around each other.

“It used to be because of my mother.” He says after a beat, and it feels strange, frankly, to admit this sort of thing. Has anybody ever asked him this question? Has Mydei himself? “She was a painter, back when she was alive, and I remember picking up her brushes and sitting myself next to her for hours on end.” A memory comes unbidden, and Mydei can’t help but chuckle. “I once painted over one of hers, you know. Made a very bad cat on top of a landscape that took her weeks to make.”

Khaslana lets out an amused breath. “Was she angry?”

“...I don’t remember.” He replies, almost distantly. “But I know she framed it.”

“Oh, she liked it, then.”

Yeah, he supposed she did. Still, “It was always embarrassing to see, to be honest.”

“Do you have a photo?”

“Hmph. You just want to make fun of me.”

“A little bit.” Khaslana admits, tying the end of the braid and letting it fall on Mydei’s back. It’s a little loose, and a few strands escaped him here and there. He wonders if pointing that out would be enough to get him to do it again. “But I also want to see it.”

Mydei sighs. “There must be one, somewhere.”

“Mm.”

The moment stretches like bubblegum pulled between teeth as silence sweeps into his house like ants underneath the floorboards. It’s not heavy, though, and not charged either. Khaslana doesn’t prod nor doesn’t push as Mydei sits quietly in front of him, lost in thought, like a sailor left ashore.

A little ‘click, click’ arises from the staircase after a while, and Mydei cranes his neck long enough to see Kopopo The Third dragging his little feet as he makes his way down. He always gets drowsy with the cold, and Mydei watches as he disappears into the kitchen just to reemerge with his mouth and paws wet.

It takes him a second to notice Khaslana, but when he does, he pins Mydei with a surprisingly judgmental look, which is remarkable considering he’s a cat.

“...What?”

Kopopo The Third sniffs, lifting his little fuzzy chin haughtily before making his way towards them. With all the grace a spoiled cat can have, jumps onto the couch and pins Khaslana with the same judgemental look he gave Mydei.

He meows once6.

Khaslana, strangely unpreoccupied considering all the time his cat has attempted to go for his jugular, tilts his head and asks, “Are you cold?”

It seems the temperature has significantly mellowed his cat out, or maybe he has finally started to warm up to Khaslana, because instead of getting hissy, Kopopo The Third simply makes a sound close to a scoff, and lays down in an empty spot in the couch, shoving himself into the wool blanket to continue sleeping.

Khaslana blinks owlishly, and, hesitantly, places a hand on top of his little fuzzy back.

Kopopo The Third meows sharply, but otherwise makes no move to bite his fingers off.

“Oh.” Khaslana lets out, a little amazed, maybe. “It’s been a while since a cat has let me pet it.”

A drop of paint falls to the floor.

Mydei looks down at the little dot of white. He makes no move to wipe it out, because then he will just have a bigger stain to clean afterwards, and places both the canvas and the brush on his coffee table before reclining once again on the couch’s welt. Khaslana keeps petting Kopopo The Third with careful movements.

It may be the weird sort of domesticity they have fallen into, or, more likely, the steadily growing trust that had grown bit by bit, that makes Mydei continue, “I didn’t paint for years after she died.”

Khaslana’s eyes shift to him.

“...How did it feel?” He asks. “Not painting, I mean.”

“Dying.” Mydei doesn’t even have to think about it, “It felt like dying a hundred times over.” To pick a brush felt like digging a nail into his hand, but to not pick it back felt as if the skin over his fingers was rotting and falling. The urge to paint clawed at him, and if there’s one thing he hated more than painting, was not doing it. But his mother was dead, his father mad with grief, and there wasn’t anything worth portraying, not until, ”My friends gifted me a box of watercolors some time after7 and they all but forced me to do it again.”

Looking back, with all the trouble he gave them, it probably felt like reanimating a corpse.

“So, you paint for others?”

Mydei shakes his head. “No, not since I moved out of Kremnos.”

“Then, why?” He asks again.

And it is easy, maybe even embarrassingly so, to answer, this time, a truth carved in his heart brought to light by a flame lit up with enough care. Why do people create, in the first place? To be heard? To be seen? To connect? Does it matter? Maybe humanity lives to create, or it creates to live, create memories, create bonds, create sadness, create happiness and all the ugly things and ugly flaws that make humanity what it is.

Mydei paints to live, and he lives, “For myself.”

Ah, he wonders how he could have forgotten that. How could he have let that urge, that passion, that beat–ing heart, flicker like a flame in the wind. Loneliness, maybe, spreading up on him like a disease, like a weed in a garden, because living for himself and living by himself are two different things. But, nevertheless, ‘if’s’ and ‘almost’s’ are not things he tends to linger on about, yesterday has passed and tomorrow is to come, and, today, Khaslana throws back his head and laughs.

“How very much like you.” He says, between laugh and laugh. His eyes crinkle at the sides as he turns to see him, and Mydei’s fingers twitch. “I should have seen that coming.”

Mydei smiles and stands up, chest light. The little spot of white paint has dried on his floor.

“What do you want for breakfast, anyways?”

Chapter End Notes

FOOTNOTES

1. Just to reemerge five minutes later with a rather sheepish admission that he has no idea how to get Mydei’s shower to work. Back

2. Which Khaslana never actually gives back. Back

3. Along with a shovel, “just in case!” Back

4. Distantly, a part of Mydei can’t help but notice that his lock screen is the picture he took of the two kites, tangled high, high up into the sky. Back

5. Equals, because there is no word for ‘lover’ in the kremonan language. Back

6. He means to say, “What are you still doing here, uh?” Khaslana does not speak cat more than he did last time, which is unfortunate because it means all the ways Kopopo The Third has threatened him fail rather miserably. It has reached the point that he has considered giving up his rivalry with the parrot from the corner shop and have it relay the very important fact that he much prefers the chicken treats rather than the fish ones he has been giving him behind his owner’s back as of late. Back

7. He still keeps the case, a scratched, dirty, and cracked thing. He had thrown it into the trash when he had first received it, just to retrieve it

from under empty cans, rotting food, and crumpled paper late at night. Back
