chapters.title: Chapter 12: Before it gets the chance to bloom
chapters.html:
“What is it?”

The question is hushed, as all words uttered during the Month of Mourning tend to be, whispered and quiet, as to not disturb the heavy grief the gray days with their weeping clouds and howling winds carry along with them. It’s a cold afternoon of a day that does not matter, not really.

Mydei’s eyes shift to Khaslana’s calm expression and instead of answering him verbally, he simply turns his phone around, where the e-mail announcing the theme for the next installment reads a single word.

Nudity.

“...Ah.”

“Mm.”

The word doesn’t land on Khaslana with the aversion Mydei thought he would have. It does not hit him like a bucket of cold water thrown on him, and neither does it land like a stone thrown into a frozen lake, but, instead, it appears like the first fissure cracking through ice.

He doesn’t answer.

Mydei stares at him even as Khaslana’s own dim blue eyes lower. He does not push, not immediately, lets him trail the patterns littering the cheap plastic surface of the table absentmindedly as the rustle of the plastic sheet the restaurant had settled to compensate for the old mall’s lack of wall in a poor attempt to keep the rain and cold away fills in the gap of their conversation.

The place is empty because of that, save for them two, and it gives the space a strange quality. Dreamy, almost, what with the dozen empty tables, the dim yellow lights casting shadows on dozen empty chairs like ghosts sat in place, and the occasional caw of the little crow that had snuck in exclusively to terrorize the kitchen.

Khaslana goes to take a bite of his hamburger. The slice of tomato in it slides out and falls to his plate with a wet ‘splat!’, followed by the meat and lettuce. He’s the type of person who can’t eat these sorts of things without them coming undone. It’s a little endearing.

He sighs, settles down the empty buns and starts reassembling it.

“I didn’t think they would have set a theme like this considering there are children in the competition.” It’s a non-answer to the underlying matter, but all the more telling because of it.

“They have a different theme.”

“Which is?”

“Beach.”

“Mm.”

A pause. A long, long pause. Distantly, the crow’s caw arises from the kitchen along with the sound of banging pots before the howling wind drowns them all out.

Mydei looks at him, brow furrowing, watches him pick a pickle and eat it on its own. Lunatic, his mind chimes in, but he pushes it down. It’s really not the time for petty squabbles.

“We don’t have to do this if you don’t want to.” He says at least.

“It’s fine.”

“Khaslana—”

“It’s fine.”

“Fine.” Mydei scoffs. “I remember you were very adamant that you ‘didn’t do nude’ when you first came to my home.”

One of his hands raises towards his mouth before he seems to think better of it and instead goes to pick at the sesame seeds scattered across the hamburger’s bun.

“That was then.”

“And now is different?”

“Yes.”

Mydei is not convinced, not really. He and Khaslana have very different ideas of what ‘fine’ means, and he has come to learn that, more often than not, whenever Khaslana says that something is fine, it is not.

He plucks one of Khaslana’s potato fries. “Have you ever modeled nude before to begin with?”

A beat.

“Once.” Khaslana replies. “Thus Burns the Dawn.”

“...Ah.”

On his tongue, the potato fry tastes stale. He swallows and it goes down like wet cardboard.

“Don’t look so grim. Nothing bad happened.” His eyes flicker. “He just— watched.”

It’s not a lie, of that, he’s sure. For all his averseness and secrecy, Khaslana is a very bad liar, and after all the time they had spent together, Mydei has come to know all his little tells. But there must be a reason why he was so adamant on the topic in the first place. A reason why he had deemed necessary to set that specific boundary.

He thinks of pinned butterflies and recurring dreams, of dying stars and burning fires, drowning corpses and crumpled statues, of a gleeful ‘will he come?’ and a hateful ‘don’t ever talk to me again’, and he wonders, intrinsically, intimately, how does Khaslana view Lygus’ painting of him1.

He takes a sip of his drink to wash down the acrid taste in his mouth and says, “I mean it, Khaslana, we don’t have to do this.”

“I know. You never say things you don’t mean.” He answers, easily, casually. It’s not surprising, not really, the fact that Khaslana has come to know Mydei as intimately as Mydei has come to know Khaslana, but there’s something to be said, perhaps, about the off-handed way he admits his care, as if it wasn’t particularly worth anything—But it does matter, of course it does, otherwise the butterflies in his gut wouldn’t be flapping so frantically. “And, as I said before, it’s fine.”

Mydei clicks his tongue. “Stop forcing yourself.”

“I’m not.”

“Mm-hm. Try that again.”

A flicker of annoyance flashes across Khaslana’s face. He shifts one of the sesame seeds he had picked out from his palm to the pad of his thumb and flicks it at him with his middle finger. It lands on his shirt.

Mydei raises an eyebrow.

Khaslana sighs. “...Maybe a little.” He concedes, before letting the sesame seeds fall from his palm onto the white porcelain plate with a ‘click-clack-clack-clack’ like falling rain. The crow caws, the pots bang again, and the lights flicker, shifting shadows like shifting patrons. They said ghosts linger as the Month of Mourning cries.

He pushes his plate towards him.

His eyes flicker to the half-eaten hamburger and the portion of cold fries he hadn’t even touched. He takes the very badly re-assembled hamburger and pushes the plate back towards him. Khaslana blinks, makes a face, but, obediently, picks one of the fries and starts eating it.

“Still.” He starts, pauses. “I think… I would like to try.”

“Why?”

Khaslana’s mouth opens, closes, and he swallows. His gaze drifts to the side before he forces himself to look Mydei in the eye.

“Because it’s you.”

Oh.

━━━━━━━━━━

“How is it?”

Khaslana blinks slowly at him, rubbing absentmindedly the red silk sheet in Mydei’s arms with his index finger and thumb2. “I am not going to keel over and die if I touch cotton, you know.” He deadpans. “My skin just gets itchy.”

“Would you have preferred to deal with an allergic reaction for hours on end, then?”

“No. That sounds awful.”

Mydei doesn’t give a verbal response to that. He jostles the silk sheet in his arms pointedly and gives a rather judgmental look at Khaslana, who makes a rather stellar job of ignoring it even as he goes to gather the sheet in his own arms.

“What I am saying is that you worry too much, that’s all.”

“Worry.” Mydei repeats slowly, almost tasting the word on his tongue. It’s not the one he would use in this situation. He doesn’t actually think Khaslana is going to burst into flames as soon as he touches cotton, despite what the man would lead you to believe. “Is it so unbelievable to think I don’t want you to be uncomfortable while we go about this?”

“...Not particularly, no.”

Mydei’s eyebrows furrow, confused, almost.

Khaslana’s mouth presses.

…Hm.

“Are you nervous?”

“No.” Khaslana says and slams closed the bathroom door on his face. The few pictures hung on his walls rattle and shake and, distantly, he manages to hear a couple of dull ‘thuds’ coming from his room.

He stares at the door, unimpressed.

“Khaslana—”

The ‘click’ of the door’s lock echoes point-ed-ly.

Mydei scoffs, still unimpressed.

Annoying, as it may be, he can’t really find it in himself to be properly mad at Khaslana for his snippy attitude. It’s a sensitive topic, that much is clear, to the point it almost even seems to have a ‘Do not touch!’ sign underlined in red. A part of him can’t help but wonder if this, all this, is a particularly wise choice, but, still, he’s not one to tell Khaslana what he should or should not be doing. The man can make his own decisions—and if he’s going through the effort of doing something that is clearly difficult for him, what can Mydei do other than commend his resilience? Self-destructive as it may be.

Besides, it would be a lie to say Mydei isn’t the least bit interested in this, him. He is not an entirely selfless being, neither is he entirely selfish, of course, but something in between.

The door is still closed.

He thinks, for a second, for a moment, on saying something reassuring, but figures it will only serve to rile Khaslana up even more, so he settles on a dry, “If you blow up the door’s hinges, I am making you fix it.”

“Don’t you want me to get the wobbly step while I am at it?”

Mydei opens his mouth, closes it and scowls. He doesn’t have a good answer to that. “Whatever.” He will fix that. “I will be waiting for you downstairs. Do you want anything to drink?”

“Coffee.” Comes the muffled reply. Mydei has barely gotten three steps in before a ‘click!’ echoes again. The door opens abruptly. Khaslana’s head pokes out, and he points a finger threateningly at him. “The good one, Mydei. The brand I brought. Not that Dirt Water thing you insist on giving me.”

“Ha! Maybe if you behaved, I would be more inclined to be nicer.”

“I’m a very well-behaved person.” He says, like a liar. “You just get mad easily.”

Mydei raises an eyebrow. Khaslana closes the door again. Somehow, it feels even more definitive than when he slammed it shut.

He goes to his own room, picks up the few books and few pictures that had fallen, before walking down to the kitchen. His hands are as firm and steady as ever as he goes through the motions, taking the pot, filling it with water, the ‘ts!’ of the stove, resisting the urge to take the bad coffee because the face Khaslana makes when he tastes it is always funny, yet, despite this, it feels like a hundred thousand ants walk and gnaw at the nerves under his skin.

He’s not jittery, not exactly, much less nervous, but there’s an undeniable surge of energy thrumming along his veins. A hard ba-thump-thump-thump pulsating at the end of his fingers. Anticipation, maybe.

It’s a little bit strange, almost, he remembers some of his classes back in art school, the quiet hum of nervous excitement washing over the room like a wave hitting shore when the model started to undress even as the professor stood on the corner with a metal pipe on hand he was very much not afraid to use at the first sign of any leering glance; and he remembers not particularly getting why. He hadn’t been moved, not really, not by the soft curves nor the hard muscles.

Then again, none of them had been Khaslana.

Five, ten, fifteen and twenty minutes pass. Time going tick-tock-tick as the coffee in his hand grows cold. A pit, then a pat, and the pitter-patter of the rain starts. The Month of Mourning cries and cries for the things that have ended, for the things that are ending, and for the things that will end.

Another five minutes pass by.

Mydei stands up.

A ‘cre–ak’ arises faintly.

He picks up the cold cup and places it in the microwave. One minute. Long enough to warm it, not enough to boil it. It comes to life with a low electric hum as the cup spins and spins.

“And here I thought you had jumped out from the window or something.”

“...Sorry for the wait.” Khaslana murmurs back, so low it’s almost lost under the sound of the rain. Mydei has to strain his ears to hear him. “Should I go to the art studio?”

Mydei stops the timer with one second remaining so that the astringent ‘pip! pip! pip!’ of the microwave’s timer doesn’t grate through his ears like nails on a board. The cup is warm against his palm, and a low puff of white steam curls and disappears in the air.

He turns around.

Damningly, the first thing Mydei notes is the presence of the purple glove around his left hand with a twinge of disappointment, ever present, ever hiding, before he forces it down. It’s fine, he thinks, whatever Khaslana will give, he will take.

And take he does.

He tries not to be too shameless as his eyes roam over Khaslana, less so because he’s ashamed of his actions and more out of consideration for the other man, because even if his face isn’t flushed bright red, the way he avoids looking at him speaks volumes. Still, it’s hard, the dark red silk draped over Khaslana’s bare body compliments him nicely, contrasting temptingly against the paleness of his body. It makes him look elegant, almost regal, tantalizing. The red pools around his feet, bringing attention to the flashes of skin from his long, long legs peeking from under it.

Khaslana clears his throat, pressing his neatly folded change of clothes further into his chest. The movement makes some of the red silk slip off one of his shoulders.

Mydei lets out a low, low breath, deliberately.

“No.” He replies, and his voice comes out rougher than he intended. He takes a sip of the coffee to wash the sudden dryness of his own mouth, wincing at the acrid taste. He still doesn’t understand why people like this stuff.

Khaslana’s eyes shift to him, fleetingly, questioningly.

Mydei doesn’t answer his question verbally, instead, he walks past him as he makes a motion for him to follow.

There is a certain place in Mydei’s home mentioned only once through the course of this mundane story. Not, of course, out of a wish for secrecy, but, rather, out of a wish to be kept. A second heart, or perhaps just the other half of the one he has, situated right in front of his art studio, under the stairs, is kept in Mydei’s library.

In all fairness, to call it a library is a rather generous description. It's certainly not as grand and magnificent as the Library of Garbaniphoro, with its hundred billion books and hundred million shelves rising tall, high and proud, where his parents used to take him and where he had holed up like a mole following his mother’s death, but it is every bit as dear to him. A piece of his prior home he had brought along to the new one.

It’s a rather modest room that gets bigger as the stairs rise. It doesn’t have any windows, and the light that illuminates the terracotta bricks of the room is a dim, cozy, yellow thing. Inside, a soft black divan is pressed flush against the wall in front of the door, along with a small coffee table on top of a plush carpet. There’s also a comfy chair and a writing desk with a lamp, shoved at the right, with an ancient computer that resembles more an old TV that he hasn’t changed because he doesn’t use it all that much, a printer, a clock that doesn’t tick and neither does it tock, and some scattered crayons.

On the left, there’s five bookshelves fitted like pages from a book, along with a sixth one shoved to the very end wall that covers it all. They aren’t filled to the brim, Mydei is rather selective with the books he decides to keep. They vary from thrillers to mysteries, horrors, novels, epics, poems, fantasy, biographies, a few very cheesy romances and, of course, dozens of art books. He keeps only the ones that have managed to make enough of an impression on him, enough of a mark. Something that matters.

Not a lot have stepped foot inside this place. Mydei is as selective to those he lets in as the books he decides to keep with him. Kopopo the Third, of course, although he’s now banned; Krateros, an old friend of his parents that had helped him cover the tuition of art school and had attended his graduation in place of his father; and his friends from Kremnos3.

And now Khaslana, who walks into the room as easily as he had walked into his heart—with ever silent steps.

Mydei places the cup of coffee on the little table with a quiet ‘tap.’

“Pick something.” Mydei says, tranquil, as if he just hadn’t revealed himself bare to him. “I will get things ready.”

“It’s wonderful.” Khaslana breathes out.

Flip-flap, make the butterflies. “I’m glad you like it.”

Khaslana disappears between the shelves, one hand trailing over the book’s spines almost reverently, while Mydei goes to retrieve some stuff from the art studio. He brings two stools, places the wooden palette, a bunch of paints and a bunch of brushes, along with a cup without a handle filled with water on one of them. Then, he brings a blank canvas, a wooden easel and, against his will, Kopopo The Third, who makes a run to the divan even though he’s still strictly banned from this place. Little fuzzy bastard. He better not find dead mice on the shelves again4.

“Have you read them all?” Khaslana calls, distantly, lost somewhere between the ink and the paper. Mydei hums an affirmative. There’s a faint rustle of cloth, and Mydei lifts his gaze to find Khaslana’s head peeking out from behind one of the shelves. He seems inclined to say something, but when he spots the easel and the white canvas placed on it, he asks, “Where should I sit?”

“The divan. I reckon it is comfier than the stool. Have you picked something?” Khaslana shakes his head, already making his way to the divan. “Pick something.” He repeats. “I will wait until you are ready. I can get started in the background in the meantime.”

Khaslana pauses. “The background, uh.”

There’s something strange in his voice when he says this—a little quiet, a little soft. He looks around his library once more, dull eyes roaming around every little corner, every little vein, before his gaze sets on Mydei once again. He must recognize something in this—the importance, the care, the piece of his heart that pulses a steady ba-thump that halts and skips when Khaslana takes a breath and brings a hand to pull the silk purple glove off the other.

He’s slow with it, methodical, almost, hesitant. He pulls at the glove’s fingers one by one in practiced motions, loosening the silk from where it clings and kisses at his skin before he drags it off.

Pitter-patter goes the rain, but it can’t be heard all the way down here, and the silence that falls over the room could almost be described as sepulchral.

Khaslana’s left arm is completely burnt.

All the way from the tip of each and every finger to the beginnings of his biceps, the pale expanse of his skin has been replaced with a bright red, angry red, burning red patch of swirling scars. Blistering and ugly, with decolored nails, and coarse-looking, like very cheap leather.

The clock doesn’t tick, and neither does it tock, but the weight of passing time is felt all the same. Heavy and crushing, tightening like a noose.

Khaslana’s burnt fingers twitch once, twice, before he pulls his arm towards his chest, and the movement pulls at his skin, stretches the red swirls, drags the scars in ways that look too tight, tight, tight, as if the skin was about to snap like a rubber band, rip apart like pulled plastic. His other hand, unmarred, pale, and flawless, goes knuckle-white as it crushes the silken glove in a death grip.

His gaze flickers from his arm to his face. Khaslana’s face is impassive, almost monotone, but not quite, not quite. His jaw is closed tight, tight, tight and his lips are sucked in slightly, as if he were digging teeth into it. Angry, he thinks, maybe. Daring.

Mydei’s eyes don’t soften.

Neither do they fall, nor do they narrow.

“Does it hurt?”

Khaslana blinks, shrugs, and lets go of his lips.

“I’m used to it.”

That’s not a no.

“I see.”

A pause.

Khaslana’s arm falls from his chest to his side. He blinks once, twice, thrice, and the beginnings of an answer form and die. He looks confused all of a sudden.

“...That’s all?”

“That’s all.”

“Oh.”

“Were you expecting something else?”

“You are not asking.”

“Do you want me to?”

“No.” Khaslana shakes his head, placing the glove on top of his pile of clothes he had set aside on the chair. “It’s rather ugly.”

Mydei raises an eyebrow. He’s not sure if Khaslana is referring to the story or the scar. Both, probably both. Still, “And it means you lived.”

Khaslana looks at him from the corner of his eye.

“I won’t be proud of it.”

“And I am not telling you to be.” Especially when he does not know the story behind it. “But you are alive, despite everything.”

“And should I be proud of that?” He replies, flatly, and immediately winces. “Don’t get me wrong, I don’t want to die, but to be proud of something as… simply being—“

“It requires strength." Mydei interrupts. “And of strength, you should be proud.”

Khaslana’s eyes lower and he sighs, walking with ever silent steps towards one of the bookshelves, and Mydei watches his slow march with ever piercing eyes, sitting down on the stool.

“I still don’t like it.”

No, of course not. Mydei is not foolish, nor idealistic, and much less romantic enough to think a few mere words will resolve the issue. But it doesn’t mean he thinks Khaslana hearing these sorts of words is useless.

“Are you ashamed?” He asks, out of mere curiosity.

“Ashamed!” Khaslana laughs, sharp and curt, like a blade cutting air. “Ha! Who do you think I am?” He shakes his head, still amused. “I just don’t like when people stare at me.”

Mydei frowns, somehow, despite the clock that doesn’t tick, and neither does it tock, and the all-encompassing silence that befalls his library, out of sight, out of this world, it feels as if suddenly all noise dies and time itself comes to a halt.

“Khaslana.” Mydei hears himself say, slowly. “Why do you model, then?”

All traces of amusement fall from his face, like a rock thrown into a frozen lake.

Time doesn’t tick. Time doesn’t tock. The rain falls outside, but its cries can’t be heard.

Khaslana doesn’t see him, eyes roaming through the spines of well-loved books.

“...I don’t know.”

Mydei looks at him.

“Liar.”

“I am not lying. I really don’t know. It’s just,” He pauses, pulls a book from one of the shelves and goes to read the back cover. “People asked.”

“And that was enough?”

“You already saw how people get with me—Felt it, even.”

Mydei lets out a low breath. “Was it always like that?”

Khaslana’s eyes shift to him before settling onto the books again. Quietly, he pulls another, reads the back cover, before placing it back. The book he had picked first remains nestled against his chest.

“No.” He replies, and, maybe, the silence, the solitude, the intimacy, of this little pocket of space peeled away his defenses like he had peeled off his clothes, because he continues, almost wistfully, almost painfully, “It started after I tried to get into art school, I think, and it wasn’t that bad at first. A few insults, thrown paint, stuff like that.” A pause. “The first to hit me was an old lady, struck me right in the jaw with her cane. Took a tooth out.” He pulls another book, though it doesn’t look as if he’s really registering any of the words on the back cover. “She was horrified—told me between tears she hadn’t even hit her kids once in her entire life.”

A pause, silence stretching like bubblegum held between teeth.

“Why—”

“People kept asking.” Khaslana interrupts him with a shrug. “It was easier. Though, of course, then Lygus appeared and—” A pause. He doesn’t finish that thought. “And then there was the whole Nanook thing,” He spits, waving the burnt hand5. “And it's just… I couldn’t do it anymore.”

A breath. One, two, three.

“Until me.”

Khaslana places the first book he had taken out back on the bookshelf, keeps the second one, and keeps looking at other titles. “Until you, yes.” He hums, tilts his head. “Perhaps it was all to meet you in the end.”

He thinks it’s supposed to be a joke, but it falls a little bit too honest, a little bit too raw.

“To be seen, you mean.”

“Don’t do that.” Khaslana bites out immediately.

“Do what?”

“That. I hate that.”

“I’m only looking.”

Khaslana opens his mouth, closes it. His expression flickers. It’s not a good thing.

“How arrogant.”

━━━━━━━━━━

“How do you want me?” Khaslana asks after a few more minutes pass.

“In whichever way you want.”

Khaslana blinks, frowns, and then nods. He moves towards the divan with a book in hand, sidestepping Kopopo The Third, who at some point had decided to move onto the carpet and simply cracks one eye open to glare at him for having disturbed his rest before falling back asleep.

He shifts from one position to the other, indecisive, before he settles in simply letting himself sink into the plushness of the seat, pulling his legs up, covering his groin.

“Ready?”

A breath.

And he lets the silk sheet fall completely off his body.

“...Ready.”

Whatever you give, I will take, Mydei had said.

I will give you everything, then, Khaslana had answered.

The grip he has around the brush goes tight, wood digging into the skin of his fingers. Butterflies flying rampant in his stomach. Khaslana is still tense, despite everything, and Mydei spends more time than he ought to mixing colors in the palette.

His mouth is dry even as he asks, “Which book did you pick?”

Khaslana lifts the book towards him. It’s a faded blue thing with pages that have started to yellow that reads in elegant calligraphy ‘An Executioner’s Last Sorrows.’

“Grim.” Mydei says, although, it’s not a bad choice. “Won’t you read it to me?”

The weight of Khaslana’s gaze is heavy as it settles on him, scrutinizing, Mydei can’t help but know it even when he doesn’t look at him, too busy mixing colors still, dragging whites and grays together.

The pages of the book flutter open.

“I am bound to die in twenty days.” He starts, a little hesitantly. The cup of coffee on the table is half-full, still warm, though it doesn’t let out steam anymore. “Drag myself to the execution ground and drive my own blade through my own chest. When I asked why I couldn’t be hanged, the count laughed and told me that there was simply no higher honor than to fall by my own hand. I don’t agree, of course, for there has never been honor in the way I live, much less love—and I heard the hangman say he did not wish to be haunted by such a wicked creature like me.”

Mydei isn’t paying attention to the story, not really. Instead, he lets the soft cadence of Khaslana’s voice wash over him like a wave hitting shore. It’s pleasant to hear, flows and drifts about in the nooks and crannies of his little library, and he wonders if, after this day comes to pass, he will come to find the words he said in between the ink and paper.

Little by little, the tension sweeps out of him like steam, and it’s only when Khaslana seems to have forgotten he’s being painted at all that Mydei presses the brush against the white linen with the softness of a kiss.

There’s no sensuality to it, not even as Mydei traces the long lines that make Khaslana’s long legs, his hips, his waist—and it feels all the more intimate because of it, almost terrifyingly so, the enormity of what he’s been given.

“—But the sky did not resent me, no, it mourned me.”

There’s a certain reverence to Mydei’s movements, his brushes, his strokes of paint, and it would be a lie, a complete, utter lie, to say said his reverence is fitting only for gods, because Khaslana is just a man, far from the divine, far from being perfect, and he’s all the more beautiful for it.

Beautiful, he thinks, repeats, breathes, as he paints the burnt swirls and decolored nails of Khaslana’s ash-filled arm, as he goes over the few birth marks that look like cracks over his chest, his crocked nose, his finger that he can’t fully bend following a basketball game, the tiny gap between his teeth that can barely be seen, the little dots of red acne littering his shoulders like constellations, you are beautiful.

I want you, he thinks, as he goes over the arch of his neck, the sun imprinted there.

I desire you, he thinks, as he goes over his bitten lips.

I love you, he knows, as he paints his face.

He settles down the brush with a quiet ‘clack.’ His heart is beat-beat-beating so fast it feels as though it might come out of his mouth any moment now, fall onto the floor with a wet ‘splat’ and a flurry of butterflies for Khaslana to pick at.

Khaslana turns to him.

“Is it done?”

“Some details of the background are missing.” He replies. “But you don’t need to naked for that.”

“Can I see?”

Mydei nods.

Khaslana doesn’t go immediately, though. He closes the book and settles it down next to the empty cup before going to gather his clothes. Respectfully, Mydei averts his eyes when Khaslana goes to put on his underwear, and, for a few minutes, the only thing that fills the lack of noise is the faint rustle of clothes.

His shoes make a squelching sound against the ground as he wiggles his feet into them, and he doesn’t bother tying them as he starts to make his way towards him. The silken glove rests in the hollow of his elbow, and he’s in the middle of putting his black choker back around his neck when he lays eyes on the painting.

And the choker slips out of his hands.

It falls to the floor with a deaf sound.

Time doesn’t tick. Time doesn’t tock. The rain cries and cries with a pitter-patter sound. It filters through the gaps of the terracotta bricks like static in his ears.

“No.” He lets out, softly.

Mydei frowns. “Khaslana—”

“That’s not me.” He lets out, all so quietly. One of his hands touches his own cheek, as if he didn’t recognize himself, and his eyes look like stars about to die. “It can’t be.”

They said ghosts linger as the Month of Mourning cries. They like to haunt people, and, maybe, that’s why when Monday comes, the one standing in the middle of the Irontomb’s exhibition is not Khaslana.

But Lygus.

Chapter End Notes

FOOTNOTES

1. A mirror. One he can’t seem to shatter. Back

2. It had been a rather spontaneous decision, a rather spontaneous want, perhaps a moment of greed. Mydei had intended to buy something in white, cream-colored, but the wine red had caught his attention, and when he had imagined Khaslana draped in it, his mouth had gone awfully, terribly dry. Back

3. His mother would have been the first to see it, were she to live, along with his father, were he to be sane. It’s a fact he used to mourn as strongly as the Month of Mourning cries every year. He doesn’t dwell much on it these days. He thinks his mother would have loved it, as for his father, well, he supposes it will be a scar that will always be a little tender—Such is life, such is a battlefield. You can’t expect to walk past a battlefield unscathed, neither can you choose the wounds you get, but you can choose whether to let them bleed and die or let them scar and walk. Back

4. Mydei finds dead mice on the shelves again. Kopopo The Third insists he wasn’t the one putting them there, but Mydei does not speak cat—which is better, because if Mydei knew he would call on the lie, and then the cat would find himself double grounded. Back

5. The Ruin Author’s mansion had burned, and with it, it had taken a piece of Khaslana. There’s only one person who knows this, however, and that’s Castorice. She had found him in the smoking area of the hospital he had been shoved into, lighting matches and letting them burn all the way down to his fingertips, and he had admitted then,

voice hoarse, that he wished nothing more than having been burnt fully —It scared her, intrinsically, intimately, and, perhaps foreboding his imminent disappearance, she had given him the silk glove, so that Khaslana would stop cutting off his circulation with the bandages; so that he could remember that, someone somewhere out there, did not want him to die. Back

━━━━━━━━━━

Maybe the real curse that impedes us from being seen as human is the love we lost for ourselves along the way or whatever people like to say

chapters.title: Chapter 13: Waiting for rain
chapters.html:
It’s quiet.

Most days on The Irontomb are—Silent until the distant old toll of the cathedral's bell echoes and resonates through the industrialized walls hidden behind the art. Every hour, from eight to nine, nine to ten, ten to twelve, the bell cries for a minute and a half before it dies. It always skips eleven.

It’s a rather gray day, and the art gallery is empty, and in the exhibition room, only he and the curator stand.

Lygus tilts his head, and he’s perfectly polite as says, “Good morning, Mydeimos.”

Mydei does not have the same reservations.

“What do you want?”

“No need to be so crude now. I just came to appreciate the art.”

In between them, the painting of Khaslana that Mydei had decided to title 'You' rests damningly, like the space where the sand and the ocean met.

“...The art.”

“Is it so unbelievable? Hm, I see his perception of me has greatly influenced yours.” Lygus shakes his head, as if the situation amused him to no end. “If I may give a word of advice, don’t let preconceived notions and biases blind you from the objective truth. After all, I, too, am an artist.”

Mydei’s eyes narrow. “Rest assured, curator, I am well aware of that fact.” How could he not?

Lygus nods, in approval, maybe, and his head shifts towards the painting. “It is a remarkable piece, I must admit.”

“Ha!”

Lygus smiles. “My compliment is sincere. The artistry of your technique is undeniable. The lighting is exceptional. The color composition, stunning— albeit soft, if you were to ask me. As for the subject,” His smile gets wider. “Vulnerability suits a thing like Khaslana so terribly well, wouldn’t you agree?”

Mydei’s face darkens.

The strange sort of helmet on top of the curator's head hides the look in his eyes as he regards You; hides the places where his gaze lingers, where it doesn’t, what it traces, what it doesn't. It’s unnerving, almost, and the uncertainty makes his palms itch and his jaw clench.

He just—watched, Khaslana said.

“I thought,” Mydei says, voice calm despite the fire licking at his ribcage, not falling for the bait. “You didn’t agree with the way I painted him.”

“And I don’t.” Lygus admits upfront. He’s still watching the painting. “But it is a well-known fact that stars shine the brightest before they die.”

Mydei’s eyes narrow. “Where is Khaslana?”

“I’m afraid, Mydeimos, I should be the one asking you that.”

“He hasn’t come?”

“Not that I know of, no—Has he left, already?” The curator asks. When Mydei does not reply, he sighs, patronizingly. “Ah, I can’t say I’m surprised about his behavior. In the distance, the old toll of the cathedral's bell arises with the solemnity of a death knell.

“How much do you want for it?”

Mydei freezes.

Something cold and ugly spreads all the way from his chest to the end of his fingertips, crawls over into his throat and rots itself deep, deep, deep into his flesh like worms would dig into rotten fruit, making him taste bile.

“It’s not on sale.”

“Price is not a problem.”

And it mixes like blood in the water with the cathedral’s old toll. Ding, then a dong. Ding, dong. Corpses without coffins and brushes without paint. All-consuming, all-alluring, all-devouring.

Khalsana’s painting is still on the wall.

“Hah, fell in love with Galatea, didn’t you?”

Mydei frowns.

Galatea?

What nonsense is this man talking about?

“I’m not Pygmalion.” Mydei replies, with a clarity that surprises even him. His nails still dig into his palms and his jaw aches from how hard he clenched it. But his voice is steady as his heart when he says, “And he has never been Galatea. I didn’t—create Khaslana, I didn’t give him life.”

Lygus chuckles, tilts his head, and turns to the painting again.

“Didn’t you?”

“I just reminded him that he already had it.” Mydei replies, certain. It’s almost laughable, how little Lygus seems to understand. “If anything,” He says, and he, too, turns to the painting. His eyes linger on Khaslana’s face, trace his chapped lips, his ash-filled arm, his beautiful imperfections, his all-present humanity. “He was the one who gave my art life.”

“What a romantic thought.” Lygus crosses his arms. In the distance, the bell gives its last toll, but the sound still clings into space with desperate hands. “But it doesn’t change the fact that you are here, and he’s not.”

Mydei’s hands close into fists.

The Month of Mourning ends with a long, exhausted sigh, as frigid as the last exhalation of a dying man, and the coin Zagreus throws lands on tails. It’s bad luck. A chaotic start to a chaotic month. Up becomes down. Left becomes right. Entire plantations are set ablaze, but weeds grow either way. Salt in place of sugar, pineapples instead of carrots. The winds laugh as they steal hats and lift skirts.

And, yet, life goes on, as it always does. Morning comes, and the sun arrives, as it always does. Time passes by, and the night comes, as it always does.

Mydei wakes up exactly at six, as he always does, stretches, goes to the bathroom and down to the kitchen. He serves Kopopo the Third his food and some water, tells him not to sink a paw into it, and sighs when his cat sinks both paws as he cooks breakfast. He changes, goes out running, and into the gym. He works out for an hour or two, runs back home, takes a bath; and so on, and so on. This or that, here and there. He goes through the same motions of a routine, of a life, with a sort of mundanity that feels— hollow.

Incomplete.

Lonely.

It’s strange, almost, the way in which Khaslana had interlinked so intimately with his life without Mydei noticing. A little puzzle piece that fitted into an empty space Mydei hadn’t realized there was, not only in his art, but in his life, in his heart.

And his presence lingers, is the thing, like the vestiges of a ghost, traces scattered like broken glass in his house. The brand of coffee he likes to drink rests next to a jar with chocolate chips on his kitchen cabinet. His art studio is filled with paintings of him, and little drops of paint lay like little planets around his couch. There are dried forget-me-nots resting on a glass box on his night desk, along with a very bad sketch of him made in pink. A well-loved black hoodie with the logo of a rock band is missing from his closet. Kopopo The Third does not eat the treats Mydei offers him and instead prefers to chew on the black choker Khaslana had left that night.

But he can not find him.

He searches for him, high and low, through the crannies of a routine, through the nooks of this city, through the places they had gone, through the people they know. But Castorice says she does not know where he is, and he has no idea where the green-haired man that had come to pick him up that far, far distant night could be. He does not answer his texts, and Mydei doesn’t even try calling him, because Khaslana has never liked phone calls, so he never picks up the phone as it is—Hell, Mydei doesn’t even know where the other man lives4.

And, so, life goes on, as it always does. The world does not stop spinning. It doesn’t even tilt on its axis.

It just continues.

Mydei’s paintings gain a bit of a melancholic edge during this time. Watercolor blues and acrylic grays. Vacant places, empty kitchens, lonely cats, and flying birds. He has a little blog he always uploads his paintings to, just so that his friends can see what he paints even when they are so far away5, and Hephaestion calls him one day to tentatively ask if he’s okay.

I am, it’s what he answers, it’s not even a lie, it’s just that someone is missing.

It feels all the more prominent when he goes back to The Irontomb a couple of weeks afterwards to retrieve his painting on his own.

The man in the reception does not comment on Khaslana’s absence as Mydei signs a little list to confirm he got the canvas back, instead, he simply taps, taps, taps a chewed pencil against a crossword missing only two words, and says,

“He comes every night, you know.”

The pen in Mydei’s hand slips right out of his fingers. It lands on the porcelain floor with a loud ‘clack!’ like the first drop of rain against a window.

There’s only one person he could be referring to, but Mydei still asks, mouth dry, “Who?”

“Your muse. He comes every night.” The man at the reception says without looking up from the crossword. “Spends his time walking back and forth all the way from there,” He makes a general motion to the exhibition room, “To there.” He motions at the west wing, where Thus Burns The Dawn rests. “Like some sort of ghost. It creeps me out, actually. Can you get him to stop?”

In the crossword, he writes haunting. It fits perfectly.

Mydei’s heart pounds in his ears. Ba-thump, it cries out, ba-thump-thump-thump. His fingers tighten around the painting in his arms.

“He probably won’t come today.”

What reason would he have?

The man’s eyes shift from the crossword to his face. His eyes, monotone things, linger a beat too long on his face, before turning to the painting in his arms and then to the west wing.

He sighs and takes out a small agenda with the image of The Little Prince from behind the reception and places it on the desk.

In the crossword, he writes kindness. It fits perfectly, and he reclines in his chair with a self-satisfied smile6.

“Don’t mention it.”

He comes every night.

Four words. Simple on their own, and, yet, they seem to carry the entire world. It strikes him like lightning, harsh and violent, and leaves his body thrumming and crackling with energy, and it repeats, over and over and over again, echoing in his mind like a broken record.

He muses, with the same piercing calculation a war general would consider a strategy in battle, what to do with this information, what to do if he comes back, tonight, what to do if he doesn’t. But all thoughts and plans vanish from his mind when a little knock, knock comes from his door.

He opens it.

“Did you guys break up?”

And immediately slams it closed.

Absolutely not.

Knock, knock, knock, comes from the door. “Mister Painter.” Says the little girl with chalks, who keeps knock-knock-knocking in-sis-tent-ly. It sounds like a war drum. “Mister Painter, Mister Painter, Mister Painter. Open the door, Mister Painter. I know you are there, Mister Painter.”

Mydei glares at the door resolutely. One minute, then two, and then three.

The little girl does not relent one bit.

“I’m not going to leave until you answer me, Mister Painter! I will sleep right here if I have to!”

“I will tell your mom you are behaving badly if you keep this up.”

“She wants to know too!”

Knock, knock, knock, comes from the door.

Each and every single one of Mydei’s survival instincts scream at him not to open the door, but, after five minutes, he relents—mostly because he feels bad about ignoring the little girl.

He opens the door again.

“We didn—”

“You guys broke up and didn’t even kiss?” Demands the kid who doesn’t eat their veggies.

Mydei closes the door again.

Slam! Slam! Slam!

He yanks the door open.

“Stop kicking—!”

“If you guys broke up, does it mean you are not going to need the shovel?” Asks the boy with the green spinning top. “Because the kind old lady says one of her friends is going to marry soon, and she told me to tell you that if you are not going to use it, then you might as well give it back so that she can give it to someone who will.”

“She will come.” Pipes the little girl with chalks.

“Don’t worry about it.” Adds the boy with the green spinning top. “Anyways, the shovel?”

Kids sure are terrifying.

“Why don’t you paint him something?”

The entire world seems to go silent, just for a second, just for a moment, Oronyx’s breath stuttering in her chest for a second too long before she exhales, long and exhausted, perhaps even surprised, as the words leave the little girl’s mouth, like a match in a dark room, like the first drop of rain after a drought.

“...What?” Mydei asks.

“Why don’t you paint him something?” Repeats the little girl, extending all her little chalks towards him. “You are a painter. That’s what you do, right? You paint.”

Mydei looks at her—Her, with her color-stained fingers and her scraped knees, with her smile with a missing tooth and wonder-filled eyes. She had drawn Khaslana, once, he remembers, and it’s surprising, how much she seems to understand at the same time she understands so little. Simple solutions to hard situations.

You don’t know what to say? Paint it.

You care? Show him.

He thinks of Khaslana, with his melancholic eyes and fragile heart, with his ash-filled arm and weight in his steps, he thinks of sleepless nights wandering on his own through the remnants of a coffin, past the isolation of a dead star, past the vulnerability of a beating heart.

The next entry for the competition none of them cared about fast approaches. The next to last one, and he thinks, briefly, of the face he would make if come to face an empty spot, empty eyes on sinking boats.

He thinks that, maybe, Khaslana does not know how to swim.

Mydei picks up the blue chalk from the little girl’s hands.

And he paints.

It’s in such manner that a rather strange painting comes to rest on the walls of The Irontomb. It doesn’t fit the theme set for this entry, and neither does it feature the muse. Instead, the picture on the canvas is of a rather unassuming home made out of warm terracotta reds, situated on middle of the seventh street of the tenth avenue of a place you don’t need to know the name of, in between the house of a man who only ever does cups without handles and teapots without spouts and the residence of kind old woman who bakes really nice cookies and most definitely killed her last three husbands.

It may be late night, or early morning, in the painting, but the light in the kitchen is turned on, a stark contrast to the blue rain made out of chalk falling around. The shadow of a man and of a cat can be seen standing against the glass, looking out, waiting for someone. Under the second stone step, one that remains perpetually wobbly, something glints like a star in the dark.

It is named, I Left a Key For You.

Chapter End Notes

FOOTNOTES

1. She will die in two days—from heartbreak, her mother will say, and her quaint little tea shop that doesn’t sell very good tea will come to be in her little brother’s hands. He doesn’t make very good tea either. Back

2. Theodoros doesn’t take it off either. The little kid always giggles at its sight every time they see it. Back

3. “I know there isn’t any worth in incomplete things,” He had said. He couldn’t have been older than seventeen. His hands had been filled with cuts, and his left eye was covered by one of those antiseptic patches. “But, it seemed important—and you broke it because of me…” Back

4. It’s just one of those things that never came up. Khaslana had always much preferred coming to Mydei’s house. To him, the cheap, little apartment on the fifth floor at the skirts of the city never felt like an actual home, and it’s not like it ever was particularly fitting to receive guests, either way. It was always a little bit too messy, a little bit too cold. It’s a safe place, all things considered, but Khaslana has never quite slept well there. Back

5. With the exception of the painting of Khaslana’s sleeping form—It felt a little bit too personal. A sight a little bit too his. Back

6. He frames it and places it right in the middle of his living room, so that everybody can see his achievement. Instead of returning to the cheap gossip magazines, filled with ambition, Mister Reception Man proceeds to try his hand at Sudoku. Back

7. Because they run a candy racketeering ring around the block and do not share their lot with other kids, considering ‘their’ street happens to be situated right next to the bus stop, Khaslana has found himself the unfortunate long-suffering victim to their schemes—not that he minds. He’s just worried about their dental health. Back

Chapter Notes

Content warning: Sex. It's nothing really freaky, I think, but if you want to know what to expect, click

here!

That night, it rains.

A faint thing, quiet, almost tender, so very unlike the mournful cries the sky let out some time ago. The little drops of water fall gently from the gray clouds like cosmic dust, shining like stars for less than a life, under the yellowing lights of the street lamps, before coming to rest on top of the petals of the flowers blooming along the way.

It’s silent, outside, save from the ‘splish-splash’ Mydei’s steps let out as he strides through puddles with remnants of chalk and the snickering winds crumpling the black plastic bag in his hand filled with small packs of cat food, a pack of rice, some snacks and a milk cartoon. It’s near the end of the month, by now, and he has to go get groceries soon enough, but for tonight, he had decided on merely grabbing a black umbrella and throwing some old pair of dirty shoes and making a last-minute trip to the store at the corner of the street before it closed. The shopkeeper had been less than pleased.

Splish-splash, echoes through the night, splish-splash, splish-splash.

Something glints from the corner of his eye. The key under the steps. He lifts his head from where he is tracing patterns through the floor just to find it is not where he left it, but where it belongs.

Right on Khaslana’s hand.

The world does not stop. Oronyx does not find the moment important enough to let out a sigh, and so cosmic dust falls, the winds laugh, and shadows dance inside the houses around them. But Mydei does, of course, how could he not? His lips part, his breath catches, and the beat-beat-beating of his picturesque heart halts.

He looks—a bit like a ghost, truth be told. He, with his solitary self and melancholic face, standing at the edge of the wobbly stone step, staring at the door. The flickering yellow lights of the street lamps dim and cast shadows all around him. The silhouettes of the tree branches extend like hands about to pull him deeper into the night, into the place between the sea foam and the sand, the thread of nonexistence, the edge of the world.

And yet the tender look in Khaslana’s eyes when he sees Mydei is so terribly, painstakingly human, all those thoughts turn into dust.

He’s here.

He, with his purple glove and picked lips, with his flaws and virtues and untied shoes—the pair Mydei gave him, that day on the ravine. He doesn’t have an umbrella, but the rain, light as it is, hasn’t soaked him yet, but it has fluffed more of his hair.

The umbrella in his hand lowers.

“Hey,” Mydei calls.

“…Hi,” Khaslana replies.

As if seeing each other for the first time.

A laugh spills out of Mydei’s chest, unbidden. It echoes and strays through the melancholy of the night like the chiming of a bell. He can’t help it, not really. He doesn’t want to help it, either.

He walks towards him with a splish-splash, splish-splash. The little specks of rain are cold against his skin.

“Why haven’t you entered?”

Khaslana gives a half-hearted shrug. “You weren’t there,” he answers, quietly. “Seemed a bit rude.”

“Well,” Mydei closes the umbrella. “I’m here now.”

The key in his hand shines like a star under the lights. He has a pack of cigarettes in the other. It isn’t opened, but his thumb digs and digs into the plastic around the cheap little white box as if he wanted to.

“Come on. It’s freezing out here.”

Khaslana hesitates, gaze scattering to the dark before going back to Mydei. Searching. He does not know what he finds, the sort of expression he has, but it is enough for Khaslana to let out a breath, turn around, and put the key in the lock.

One click, and the door unlocks. Another, and it opens.

He takes one step to the side, perching precariously on the very edge of the stone step, intent on letting him pass. Mydei places a hand on the small of Khaslana’s back and leads him into their home, just to make sure he remains at his side when the door closes again.

Inside, he kicks off his drenched shoes and places them next to the door. Khaslana does the same, revealing a pair of horribly mismatched socks underneath. It makes his steps silent as he follows him into the kitchen, so, so terribly, awfully silent that Mydei could almost let himself believe he was never here—and he thinks, briefly, perhaps pretentiously, that if this is how Orpheus felt when he led Eurydice out of death, then it is no wonder he looked back.

It is a rather foolish wonder, admittedly. Mydei is not Orpheus as much as he isn’t Pygmalion, and he has no intentions of letting Khaslana vanish.

“I still have the coffee you like if you want some. Though,” he makes a general motion towards the pot on the stove, still oozing steam. “I made hot chocolate.”

“I’m fine. Thank you.”

Mydei still takes two cups out. One red, one blue. None of them has handles.

Khaslana sighs.

“...Hot chocolate.”

“Sit down, then.”

Once again, Khaslana hesitates.

Mydei lets out a faint scoff and pats the empty space on the kitchen counter beside him, between the sink and the stove, before he grabs a wooden ladle. In practiced motions, he fills both cups while Khaslana pushes himself up to sit on the counter with a ‘bam!’ as the heels of his feet collide against the wooden cabinets. He gives him the red cup and keeps the blue one.

The rain outside starts to pick up as tiny little fragments of stars fall to the ground. In the lull of silence that befalls them, it’s not the pitter-patter sound that accompanies it, but something that resembles static more.

He does not know what to do.

It’s a rather strange sensation, come to think of it. Mydei had spent some time wondering how things would go once Khaslana came back, what things he would do, what he would say. Not anxiously, not really, but with the sort of precision a war general would plan their movements. And, yet, right now, with the warmth of the cup sweeping into his hands, watching Khaslana kick his legs almost absentmindedly in the air, all plans have promptly evaporated from his mind and the fragments of what he can remember don’t seem right.

That’s alright, maybe.

A part of Mydei is happy just to let the moment be.

“I saw the painting,” Khaslana says, eventually, rolling the cup in his palms. Both the key and the pack of cigarettes rest beside him. “It was nice.”

Mydei raises an eyebrow. “Only nice?”

A sound close to a scoff comes out of his mouth.

“Are you fishing for compliments? You know it wasn’t just nice.”

“No,” Mydei replies, not arrogantly, but plainly. He knows of his skill, knows of the sentiments he poured on each stroke of paint. “But I want to know what you think of it.”

“Why?”

“I made it for you.”

Khaslana lets out a breath and takes a sip of his drink. It’s still steaming, white clouds curling in loops in the air, and there’s no chance he hadn’t burned both his tongue and throat horribly. Khaslana doesn’t flinch as he swallows, though, but he does lick his lips. Mydei wonders if the liquid stung against the new wounds he picked out.

“I know,” he answers, and it is not a lie. “I liked it.”

“Yeah?”

“...Don’t sound so smug about it.”

Mydei chuckles. “I did not mean to.” If anything, he would think it came out more as giddy, embarrassingly enough. “I’m just glad.”

Khaslana lets out a faint ‘hmph’ and then, almost off-handedly, as if it didn’t matter, “I do believe it’s a little—embellished, maybe. I don’t think Kopopo would bother with someone like me.”

“Do you still think he doesn’t like you?”

“I think he tolerates me.”

“He lets you pet him.”

“He’s a very strange cat. That’s all.” He takes another sip, still piping hot. “As strange as his owner, maybe.”

Mydei lets out a hum. “Perhaps that’s why he missed you, too.”

Khaslana’s eyes lower. His thumb goes over the rim of the red cup in his hand almost absentmindedly while he watches his own reflection in the water.

“I wasn’t gone for that long.”

“It felt that way.”

“I’m sorry.” It’s nearly a whisper. “It’s just…” He pauses, starts again. “I didn’t mean—” And yet again. “I shouldn’t have—” And one last time, before he repeats. “...Sorry.” He slides the key towards him. “Here’s your key.”

Mydei looks at it for a beat far, far too long.

He slides it back towards him.

“Why are you giving it to me? It’s yours. It’s always been yours.”

Khaslana’s voice is nearly flat, but not quite, when he replies, “But I left.”

“And you came back.”

“But I left.” He repeats, and his voice is nearly angry, but not quite. “How can you trust me with something so important? I left once, I could leave again.”

Something squeezes harshly against his ribcage, and Mydei has to let out a breath to avoid whatever that painful, tender something is to burst out of him like jagged crystals.

To vanish and to leave are two very different things. He has no intention of letting Khaslana do the first, not now, not ever—but if he ever truly ever wished to leave, if he ever truly decided he did not want to be with Mydei, he does not think he could stop him, wouldn’t ever dream of clipping his wings.

Still, still, still, “And I would be happy to know you keep it with you even if you did so.”

Just in case you change your mind.

Just in case you need a safe place.

Carry with you a piece of my heart.

Khaslana stares at him. His eyes, deep blue things, holding both the immensity of the sea and the sky, go through every inch of Mydei’s face, piercing his very soul, searching for a lie, perhaps, or something he can’t hope to understand.

Outside, the rain goes on, static falling like a television with a very bad signal, perhaps the channel it would be on would be a very bad one too.

Khaslana settles his cup to the side.

“I’m not in love with you.”

Mydei’s heart breaks into pieces.

Butterflies fall limply to the bottom of his stomach. Their little blue and white wings flutter once, twice, before the cold exhale of death takes them with it. The sensation extends past his stomach, past his arms, and all the way to the ends of his fingers. Static fills his ears. The world seems to have reduced to merely six words, echoing around like a broken echo, as if the gasp Oronyx let out made the moment repeat forever while Zagreus laughed.

The pieces of his heart beat and dig into his chest like pieces of broken glass, perhaps this is what dying feels like.

It’s a stupid, foolish thought, but love, ah, treacherous thing, has a way to make even the smartest of people turn into the foolest of fools.

Still, still, still, “I never said anything about love.”

“But you did,” Khaslana replies, vehemently. “But you have, ever since…” A pause, and his brow furrows, as if he didn’t quite know. “Ever since…”

Since when, exactly?

When did love become so deeply, intrinsically interconnected between them that now it is unfathomable to think of a time where it wasn’t there? Where is it impossible to pinpoint when it bloomed to life? How did that happen?

Does it even matter?

“It doesn’t matter.” It’s what Khaslana decides, but not for reasons Mydei would agree with.

He takes a sip of his drink. It’s not piping hot, but it is still warm enough to chase away the exhale of death, though the taste of chocolate feels nearly cloying. “I think it does,” he answers.

“It doesn’t.” His hand closes around the key, and there’s one fleeting, terrifying moment where Mydei thinks he’s going to throw it out, but he just clutches it tightly—tight enough that it might actually draw blood. “Because I am not in love with you.”

Mydei does not reply.

“I’m not,” he repeats, sounding more as if he was trying to convince himself, this time. “Stop looking at me like that1. I’m not. I’m really not.”

Mydei still does not reply.

Khaslana’s face twists into something ugly, for a second or two, before he sighs. His gloved hand lets go of the key and drifts towards the pack of cigarettes. He’s saying something or another, but Mydei is not listening to him anymore, catching the slight shift of his body as he starts to the edge of the counter.

He sets down his own cup and, just as Khaslana hops off the counter, he cages him against it.

Khaslana lets out a sound that resembles a squeaky toy being stepped on, and his hands fly towards Mydei’s chest to try to put some distance between them. Mydei doesn’t budge one bit, tightening the hold he has on the counter when Khaslana pushes harder.

“Again,” he demands.

Khaslana blinks once, twice. They are so close that Mydei could count each and every one of his fluttering lashes. “What?”

“Say it again. Just one more time. Say it, and I will believe you—let you go, if that’s what you want.”

Khaslana’s eyes narrow and his head shifts to the side. “I am not—”

“Look at me,” Mydei interrupts. He grabs his face and tilts his head back towards him before he places his hand back on the counter, right next to Khaslana’s hip, while pretending he did not notice the way Khaslana’s breath fully stopped. “When you say it.”

Khaslana’s mouth presses into a thin, thin line and raises his nose, pridefully, almost haughtily, at him.

“I—” He breaks off, gaze drifting before he forces himself to look back at Mydei. He tries again. “I am not—” And breaks again. He licks his lips, swallows, and one more time. “I do not—” He closes his eyes, and his face shifts into something softer, quieter, tender, like surrender. “I can’t.”

He lets himself fall, like a puppet whose strings have finally been cut off.

Mydei catches him, of course he does, brings one hand around his body and places the other in his hair, soft, slightly damp, as Khaslana hides his face in the space between his neck and his shoulder. His exhalations are warm against his skin.

He closes his eyes and buries his nose in the mess of white curls.

He smells like rain.

“You are a very cruel man,” Khaslana whispers. “I never had a chance.”

Mydei sighs.

“You are so dramatic. It’s only love.”

“It’s unfair, that’s what it is.”

He twirls a curl of white hair around his finger and pulls it lightly. “Stop whining,” he demands, but it comes far too fondly. Under his ribcage, he can feel the little butterflies start to flutter around again, cautiously, hopefully, picking back together the scattered pieces of his heart. “It’s not like you ever gave me much of a chance either.”

“Don’t lie to me.”

“You know I am not.”

A pause. One of Khaslana’s hands comes to rest in Mydei’s chest, right over his heart.

“Perhaps that’s the worst part.”

“Is it?”

“Yes, because I'm an awful being, and you are just… so wonderful, Mydei.” He exhales, and when he talks again, it’s as if it pained him. “I don’t think I know how to love. Not anymore. Not with the ease it comes to you.”

“Ease.” The word tastes like chalk on his tongue. Easy would have been to look at the abyss below and let himself drown. Easy would have been to let him go. “I don’t know about that.”

“Really.”

“Love isn’t easy, no. It’s about the willingness to try, I think.”

“To have it?”

Mydei hugs him tighter.

“To keep it.”

Khaslana goes silent, for a minute or two, before he admits, quietly, “I wish you had met me earlier.” And he lets out a sound, amused, almost, but each word he lets out sounds as if he were grieving a dead man. “Ah, how would you have loved me back then.”

And Mydei replies, “But I love you now.”

The world does not stop, not even for the magnitude of his words, his confession, his fluttering heart, but that doesn’t matter, it never did, not like the man that peels away from his hold to look his face with such deep, buried longing in his deep, blue eyes it threatens to fall like shooting stars any minute now.

“And I will have you, awful parts and all,” he continues, “if you just let me.”

Khaslana’s breath stutters in his chest.

The strokes of conflict paint themselves over his expression, and his whole frame starts to tremble as he comes to odds with his own self. The beginnings of misery, of a life, of a curse in and of itself clashing with the terrible, selfish want to be loved.

To be happy.

And it seems Khaslana is all too eager to finally pull himself out of that abyss, because he answers, tentatively, tethering right on the edge. “Only if you let me have you too.”

And Mydei laughs, oh, how he laughs! Long and loud, he laughs, drowning out the static outside.

“Oh, Khaslana.” He smiles. “You have had me for a long time now.”

Khaslana kisses like someone who wants to be consumed and consume in return.

It’s nearly violent. Their teeth clatter harshly against each other. The force with which Khaslana surged forward sends Mydei slamming down onto the floor. It’s an ugly, desperate thing, nearly anguished, and Mydei doesn’t even think for a second of letting him go until all oxygen evaporates from their lungs.

When they part, a thin string of saliva connects them for a second longer before it breaks.

Khaslana pants heavily over him, overwhelmed, as if he has forgotten how to breathe. Chest rising up and down, up and down, harshly. His cheeks have gained a faint pink tint, and his eyes are glassy.

A bit of saliva sticks to his chin, and, instinctively, Mydei cleans it with his thumb.

Khaslana blinks once, twice, and one tear falls out of his eye, followed by another, and another, and another still, and then it is like he can’t stop. Little tears falling onto Mydei’s face like the 'pitty-patter' rain.

And he laughs.

It starts small. A snicker, then a chuckle, and then a laugh. A little shaky around the edges but bright all the same, warm and free, even as he hiccups between breaths. It’s a beautiful sound.

Nothing will ever fit Khaslana quite as well as happiness does.

The urge to kiss him again surges through him like an electric current, but Mydei does not want to cut his happiness short. His hands cup Khaslana’s face, feeling the vibrations of the sound at the edge of his fingertips before he pulls him down to kiss the tip of his nose.

Khaslana laughs harder. His ears redden.

Delighted at the revelation, Mydei peppers his face with kisses. He places one on his forehead, on the space between his eyes, on his eyelids, on his cheeks, on his tears. He makes him laugh so much that the sound etches itself into the quaint red walls of his kitchen and worms itself into the little gaps of his mended heart.

Only once Khaslana has calmed down, he kisses his lips.

It’s a gentle thing, this one, soft and tender. He leads it, this time, passes his tongue over the little nicks and scars adorning the dry tissue and feels Khaslana tremble all over before he parts his mouth for him. He tastes of hot chocolate with a little bit of ash, and Mydei thinks he can taste the remnants of his joy hidden between his teeth.

It’s contagious. Mydei chuckles into the kiss.

They part, for less than an instance, just to get enough air before they kiss again. The rain might have picked up, or it might have lessened. It doesn’t matter, the world outside does not exist, not for tonight, not when Khaslana starts to breathe heat into him with every kiss, like a furnace melting gold.

Hands start to roam. Mydei lets go of his face in favor of his waist, trailing past his ribs, and when he absentmindedly rubs circles in the skin exposed with his thumb, Khaslana shudders.

Sensitive, a part of his mind supplies, and the knowledge makes him heady.

They don’t go for another kiss when they part this time. Khaslana swallows, lips shiny and swollen, and tugs his shirt slightly in a tentative, almost shy, motion. It’s a silent petition, one Mydei understands, and understands with every beat of his heart.

Ah, but alas, he’s a rather cruel man, so he asks, “What is it?” Khaslana blushes, tugs again. Mydei remains unfazed. “I can’t understand you if you don’t use your words.”

“…You know what I want.”

“I do. I just want to hear you say it," he admits. Khaslana scrunches his nose. He can be so stubborn sometimes. “Indulge me this once, won’t you?”

Khaslana’s eyes flicker to the side, still flighty despite everything. Mydei keeps rubbing circles with his thumb on waist as he waits for him to gather himself. He’s in no real hurry.

Frankly, for Khaslana, Mydei would be more than willing to wait for the end of eternity itself.

He opens his mouth.

A harsh, almost petulant ‘meow!’ arises and pops their little bubble with the precision of a sharp needle. They both jolt, and when Mydei shifts his head to the side, he’s met with Kopopo The Third in all his fuzzy glory sitting a couple of meters away from them, giving them his back.

A second passes where nothing really happens. Kopopo The Third shifts his head to the side to watch them from the corner of his eye. Once he notices they are already looking at him, his head snaps forwards and he lets out another mewl2.

Khaslana pushes himself off from where he’s laying on Mydei and sits down, straddling him, and reaches a hand towards his cat with a little ‘psps’ sound.

Kopopo The Third gives him a sideways glance, playing the part of a very haughty cat for approximately twenty seconds before he caves in and turns around. He walks towards Khaslana with languid steps, doing a very bad job of pretending he does not care, before coming to sit right next to him.

Khaslana blinks.

Kopopo The Third mewls at him.

Slowly, Khaslana brings the hand he had extended forwards towards a little fuzzy head, petting it lightly—too lightly for Kopopo The Third’s liking, it seems, who lets out a growl and pushes his head further into his palm.

Khaslana freezes.

And then makes the rather bold decision to pick Kopopo The Third up into his arms. Miraculously, his menace of a cat, who has attempted to kill Khaslana at least four times, does not go for the jugular, but, instead, starts purring.

“Oh,” Khaslana lets out and just… kind of holds Kopopo The Third against his chest, like a child that doesn’t want to part with a very dear plush toy. His cat looks wholly unamused, but keeps purring nevertheless.

It's a terribly, awfully domestic sight. Mydei would not mind seeing it more often, getting used to it, and, for a while, he is content with simply laying on the floor and watching Khaslana squeeze his cat half to death, like a very gentle revenge, before he pushes himself up.

“Bedroom?” he asks. Khaslana blinks, and actually seems to consider the options, looking, for a second, more inclined to keep pampering Kopopo The Third. Mydei is not as ridiculous as to get jealous of a cat. He really isn’t. “Come on,” he continues, eyebrow twitching at the glare his cat sends him. “I want you.”

An array of different emotions crosses Khaslana’s expression, ranging all the way from disbelief to doubt, before settling into embarrassment. He stares at Mydei, seemingly at a loss on what to do next.

Mydei doesn’t give him time to ponder much longer. He stands up, pulling Khaslana up with him. A faint impulse spreads through his body, almost childish, definitely love-sick. It makes the tips of his fingers twitch before he realizes there’s no real need to restrain such things any longer.

Before Khaslana can even take one step forwards, Mydei bends slightly, passes an arm behind his knees and sweeps him into a bridal carry, taking a bit too much enjoyment in the startled sound he lets out as he starts to walk towards his room and Kopopo The Third jumps out of his arms.

He scoffs. “Show-off.”

“You like it,” he answers. Khaslana is not exactly subtle with how he’s squeezing one of his arms appreciably. Immediately, he lets go and tugs harshly at his braid. Mydei rolls his eyes. “Don’t be petty. You can carry me next time if you want.”

Khaslana goes quiet.

Outside, it might still be raining—he thinks it’s still raining, static and stars falling onto the streets outside. It still doesn’t matter, but he can’t help but wonder if it will make the flowers shine tomorrow.

“Next time…” Khaslana repeats, faintly. He twirls a strand of orange hair around his index finger and lets it rest there like a ring. “I would like that.”

The door to his room opens with a creak.

There is a strange sort of quiet intimacy in the action, a strange sort of trust, perhaps, one that’s always present in having someone come into your room and letting them see the basket of dirty laundry in the corner, the seal plush toy won in a fair resting on the bed, the books yet to be read.

Khaslana has never been in his room before, though he has caught glimpses, and his eyes go through every little piece with a sense of curiosity that is all too present; through the scratched yoga mat in the floor his cat much prefers instead of the scratching post next to it, through the little green plant sitting next to a few knick-knacks on the shelves, through the television on the wall he barely uses, through the few canvas and art supplies strewn along the floor. It’s a broad bedroom, truth be told, but is not something that could be described as luxurious, much less sumptuous, but, rather, cozy. A place where he lives, a place where he sleeps, a place that is his.

A place that could be theirs.

Something in his chest sings like a little bird at the thought.

“You kept those?”

His eyes drift down and follow Khaslana’s line of sight, right to his night desk, next to his bed, where a little glass box with pressed forget-me-nots rests, a little thing lost between the gaps of the story, a little footnote at the margins of a life.

Mydei hums and lowers Khaslana down into the bed gently. “I keep everything you give me,” he replies, throwing some of the pillows he’s pretty sure are made out of cotton onto the floor.

Khaslana shakes his head. “No, I’m fine,” he says, breathless again. He’s gripping Mydei’s hand so strongly it feels as if he might break a bone or two. “I’m fine. It’s just—it feels weird.”

“Weird how?”

“I don’t know. Weird.”

Mydei stares at him, doubtful. He thinks—reflects, really, back on all the little instances of tonight that have led him to this point, all the little moments. He thinks of Khaslana’s apparent inexperience, his hesitation, his embarrassment. His sensibility, even. He’s not used to pleasure.

A small, sudden moment of clarity overcomes him.

“Are you—is this your first time?” He asks. Khaslana attempts to kneecap him again, gentler, this time, though it only serves him to take Mydei deeper, and he lets out a strangled sound. “It is, isn’t it?”

Khaslana glares at him, tries to, at least. “So, what if it is?” He asks, defensive, somewhat embarrassed. “It wouldn’t have changed anything.”

“I would have insisted on the lube, for starters.”

He scoffs. “Funny.”

“I’m serious.”

“Wasn’t it obvious?” He sighs. “It’s not like there was anyone who I could trust this with.”

“...Until me.”

Khaslana looks at him. “I love you, Mydei.”

Oh, love.

The words hit him hard. He’s not sure why. Mydei already knows it, intrinsically, intimately, infinitely. But, there’s just something about this time, about it now, about hearing without any sort of fanfare, in the confines of his room, his life, a confession uttered said so plainly, so casually, so mundanely, as if it was second nature, that makes Mydei’s heart burst and spill out from his eyes.

Oh, love! What has it done to him? Why can’t he bring himself to resent it? How could he, when it makes him so happy?

Two hands settle on his cheeks again. One soft, one coarse like sandpaper scraped raw, and he is pulled down so that Khaslana, he who trusts Mydei enough to give him his whole being, can kiss away the wetness gathering at the corners of his eyes, make them his own.

“Khaslana,” his heart calls, and he places a kiss on his forehead. “My muse,” his soul calls, and he places a kiss on his nose. “My love,” Mydei calls, and he places a kiss on his lips. “Oh, how I adore you.”

It’s a gentle rhythm, what they settle into. Slow and tender. Lost, beneath the night. Insignificant, underneath the stars. Hidden, under the falling rain. The world won’t stop for them, it hasn’t before, and it won’t start now. Time will pass, and, in a couple of hours, the sun will arise, and none will know what else happened in that little room.

For there’s no need for any other witness than their own hearts.

Still, before the end comes, you may find yourself pleased to know that a rather mundane painting comes to rest on the walls of The Irontomb for the very last entry of a competition which a purple butterfly and her sister won —for those who wish to know. It is of a rather cozy kitchen of a rather unassuming home made out of warm terracotta reds. On the counter, there sat a rather simple man with a coffee cup without a handle in hand, saying something that, overall, simply does not matter, to another man making breakfast. They both look rather drowsy by the early morning, and even the cat stretching on the table, next to a pair of keys with matching keychains, looks much more inclined to simply turn tail and go back to sleep.

It is named, Love.
